For an ideal gas enthalpy depends only on temperature, so an isenthalpic pressure drop gives no temperature change. A real gas can cool or warm because enthalpy also depends on pressure through non-ideal molecular interactions.
This distinguishes Joule–Thomson throttling from reversible adiabatic expansion, which can cool even an ideal gas.
The sign convention and the inversion curve

μJT = (∂T/∂P)h. In a pressure reduction, P₂ − P₁ is negative. A positive μJT therefore gives a negative temperature change; a negative coefficient gives warming. The coefficient depends on the initial state and changes along the path.
The inversion condition μJT = 0 is a pressure–temperature curve, not one pressure-independent number for every use of a gas.
Calculated example, not a measured gas property:

if a hypothetical gas has an approximately constant μJT of +0.20 K/bar over a 10 bar pressure decrease, ΔT ≈ 0.20 × (−10) = −2 K. Using a quoted coefficient over a much larger pressure drop without checking its state dependence may be misleading.
If condensation occurs, a single-phase linear calculation is insufficient.
Interpret cylinder and cryoprobe observations cautiously

At a regulator, assess the throttling process. In a cylinder containing liquid and vapour, withdrawal also drives evaporation and removes latent heat from the remaining contents and wall. In the remaining gas of a rapidly emptying cylinder, use an unsteady energy balance.
These mechanisms can coexist, but they must not be collapsed into one “adiabatic” formula or one universal Joule–Thomson coefficient.
Frost depends on wall temperature, humidity, heat transfer and flow history; it is not a reliable quantitative contents gauge. Use the appropriate cylinder contents method.

Likewise cryoprobe temperature depends on the working fluid, inlet conditions, heat exchanger, phase behaviour and tissue heat load, not merely the word “expansion.” The source establishes thermodynamic relationships, not a clinical device’s operating specification.

Learning check: does adiabatic always mean isentropic?
No. Reversible adiabatic change is isentropic. Irreversible adiabatic throttling instead conserves enthalpy under the stated steady-flow assumptions and generates entropy.

A separate-winding isolation transformer removes the intentional earth reference from its secondary circuit; an autotransformer with a shared winding does not provide this separation. In an isolated supply, a single contact to earth does not have the same return path as in an earth-referenced supply.
Real equipment still has leakage paths. Contact between both secondary conductors can complete a dangerous circuit regardless of earth isolation.
OpenAnesthesia OR Electrical Safety

A first insulation fault can earth-reference the previously isolated system. A further contact or fault may then complete a current path. A line isolation monitor detects the potential for hazardous current to flow to earth; it is an alarm, not an overcurrent trip or proof that every connected device is safe.

Do not ignore the alarm or disconnect life-support equipment indiscriminately: preserve patient support, identify newly connected suspect equipment and obtain trained technical assistance according to the local electrical-safety procedure.

Mean pressure is often less affected than the extremes, but “less affected” does not mean always reliable. An incorrect zero or level, catheter obstruction or monitor-processing error can also distort the clinical interpretation.
What the fast-flush test actually tells you

A brief flush produces a square-wave perturbation; after release, inspect the return and any decaying oscillations. Ringing suggests inadequate damping; a slow return without discernible oscillations suggests excessive damping. Counting oscillations is a useful screen, not a universal pass/fail rule.
The source describes evaluating both oscillation spacing and the amplitude ratio of successive waves against the system’s response characteristics.
Calculated example:

at a displayed sweep speed of 25 mm/s, successive peaks 5 mm apart represent a period of 0.20 s and an oscillation frequency of 5 Hz. At 1 mm separation the frequency is 25 Hz. These are calculations from a trace, not alternative “safe” thresholds.
Screen rescaling, filtering and an unclear response can invalidate a simple measurement; use the monitor’s supported method.
>Troubleshoot methodically before changing treatment
Troubleshoot methodically before changing treatment
Check the patient:
examine perfusion and the clinical context. Do not delay resuscitation while investigating a clearly deteriorating patient.
Check reference and display:
inspect level, zero, units, scale, cables and connections. Repeat assessment after a position change.
Inspect the circuit:

look for low flush pressure, bubbles, blood, loose/open connections and catheter or tubing kinks. Address these using the trained arterial-line procedure; do not force suspected clot into the patient.
Assess the complete kit:
retain approved short, non-compliant pressure tubing and avoid unnecessary stopcocks or extensions. Arbitrarily adding tubing to “fix” ringing changes both frequency and damping.
repeat the trace and flush response, compare with a suitable cuff measurement and document unresolved disagreement. Consider catheter/site replacement or an approved damping device when appropriate.
The source identifies these circuit and waveform checks; safe manipulation and escalation remain subject to local arterial-line procedures.
Keep artefact separate from physiology

A changed pulse contour may also reflect genuine changes in stroke volume, vascular tone or the arterial recording site. Peripheral amplification and radial–central differences are not necessarily equipment failures. Conversely a plausible mean number does not validate an implausibly wide pulse pressure.
Describe the signal limitation in the handover rather than titrating treatment to an unverified systolic value.

Real respiratory flow may include inertial and turbulent losses, so the result is a mechanism illustration, not a prediction of a patient’s minute ventilation.
>Reynolds number compares inertia with viscous effects<InlineRef topicId=
Reynolds number compares inertia with viscous effects

Re = ρvd/η uses density, mean velocity, characteristic diameter and dynamic viscosity. It is dimensionless. Faster flow and greater density tend to increase inertial effects; greater viscosity tends to suppress disturbances.

Pipe-flow transition values are approximate and depend on the apparatus, entrance conditions and disturbance. A number calculated for a straight laboratory tube does not locate the regime everywhere in a branching, deformable airway.

Turbulent pressure losses are more strongly influenced by density than the laminar Poiseuille model, but “turbulence depends on density, not viscosity” is too absolute: viscosity remains part of Reynolds number and the transition behaviour.
At fixed flow a smaller lumen can markedly increase velocity and pressure loss even though diameter alone appears in the Reynolds expression.

>Heliox: a physiological rationale, not a guaranteed outcome

Replacing nitrogen with lower-density helium can reduce the pressure needed for flow where inertial/turbulent losses are important. That can reduce work of breathing in selected obstructive conditions.

It does not remove obstruction or replace oxygen, ventilation support or definitive airway management. Evidence varies by indication, and a theoretical flow calculation must not be converted into a promised percentage improvement in minute ventilation.<R label=

Do not equate every filled window with stenosis or a particular percentage narrowing. Assess B-mode anatomy, gate position, beam alignment, reproducibility and a validated vascular-laboratory protocol. A spectrum from an oversized gate and one from a carefully positioned small gate are not directly interchangeable.
The cited engineering review explains error mechanisms; it is not a current carotid-grading guideline.
Aliasing is a sampling limit, not spectral broadening

With pulsed-wave sampling, a Doppler frequency beyond half the pulse repetition frequency cannot be represented unambiguously and wraps across the display. Greater sample depth limits how rapidly pulses can be sent because echoes must return before the next pulse.
Increase the scale/PRF where feasible, reduce depth when anatomically possible, use a lower transmitted frequency or use continuous-wave Doppler if depth localisation is no longer required.

A baseline shift reallocates the available display range between positive and negative directions; it does not increase the underlying sampling rate or recover the true velocity from an ambiguous trace. Colour aliasing can help locate a high-shift region, but the colour map, scale and direction must be checked.
Red and blue are configurable display conventions, not intrinsic markers of arteries and veins.
Angle correction: mathematical precision cannot rescue poor alignment
The Doppler equation gives v = cΔf/(2f₀cosθ). The correction cursor must describe actual flow direction, not automatically the vessel wall. Error is magnified as the angle approaches a right angle.
For cardiac spectral measurements, align the beam as parallel to flow as possible; applying a vascular angle-correction convention is not a substitute for correct echocardiographic alignment.

AC / CMV (Pressure-controlled assist-control)
What is the difference between volume-controlled and pressure-controlled ventilation?
Every breath fully supported to the same target pressure.

VCV — set tidal volume guaranteed, airway pressure varies with compliance/resistance. Risk: barotrauma if compliance falls (pressure rises). PCV — set inspiratory pressure, tidal volume varies with compliance/resistance.
Variable tidal volume (depends on compliance & resistance)
Decelerating flow improves gas distribution; risk: hypoventilation if compliance falls (volume drops). Modern hybrid modes (PRVC, VC+) target a set volume at the lowest pressure.
Apnoeic or deeply sedated patient; lung-protective ventilation in ARDS with set plateau pressure.
What is pressure support and when is it used?
Vt is not guaranteed — if compliance falls, Vt falls. Patient–ventilator dyssynchrony (double-triggering, breath-stacking) is common if respiratory drive is high.

Patient-triggered breaths are augmented to a set pressure; the patient sets rate, depth and inspiratory time, cycling to expiration at a flow threshold (typically 25 % of peak). Used for weaning, in spontaneously breathing patients on a SAD, and in NIV. Reduces work of breathing while preserving patient control.
SIMV + PS (Synchronised Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation)
Apnoea backup must always be enabled.
What lung-protective ventilation settings are recommended in ARDS?
Set number of mandatory breaths; any extra patient breaths are pressure-supported.

Tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau pressure ≤30 cmH₂O, driving pressure ≤15 cmH₂O, PEEP titrated to oxygenation (FiO₂/PEEP table), permissive hypercapnia (pH ≥7.20), and prone positioning for P/F <150 (PROSEVA trial — 28-day mortality 16 % vs 33 %).
Smaller pressure-supported spontaneous breaths in between
Apply to all mechanically ventilated patients, not just those with ARDS (lung-protective by default).

pH — Sanz (glass) electrode; potential difference across pH-sensitive glass. PCO₂ — Severinghaus (modified pH electrode separated from blood by CO₂-permeable membrane; CO₂ alters pH of bicarbonate solution inside).

PO₂ — Clark polarographic electrode; O₂ reduced at platinum cathode under 0.6 V polarising voltage, current proportional to PO₂.
> <button onClick={() => setAnimating(!animating)} className=

The analyser measures whatever blood you give it, so the physics is identical. The difference is physiological: venous blood has already given up oxygen to the tissues, so venous PO₂ says nothing reliable about lung gas exchange.

Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ and ionised Ca²⁺ are measured potentiometrically: a membrane that lets through only one ion develops a voltage that follows the Nernst equation, read against a reference electrode with no current flowing.

A heated sensor on the skin warms the capillary bed, increasing local blood flow and making the skin more permeable to gases. Gas diffusing through the skin reaches a miniature electrode underneath: a Clark-type electrode for PtcO₂ and a Severinghaus-type electrode for PtcCO₂. Newer sensors use optical methods instead.

A bubble lets the sample equilibrate with air. PCO₂ falls because room air contains almost no CO₂, and pH rises with it. PO₂ moves towards the air value (about 21 kPa at sea level): it rises in a hypoxaemic sample but falls in a sample from a patient breathing high oxygen.

The blood gas analyser measures directly on undiluted whole blood, so it reports ion activity in plasma water. This avoids the falsely low sodium (pseudohyponatraemia) that diluted laboratory methods can give when protein or lipid levels are very high.

Essential for suspected CO poisoning, methaemoglobinaemia, or after methylene blue.

Venous PO₂ reflects tissue extraction downstream of the lungs, not how well the lungs oxygenate arterial blood. Oxygenation needs an arterial sample or pulse oximetry.

Not necessarily. PtcO₂ depends on skin blood flow; poor perfusion lowers it even when arterial oxygenation is fine.
Delay and "leucocyte larceny"

Cells in the syringe keep metabolising: PO₂ and glucose fall, PCO₂ and lactate rise, pH falls. The effect is much larger with very high white cell or platelet counts, which can make a well-oxygenated patient look hypoxaemic.
Ice and plastic syringes
cooling slows metabolism, but plastic is slightly permeable to oxygen and oxygen is more soluble when cold, so an iced plastic syringe can gain O₂ from the surrounding air.

Analysing promptly at room temperature is usually better than icing a plastic syringe; follow the analyser manufacturer and local laboratory guidance on time limits. This paragraph is standard laboratory teaching, not part of the quotation above.
Falsely low. The bubble pulls PO₂ towards about 21 kPa, so a very high true value is under-read. PCO₂ is falsely low too.

Physiology is the study of how the body keeps its internal environment steady while the outside world changes. The OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology textbook (openly licensed, CC BY) puts it like this:
OpenStax: a set point is the physiological value around which the normal range fluctuates; the body defends a range, not one number.
A negative feedback loop has three working parts, defined in the source:
the eleven systems are a useful filing scheme, but no system works alone, and the boundaries are imprecise — the pancreas belongs to both the digestive and endocrine systems.

In exams and at the bedside, the skill is tracing one variable across systems: arterial oxygen content depends on the lungs, the blood, the heart and the circulation together.

a set point is not a single fixed value. Body temperature, blood pressure, blood glucose and plasma sodium each sit inside a normal range, and the body defends that range rather than one exact number. For temperature the set point is about 37°C; for mean arterial pressure, roughly 90–100 mmHg in a resting adult.

between them sits the control centre, which compares the sensed value with the normal range and decides how strongly to drive the effector.

The baroreflex is the classic anaesthetic example: stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch (sensors) report pressure to the medulla (control centre), which adjusts heart rate and vascular tone (effectors) through the autonomic nervous system — see

almost everything anaesthesia does disturbs homeostasis, and almost every monitor exists to watch it happen. Induction drops blood pressure; positive-pressure ventilation changes venous return; surgery triggers a stress response; blood loss threatens oxygen delivery.
The sensor monitors, the control centre compares, and the effector acts to reverse the deviation.

The value has moved outside its normal range around the set point (about 37°C). Sensors in the skin and hypothalamus detect the deviation, and effectors — shivering, vasoconstriction, increased metabolic rate — act to return it. Anaesthesia blunts these responses, which is why active warming is needed.
An organ system is a group of organs working together; assignment can be imprecise because organs such as the pancreas serve more than one system.

a worked example of integration: a fit adult haemorrhages. Baroreflex (nervous system) raises heart rate and vasoconstricts; adrenaline and cortisol (endocrine) reinforce this; the kidney retains salt and water (renal); breathing quickens as acidosis develops (respiratory); clotting activates (haematology).
Every one of those responses is a negative feedback loop defending oxygen delivery — and each has a page above.
why can no single organ system maintain homeostasis on its own?

>

Because each defended variable crosses system boundaries. Blood pressure, for example, is sensed by the nervous system, adjusted by the heart and vessels, supported by renal salt and water handling, and modulated by hormones.
Organ systems share sensors, effectors and messengers, so homeostasis is a property of the whole body, not of any one system.

Free hydrogen-ion excretion is quantitatively small even in very acidic urine: buffers allow much more acid to be removed without requiring an impossibly low urine pH. A low urine pH therefore does not prove adequate total acid excretion.
Distal secretion, phosphate buffering and the bicarbonate exit route

In α-intercalated cells, carbonic anhydrase generates hydrogen and bicarbonate. Apical H⁺-ATPase and H⁺/K⁺-ATPase secrete hydrogen; basolateral AE1 exchanges bicarbonate for chloride, returning bicarbonate to blood. Hydrogen that protonates phosphate is excreted as titratable acid.

The capacity of this pathway depends on buffer delivery and tubular handling: it cannot increase as flexibly as ammonium excretion during sustained acid loading. β-intercalated cells have a different transporter arrangement and can secrete bicarbonate through apical pendrin when bicarbonate disposal is required.
Ammonium is produced by the kidney, not just filtered

Proximal glutamine metabolism can generate two ammonium ions and two bicarbonate equivalents. Ammonium enters tubular fluid, with NHE3 contributing to proximal secretion. In the thick ascending limb it can substitute for potassium on NKCC2, establishing a medullary reservoir.

Collecting-duct ammonia transport and hydrogen secretion then permit ammonium excretion. Urinary excretion is essential to the net bicarbonate gain; ammonia returned to the circulation and metabolised elsewhere does not have the same acid–base effect.
Kim 2009 Renal Ammonium

“Diffusion trapping” is a useful chemical explanation of NH₃ becoming NH₄⁺ in acidic fluid, but is not the entire transport mechanism. Specific proteins, including Rh glycoproteins, contribute to epithelial ammonia transport. Persistent acidosis increases ammoniagenesis and transport capacity.
Hyperkalaemia suppresses renal ammonia production and transport, while hypokalaemia promotes them; potassium disturbance can therefore sustain an acid–base disorder rather than merely accompany it.
>Interpret renal acidification in the patient
Interpret renal acidification in the patient's whole context
Establish the systemic disorder first: blood pH, bicarbonate, carbon dioxide and the plasma anion gap distinguish the problem from its compensation.
Ask whether the kidney is losing bicarbonate, failing to excrete ammonium or failing to sustain distal hydrogen secretion; these are not interchangeable defects.
Interpret urine pH together with potassium, renal function and the clinical setting. An acidic sample can coexist with low ammonium output, notably in hyperkalaemic acidification disorders.

Remember that reduced functioning nephron mass limits whole-kidney acid disposal even when surviving nephrons adapt. A single urine pH is neither a measure of that adaptation nor a stand-alone renal tubular acidosis diagnosis.

Learning check: does normal arterial saturation exclude hepatic hypoxia?

No. Saturation is only one determinant of oxygen content, and delivery also requires adequate blood flow. Anaemia, reduced cardiac output and impaired hepatic perfusion can compromise oxygen delivery despite normal saturation; downstream cells start with less oxygen reserve.

Describe the three fetal shunts and what they become postnatally.

Aeration and falling pulmonary resistance increase pulmonary blood flow. Pulmonary venous return then becomes the major source of left ventricular preload. This is not merely a change of oxygen source: it is a handover in the circulation supplying the left heart.

Ductus venosus — bypasses liver from umbilical vein to IVC; becomes ligamentum venosum. Foramen ovale — bypasses pulmonary circulation, RA → LA; becomes fossa ovalis (patent in 25 % of adults). Ductus arteriosus — bypasses lungs, pulmonary artery → aorta; becomes ligamentum arteriosum.

What triggers closure of the ductus arteriosus and how is it managed if it fails?

This is mechanistic animal evidence, not a human trial establishing a universal cord-clamping interval or a reason to delay necessary resuscitation. It does not compare every modern cord-management strategy.

At birth: ↑PaO₂, ↓pulmonary vascular resistance, ↓circulating prostaglandins (placenta removed). Functional closure within 24 h, anatomical closure by 3 weeks. Persistent PDA in preterm infants is treated with indomethacin or ibuprofen (COX inhibitors reducing PGE₂).

Flow through a patent communication follows its pressure gradient. As pulmonary and systemic resistances change, shunt direction can change before anatomical closure occurs. Increasing pulmonary venous return changes atrial pressure relationships.

Neonatal cardiac output is 200–250 mL/kg/min (2–3× adult per kg) and is rate-dependent — stroke volume is ~1.5 mL/kg and relatively fixed, so bradycardia is a pre-arrest sign

The immature myocardium has fewer myofibrils (~30% vs 60%), disorganised sarcomeres, immature sarcoplasmic reticulum and depends on extracellular calcium — poor compliance and limited contractile reserve
Transitional circulation: hypoxia, acidosis, hypercarbia and hypothermia raise pulmonary vascular resistance and can reopen the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale, causing right-to-left shunt (PPHN)

Oxygen consumption is 6–9 mL/kg/min (adult ~3) with alveolar ventilation 100–150 mL/kg/min and FRC ~30 mL/kg — a ventilation:FRC ratio of about 5:1 means rapid desaturation and fast inhalational induction

Fetal haemoglobin (60–80% at birth) has a LEFT-shifted curve (P50 ~19 mmHg) because it binds 2,3-DPG poorly — high oxygen affinity but impaired tissue unloading; HbF falls to ~5% by 6 months with a physiological nadir of Hb 9.5–11 g/dL at 8–12 weeks
Neonates have ~3× the adult surface area to mass ratio, thin skin, little subcutaneous fat and cannot shiver — heat loss is dominated by radiation, then convection and evaporation

Non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue (uncoupling protein-1, sympathetically driven, thyroid-dependent) is the main heat source; it raises oxygen consumption up to 2–3× and is impaired by volatile agents, prematurity and beta-blockade

Target core temperature 36.5–37.5 °C with a neutral thermal environment (theatre 26–28 °C, higher for preterm); hypothermia causes acidosis, apnoea, coagulopathy, delayed drug clearance and increased mortality

Why is cardiac output in the neonate described as heart-rate dependent?
Because neonatal systemic vascular resistance is fixed
Because the immature myocardium has limited contractile reserve and poor compliance, giving a relatively fixed stroke volume
Because the neonatal heart lacks sympathetic innervation entirely
Because neonatal blood volume per kilogram is lower than in adults

Fewer and disorganised contractile elements (~30% myofibrils vs 60% in adults), an immature sarcoplasmic reticulum and a stiff ventricle mean stroke volume (~1.5 mL/kg) cannot rise significantly. Output of 200–250 mL/kg/min is therefore maintained by rate, and bradycardia causes a near-proportional fall in output.
A term neonate has an oxygen consumption of about 7 mL/kg/min and an FRC of 30 mL/kg. What is the main clinical consequence?
Slow inhalational induction and slow desaturation
Rapid desaturation during apnoea and rapid inhalational induction
Resistance to hypoxaemia because of fetal haemoglobin
A high risk of oxygen toxicity during preoxygenation

High oxygen consumption with a small FRC reservoir and a ventilation:FRC ratio of about 5:1 means the oxygen store lasts seconds, while alveolar concentration of volatile agent equilibrates quickly — rapid desaturation and rapid induction/emergence.

The review recommends early consideration of continuous haemofiltration.

Standard supportive steps — stop propofol, change to an alternative sedative, support the circulation and treat hyperkalaemia — reflect usual practice rather than trial evidence. Brugada-like ECG changes and progression to bradyarrhythmia are described in case reports.

Concentration, not just volume:

a dilute epidural solution may sit near the threshold for some fibre groups but below it for others, which is why labour regimens can spare motor function. Increasing concentration narrows the differential.
Time course:

during onset and regression, partial block is common — temperature sensation may be lost while sharp pain is incompletely blocked. Test the modality relevant to surgery and repeat after adequate time.
Neuraxial levels:
sympathetic block typically extends above sensory block, and motor block lies below it; haemodynamic effects can therefore exceed what the sensory level suggests.
>Evidence limits: most fibre-sensitivity data are animal electrophysiology with lidocaine; extrapolation to human peripheral and neuraxial blocks with long-acting agents is inferential.

Learning check: is loss of cold sensation proof the block is ready for incision?

No. Cold sensation can be lost before full block of the fibres carrying sharp or surgical pain. Confirm with the relevant modality (e.g. pinprick or touch for caesarean section, per local practice) at the required level, and have a supplementation plan.
Learning check: do C fibres always block first?
No. Single-axon and in vivo studies found small myelinated (Aδ, Aγ) fibres more sensitive to lidocaine than unmyelinated C fibres. “Small fibres first” is a simplification.

Artemisinin derivatives such as artesunate act rapidly against a broad range of parasite stages, including the young circulating ring forms. They clear parasitaemia faster than quinine. Two large randomised trials changed practice.
In SEAQUAMAT (mainly Asian adults), in-hospital mortality was 15% with artesunate versus 22% with quinine.

In AQUAMAT (African children), mortality was 8.5% versus 10.9%, and artesunate also reduced coma, convulsions and hypoglycaemia during treatment.

It also has a narrow therapeutic index with cardiac conduction effects, so check glucose frequently and monitor the ECG if it has to be used.

Procalcitonin (PCT) rises more in bacterial infection than in most other inflammation. Two large ICU trials tested using falling PCT levels to stop antibiotics earlier.
Median duration of treatment was 5 days (3-9) in the procalcitonin-guided group and 7 days (4-11) in the standard-of-care group (between-group absolute difference 1·22, 0·65-1·78, p<0·0001).

Scale, definitions and how resistance spreads

A global analysis estimated that in 2019 bacterial antimicrobial resistance was directly attributable to about 1.27 million deaths and associated with about 4.95 million. Most of the burden came from lower respiratory, bloodstream and intra-abdominal infections — the core of ICU practice.

Use the standard terms precisely.
>MDR means non-susceptible to at least one agent in three or more antimicrobial categories.
means non-susceptible to at least one agent in three or more antimicrobial categories.
>XDR means non-susceptible to at least one agent in all but two or fewer categories.
means non-susceptible to at least one agent in all but two or fewer categories.
>PDR means non-susceptible to all agents in all categories.
means non-susceptible to all agents in all categories.

“MDR” is therefore a laboratory category, not a statement about which drug will work.
Vertical vs horizontal:

chromosomal mutations (for example gyrase changes or porin loss) are selected within a strain. Plasmid- or transposon-borne genes (ESBLs, carbapenemases) can move between species. That is why a carbapenemase can appear in several organisms in one unit.
Mechanisms combine:
porin loss plus an ESBL or AmpC enzyme can produce carbapenem resistance without a carbapenemase. Phenotypic results, not presumed mechanism, guide treatment.

every course selects for resistance in the patient's own flora. Shorter, targeted courses and de-escalation are resistance interventions as well as cost measures.
>Infection control: because resistance genes spread between patients, hand hygiene, screening and isolation per local policy are as important as drug choice.

because resistance genes spread between patients, hand hygiene, screening and isolation per local policy are as important as drug choice.

Aciclovir is a prodrug. Herpes simplex virus-encoded thymidine kinase phosphorylates it far more efficiently than host enzymes do, so the monophosphate forms mainly in infected cells. Cellular kinases then convert it to aciclovir triphosphate, which inhibits the viral DNA polymerase more strongly than host polymerases.

The two steps — activation by a viral enzyme and preference for the viral polymerase — explain its wide therapeutic margin.

The 5th National Audit Project (NAP5) collected every reported case of accidental awareness during general anaesthesia in the UK and Ireland and matched it to a national activity survey.

Volatile maintenance remains the commonest technique in the UK and Ireland. But an inhalational technique is sometimes not possible, and sometimes contraindicated, so the joint Association of Anaesthetists and Society for Intravenous Anaesthesia guideline says

Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) is the end-expired concentration used to compare the potency of inhaled agents. Nickalls and Mapleson turned Mapleson's 1996 meta-analysis of MAC data into age-related iso-MAC charts for isoflurane, sevoflurane and desflurane.
Bouillon and colleagues gave 20 volunteers propofol and remifentanil by target-controlled infusion, alone and together.

Does a BIS monitor prevent it? The trials disagree
B-Aware (2004):
2,463 at-risk adults given relaxant anaesthesia. Awareness occurred in 2 patients in the BIS group and 11 with routine care, an 82% risk reduction.
B-Aware 2004
B-Unaware (2008):

high-risk patients randomised to BIS-guided (target 40–60) or end-tidal gas-guided anaesthesia (0.7–1.3 MAC). There were 2 definite cases in each group, and awareness happened even with both values in range. The authors concluded their findings did not support routine BIS monitoring.
B-Unaware 2008
BAG-RECALL (2011):
6,041 high-risk patients. Definite awareness occurred in 7 of 2,861 in the BIS group and 2 of 2,852 in the end-tidal group, so BIS was not shown to be superior.

The difference is the comparator. B-Aware compared BIS with routine care, while the US trials compared BIS with a structured end-tidal gas protocol. With a volatile agent, a measured end-tidal concentration with alarms performs at least as well as BIS.

Nitrous oxide: ENIGMA-II

ENIGMA-II randomised 7,112 patients aged 45 or over with known or suspected coronary artery disease, having major non-cardiac surgery, to anaesthesia with or without nitrous oxide.
Death and cardiovascular complications at 30 days occurred in 8% of each group (relative risk 0.96). Surgical site infection was also no different (9% each).

Severe nausea and vomiting was higher with nitrous oxide: 15% versus 11%. The authors concluded the findings support its safety in major non-cardiac surgery, that its emetogenic effect can be controlled with antiemetic prophylaxis, and that it reduced volatile use.

Propofol reduced the risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting by 19%, and avoiding nitrous oxide (nitrogen) by 12%.

So an opioid-heavy technique can produce an unresponsive patient with a higher index than you might expect. That last inference is teaching reasoning, linking back to the EEG lesson.
Volatile plus nitrous oxide: MAC fractions add up

The iso-MAC charts let the contribution of nitrous oxide be counted towards total MAC. If nitrous oxide is turned down or off, the volatile must go up to keep the same total, or awareness risk rises, particularly at the extremes of age.
Gabapentinoids plus opioids: respiratory depression
In 8,567 patients having major laparoscopic surgery, Cavalcante and colleagues found
gabapentin was associated with respiratory depression in recovery (odds ratio 1.47)

, confirmed in a propensity-matched subset. Older patients and those given more intraoperative opioid were at higher risk, and respiratory depression lengthened recovery and increased admission to a higher level of care. The authors advise that when gabapentinoids are used,
intraoperative opioids must be reduced
, with increased vigilance, especially in the elderly.
Cavalcante 2017
This was a retrospective single-centre study, so it shows an association, not proof of cause.
The two drugs are synergistic: remifentanil alone barely suppresses the response to laryngoscopy, but modest concentrations dramatically reduce the propofol needed to ablate it (Bouillon 2004).

Alternative 2: the isolated forearm technique

The isolated forearm technique inflates a tourniquet on one arm before neuromuscular block, so that hand can still move, then asks the patient to squeeze on command. It tests consciousness of the outside world, called connected consciousness. In a six-centre study of 260 adults,
4.6% (12 of 260) responded to command after intubation, and 5 of the 12 signalled pain
. Responders were younger, and their depth-monitor values were higher, but the values overlapped widely.
No participant had explicit recall afterwards.
In patients not on TIVA, volatile exposure before intubation reduced the odds of responding.
Sanders 2017 IFT
So connected consciousness without later recall is far commoner than the 1 in 8,200 reported awareness in NAP5.
The two measure different things: response during anaesthesia versus reported memory afterwards. That comparison is teaching reasoning, not stated in either source.

What NICE recommends

NICE recommends EEG-based depth-of-anaesthesia monitors as an option during any general anaesthetic in patients at higher risk of adverse outcomes. That includes patients at higher risk of awareness and those at higher risk of excessively deep anaesthesia. NICE also recommends them as an option in
all patients receiving TIVA
. BIS, E-Entropy and Narcotrend-Compact M are treated as broadly equivalent.
NICE adds that users need training and must understand the monitors' limitations. It lists high opiate or alcohol use, airway problems and previous awareness as higher-risk groups for awareness.

reassess the illness and optimise the child. For elective surgery, discuss deferral with the senior anaesthetist and surgeon. Treat the underlying condition where indicated; cancellation alone is not treatment.
Mild symptoms but multiple risk modifiers:

make a senior, individualised decision. Consider changing timing, location or technique. A well appearance does not cancel the added risk of young age, reactive airways, airway surgery and necessary tracheal instrumentation.

proceeding may be reasonable after shared discussion and a documented risk-reduction plan. Explain the increased possibility of coughing, desaturation, airway intervention and prolonged recovery, not just the inconvenience of cancellation.

When proceeding: reduce provocation without compromising the airway

Optimise established respiratory disease; bronchodilator treatment may be appropriate according to the child’s condition and local plan, but is not a universal substitute for reassessment. Use an experienced clinician and minimise repeated instrumentation.

For children and young people needing IV-fluid resuscitation, NICE recommends glucose-free crystalloid containing sodium 131–154 mmol/L, initially 10 mL/kg over less than ten minutes. Cardiac or kidney disease may require smaller volumes. Term neonates have a separate 10–20 mL/kg recommendation.

Reassess circulation and signs of overload after each bolus; seek expert advice if 40–60 mL/kg or more is needed during initial resuscitation. Do not wait for that cumulative volume before calling for help in a deteriorating child.
NICE NG29 Resuscitation

Haemorrhage needs haemorrhage control and appropriate blood replacement, not repeated crystalloid solely because a generic bolus calculation exists. DKA, neonatal physiology and other specialist conditions require their specific pathways; NG29 explicitly directs DKA care to the diabetes guideline.
Maintenance: daily formula versus the hourly shortcut

NICE uses Holliday–Segar: 100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg, 50 mL/kg/day for the next 10 kg and 20 mL/kg/day above 20 kg. The familiar hourly 4–2–1 rule is an approximation, not an exact division of those daily values by 24. Term neonates use age-dependent volumes; do not apply the older-child shortcut automatically.
Worked example, 25 kg:

1,000 + 500 + 100 = 1,600 mL/day, or approximately 66.7 mL/hour. The 4–2–1 shortcut gives 40 + 20 + 5 = 65 mL/hour. Both describe an initial maintenance estimate, not the amount that must be infused regardless of examination, oral intake, urine output or perioperative water retention.

Initially use isotonic crystalloids with sodium 131–154 mmol/L for routine maintenance in children and young people. Non-osmotic ADH secretion can cause water retention; NICE advises considering 50–80% of routine maintenance in that context, or an insensible-loss-plus-urine approach.
This restriction concerns maintenance, not withholding necessary resuscitation from a shocked child.
NICE NG29 ADH
Glucose, potassium and neonatal exceptions

Glucose provision and electrolyte composition must match age, intake, metabolic risk and measured results. “Isotonic” describes sodium/tonicity, not an assurance of appropriate glucose or potassium content.

NICE recommends isotonic fluid with 5–10% glucose for maintenance in term neonates aged eight days or more; in the first seven days it explicitly requires professional judgement because sodium may be unnecessary or too high and that glucose content may be insufficient.
Preterm neonatal care needs its specialist pathway.

>Deficits and ongoing losses

Assess the type of loss: vomiting or gastric drainage, diarrhoea, urine, drains and bleeding have different compositions. Adjust the prescription in addition to maintenance, using the child’s fluid status, balance and laboratory results.

Avoid adding an assumed fasting deficit or unmeasured “third-space” allowance automatically; account for oral intake and reassess the clinical need. Do not put every loss into the same replacement category.<R label=

>Monitoring and troubleshooting

Record weight, fluid status, the reason for each fluid component, hourly inputs and outputs, running totals, 12-hourly subtotals and 24-hourly balance. Review the prescription and whether oral fluids can resume.

Check electrolytes and glucose when IV fluids start and at least daily thereafter, more often with disturbances; routine baseline tests are not required before most elective surgery unless the condition or operation warrants them.<R label=

= [ [ "What are the haemodynamic consequences of aortic cross-clamping and unclamping?", "Cross-clamping the aorta abruptly increases systemic vascular resistance and afterload (40–60% rise in SVR), which raises myocardial oxygen demand and can precipitate LV failure or ischaemia in patients with coronary disease.

Distal to the clamp, organs (kidneys, gut, spinal cord, lower limbs) become ischaemic, producing lactic acidosis and releasing potassium. Unclamping causes a sudden fall in SVR due to vasodilatation and washout of acidic metabolites, plus a fall in preload as blood pools in the revascularised lower body.
This produces hypotension, hyperkalaemia, myocardial depression, and reperfusion injury.

What is the evidence for general anaesthesia versus cervical plexus block in carotid endarterectomy?

The GALA trial (Lancet 2008, n=3526) found no significant difference in the composite of stroke, myocardial infarction, or death at 30 days between general anaesthesia and local anaesthesia/regional techniques (4.5% GA vs 4.8% LA).

Under GA, no single surrogate monitor (stump pressure, TCD, EEG, NIRS) has been proven to reduce stroke when used alone. The ESVS 2023 guidelines recommend offering both techniques and individualising the choice.
How is cerebral perfusion monitored during carotid endarterectomy under general anaesthesia?

Because the awake neurological exam is unavailable under GA, surrogate monitors are used, often in combination: (1) Carotid stump pressure — measures back-pressure in the distal ICA; <40–50 mmHg suggests inadequate collateral flow.

(2) Transcranial Doppler — continuous MCA velocity monitoring; a >50% drop from baseline or embolic signals (HITS) triggers shunt insertion. (3) Processed EEG — ipsilateral attenuation or slowing indicates cortical ischaemia. (4) Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) — frontal rSO₂; alarm if >20% fall from baseline.

(5) SSEPs — detect subcortical white-matter ischaemia but are slow and affected by anaesthetics. No single monitor has been shown to reduce stroke compared with awake testing; most centres combine two modalities.

It is standard of care in ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, where systolic blood pressure is maintained at 70–80 mmHg (or the lowest pressure compatible with conscious mentation) until the aorta is cross-clamped.

The rationale is that aggressive fluid resuscitation before surgical control raises blood pressure, dislodges clots, and increases uncontrolled bleeding. Once the aorta is clamped, full resuscitation can proceed.

Permissive hypotension should NOT be used in traumatic brain injury or spinal cord injury, where perfusion must be maintained.", ], [ "How is spinal cord protected during thoracoabdominal aortic surgery?", "Spinal cord ischaemia is the most feared complication of thoracoabdominal aortic repair.

Protective strategies include: (1) CSF drainage — maintains a lumbar drain to keep CSF pressure low and improve spinal perfusion pressure; target drainage 10–15 ml/h. (2) MAP maintenance ≥80 mmHg (some centres ≥85–90) throughout the procedure and for 24–48 hours postoperatively.

(3) Motor evoked potential (MEP) or SSEP monitoring to detect ischaemia in real time. (4) Reimplantation of critical intercostal and lumbar arteries (open repair) or staging of the procedure. (5) Avoidance of hypothermia and hypotension.

(6) Some centres use distal aortic perfusion or left-heart bypass to maintain spinal perfusion during the clamp period.", ], [ "What is the difference between open AAA repair and EVAR?", "Open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair involves a laparotomy, aortic cross-clamping, and graft insertion, with a 30-day mortality of 4–6% and significant physiological stress.

Remove a stoma cover and any removable inner tube. Some tubes require the inner cannula to connect to a breathing circuit; know the device, but do not leave an obstructed cannula in place just to preserve the connector. Leave the TEP prosthesis in situ.
Test patency with a suction catheter.

If a catheter passes, perform tracheal suction, consider partial obstruction and reassess breathing. Passage indicates patency but does not prove adequate ventilation or exclude a distal mucus plug. If the patient is not breathing, ventilate via the stoma.
If the catheter will not pass, deflate a cuff if present.

Reassess at the stoma or tube with capnography where available. If the patient is not stable or improving, remove the tube from the laryngectomy stoma if one is present, reapply oxygen to the exposed stoma and reassess. Do not persist in ventilating through a potentially blocked or displaced tube.
Primary rescue ventilation.
Seal a paediatric face mask or a laryngeal mask over the neck stoma and ventilate through it. The laryngeal mask is applied externally to the stoma, not inserted into the mouth.
Assess chest movement and exhaled carbon dioxide; reassess a poor seal, obstruction or ineffective ventilation rather than assuming oxygen flow alone is sufficient.
Secondary rescue airway.

An airway-skilled clinician may intubate the stoma with a small tracheostomy tube or a 6.0 cuffed tracheal tube, as illustrated in the adult NTSP algorithm. This is an algorithm example, not a size guaranteed to fit every stoma. A flexible scope, Aintree catheter, bougie or airway-exchange catheter may assist.
Confirm effective ventilation with waveform capnography and avoid an excessively deep tube in the short stomal-to-carinal distance.
After oxygenation is restored

Continue ABCDE assessment: resolving a blocked cannula does not exclude infection, distal obstruction or another cause of deterioration. Document the anatomy, airway device and intervention; restore the appropriate bedhead sign, suction, humidification and emergency equipment before handover.
The official algorithm is consensus emergency guidance, not a substitute for device-specific training or specialist assessment.
Viva application

“A neck-breather is cyanosed and the catheter will not pass. I call for help and give oxygen to the stoma, adding face oxygen if the anatomy is uncertain. I remove the cover and inner cannula, leave the voice prosthesis alone, deflate any cuff and reassess.

If there is no improvement I remove the obstructing tube, then ventilate over the stoma and escalate to a capnography-confirmed stomal airway. Oral intubation cannot help a confirmed total laryngectomy.”

No increase was identified.
Name one limitation of this evidence.
Observational; no data on direct oral anticoagulants.

Roughly what proportion of children vomit after squint surgery without prophylaxis?
About two-thirds (65–68% in placebo groups).
What did the meta-analysis recommend?
Combined dexamethasone and ondansetron.
In Splinter 2001, what was vomiting with dexamethasone alone vs combined?
UK practice favours sub-Tenon's or topical techniques for this reason — the review does not show retrobulbar block is unsafe, only that it offers no measured advantage.
Which complication was more common after peribulbar block?
Conjunctival chemosis.
Did peribulbar block give less complete akinesia?
No — no evidence of a difference.
Why can this review not settle globe-perforation risk?
1,438 patients is far too few for a rare event.
Surgeon and patient satisfaction:
both were lower with topical anaesthesia (moderate and low quality evidence respectively) — relevant because a moving eye under a microscope is a surgical problem, not just a comfort problem.

there was not enough evidence to say whether one technique causes more intra-operative complications than the other. The safety advantage of avoiding a needle is biologically plausible but has never been demonstrated in a randomised trial at the frequencies involved.

"needle blocks are dangerous, drops are safer" overstates the evidence. The honest position is that both are safe and effective in trained hands, topical is more painful during surgery, and the choice should reflect patient cooperation, surgical requirements and local complication experience.

The reflex is conventionally quoted as occurring in 30–90% of strabismus operations.

Review the blood count and investigate iron deficiency, inflammation, renal disease, bleeding or other causes as indicated. NICE NG24 advises oral iron before and after surgery for iron-deficiency anaemia.

Agree timing with the surgical team, particularly in cancer or emergency surgery. An iron-treatment plan is not a transfusion decision; active bleeding, symptoms, physiology and procedure-specific risks require their own assessment.
Document the expected response and follow-up rather than assuming an infusion completes optimisation.
Nutrition, prehabilitation and medicines

NG180 recommends nutritional screening before intermediate, major or complex surgery and directs at-risk patients to NICE nutrition-support guidance. Establish intake, weight loss and the underlying cause; request dietetic input and an appropriate oral, enteral or parenteral plan when indicated.
Malnutrition is not corrected by carbohydrate loading alone.
NICE CG32 Colorectal Nutrition

Discuss smoking cessation, alcohol reduction and physical preparation suited to the person and time available. Avoid presenting a fixed cessation interval as a condition for every operation. Reconcile anticoagulants, diabetes medicines and steroids, and agree interruption/restart and monitoring plans.
Follow the VTE pathway and the colorectal team’s bowel-preparation and fasting instructions rather than applying an unqualified default to obstruction or delayed gastric emptying.
NICE NG89
>Complete a practical handover plan
Complete a practical handover plan
Define unresolved risks:
illness requiring optimisation, aspiration risk, vascular access, monitoring and blood availability.
Agree intraoperative priorities:
position changes, analgesia by incision and approach, individualised fluid support and haemorrhage contingency.
Agree recovery:
observation level, pain strategy, mobilisation/nutrition goals, medicine restart and escalation if recovery deviates from the expected course.
Record shared decisions:
patient priorities, realistic risks and any agreed limits of treatment; a risk calculator does not make these decisions for the patient.

These steps translate NG180’s shared decision-making and enhanced-recovery principles into a case-specific plan; they are not mandatory numerical cut-offs or a substitute for local colorectal pathways.

reconfirm waveform capnography, ventilation, circuit connections, tube position, blood pressure, line function, eye protection and pressure points. Investigate a new ventilation or haemodynamic change; do not attribute it to “the turn” without checking reversible problems.

Document position changes and review limb pain, swelling or neurological symptoms after surgery.
Why presacral bleeding can become torrential
Presacral and communicating veins can bleed briskly during pelvic dissection and are difficult to control in a confined field.

Conventional haemostasis can extend tears in delicate vessels; the review describes direct pressure with aspiration as the first temporary manoeuvre, followed by several possible surgical techniques rather than one universally superior method.

The anaesthetist should recognise the bleeding promptly, communicate and activate the local major-haemorrhage pathway when appropriate, secure effective access, coordinate blood delivery and warming, and follow coagulation, physiology and electrolyte assessment.
Surgical haemorrhage control and resuscitation proceed together. Do not delay resuscitation while waiting for an exact blood-loss estimate.

Packing, tacking, topical haemostatic agents, muscle-based methods and cautery/suture techniques are options selected by the surgeon according to the bleeding site and stability. They are not a mandatory linear sequence.
The review stresses timely packing when physiological deterioration makes prolonged attempts unsafe. If packs remain, handover the planned return to theatre and postoperative observation needs.

A cuff-leak test should be performed before extubation; if absent, the patient may remain intubated until oedema resolves. Re-intubation after robotic surgery can be difficult because of laryngeal swelling and the supine-to-sitting transition.

Glycine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter at retinal level → blurred vision and transient blindness with normal pupillary reflexes (post-chiasmatic origin). Resolves within 24–48 h. Pathognomonic when present.

Prophylactic measures include limiting head-down time where possible, maintaining normovolaemia, and using slight reverse Trendelenburg before extubation.", ], [ "How does hysteroscopy fluid absorption differ from TURP syndrome?", "The mechanism is identical: hypotonic, electrolyte-free distension fluid (classically 1.5% glycine) is absorbed through open venous sinuses when intrauterine pressure exceeds mean arterial pressure.

↑ IOP up to 30+ mmHg — risk of postoperative ischaemic optic neuropathy

The low CVP technique aims to reduce central venous pressure below 5 cmH₂O during hepatic parenchymal transection. By lowering CVP, the back-pressure in the hepatic veins and sinusoids is reduced, which minimises bleeding from the cut surface of the liver.
Maintain euvolaemia — avoid splanchnic congestion

Methods to achieve low CVP include: fluid restriction (maintenance only crystalloid), head-up (reverse Trendelenburg) positioning, and vasodilators such as glyceryl trinitrate or phlebotomy in extreme cases. The technique requires careful monitoring with an arterial line and central venous catheter.
Over-transfusion in this phase worsens venous bleeding when the IVC is later clamped.

Caution is needed because excessive hypovolaemia risks renal dysfunction and air embolism through open hepatic veins. After resection is complete, fluids are liberalised to restore normovolaemia and support perfusion of the remaining liver.
Phase 2 — Anhepatic
What is the Pringle manoeuvre and what are its limitations?
IVC + portal vein cross-clamp → ↓↓ preload, CO can fall 50%

The Pringle manoeuvre involves clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament, which contains the hepatic artery, portal vein, and common bile duct. This occludes the inflow to the liver and dramatically reduces bleeding during parenchymal transection.
No hepatic metabolism: lactate, citrate, drugs accumulate
The manoeuvre can be applied intermittently (15–20 minutes clamped, 5 minutes released) or continuously for up to 60 minutes in healthy livers.
Progressive metabolic acidosis and hypocalcaemia

Limitations include: (1) ischaemia-reperfusion injury to the liver — the cirrhotic liver tolerates ischaemia poorly; (2) intestinal congestion from portal venous occlusion; (3) haemodynamic effects from reduced venous return (portal vein carries ~75% of hepatic blood flow); and (4) in chronic liver disease, even short periods of ischaemia may cause significant hepatocyte damage.
Hypothermia from cold graft + open abdomen
Some surgeons use selective inflow occlusion (hepatic artery only) to preserve portal venous return.
Decision: full cross-clamp vs piggy-back vs venovenous bypass
What are the three phases of liver transplantation and their key physiological changes?
Vasopressor + judicious volume; avoid fluid overload before reperfusion

Phase 1 — Dissection (pre-anhepatic): mobilisation of the diseased liver with division of hilar structures and hepatic veins. Portal hypertension and coagulopathy cause significant bleeding. Ascites drainage produces haemodynamic shifts.
Active warming (forced air + fluid warmer) — target ≥ 36 °C

Rapid transfusion leads to citrate toxicity (hypocalcaemia), hypothermia, and acidosis. Phase 2 — Anhepatic: the native liver is removed and venous return is interrupted by IVC clamping (or maintained with venovenous bypass). Cardiac output falls 30–50%.
Bicarbonate + calcium chloride boluses; insulin if hyperglycaemia

There is no hepatic metabolism, so lactate, citrate, and drugs accumulate. Hypocalcaemia and acidosis worsen. Hypothermia is common from the cold donor organ and reduced metabolic heat production. Phase 3 — Reperfusion (neo-hepatic): the donor liver is revascularised.
hypotension here is dangerous — you will cause RV overload at unclamping.

Cold, acidotic, hyperkalaemic preservative fluid and blood from the graft enter the systemic circulation, causing post-reperfusion syndrome — a precipitous fall in MAP, arrhythmias, and myocardial depression.
Phase 3 — Reperfusion (Neo-hepatic)
How is post-reperfusion syndrome managed?
Post-reperfusion syndrome: ↓ MAP > 30% lasting > 1 min within 5 min of unclamping

Post-reperfusion syndrome is defined as a >30% fall in MAP for >1 minute within 5 minutes of graft reperfusion. Management is pre-emptive and reactive: (1) Pre-emptive — before unclamping, ensure ionised calcium is normal (citrate chelation), pH >7.25, K⁺ <5.5 mmol/L, and core temperature >35.5 °C.
Hyperkalaemia + acidosis + hypothermia bolus from preservation fluid
Have vasopressors, calcium, and bicarbonate drawn up.
Hyperfibrinolysis from graft tPA release — diffuse oozing

(2) Reactive — if MAP falls precipitously: give 10 mL 10% calcium chloride IV for cardiac membrane stabilisation and inotropy; administer vasopressors (noradrenaline bolus 10–20 µg, then infusion; adrenaline if severe); treat hyperkalaemia with insulin 10 U + 50 mL 50% glucose and 50 mmol sodium bicarbonate; manage arrhythmias according to ACLS; check TEG/ROTEM for fibrinolysis (graft releases tPA) and give tranexamic acid 1 g if indicated.

What is cyanide poisoning and how is it recognised in burn patients?

Cyanide (CN⁻) can be released when nitrogen-containing materials burn, especially in enclosed-space fires. It inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase, causing cellular hypoxia and marked lactic acidosis; lactate >10 mmol/L increases suspicion but is not diagnostic.

Free flap principles

Maintain adequate perfusion pressure across the microvascular anastomosis. Hypotension reduces flow through small-calibre vessels. Use arterial line for continuous monitoring. Fluid boluses first; vasopressors as second line.
Prolonged surgery
Specific procedures

Both hypovolaemia (↓preload → ↓CO → ↓flap perfusion) and hypervolaemia (tissue oedema → ↑interstitial pressure → venous congestion) impair flap survival. Use stroke volume variation or pulse pressure variation to guide fluid therapy. Target crystalloid 1–2 ml/kg/h maintenance.
Flap-specific regional blocks
Anticoagulation & monitoring

Hypothermia causes vasoconstriction (↓flow through anastomosis), platelet dysfunction (↑thrombosis risk), coagulopathy, and shivering (↑O₂ consumption). Forced-air warming, warmed IV fluids, theatre temperature ≥23°C. Monitor core temperature continuously.
DVT prophylaxis & Caprini risk
Postoperative complications

Mild haemodilution reduces blood viscosity (Poiseuille's law: flow ∝ 1/viscosity) improving microcirculatory flow through 1–3 mm diameter anastomosed vessels. Excessive haemodilution (<25%) reduces O₂-carrying capacity. Transfuse to maintain Hb >80 g/L.

Learning check: why is a high STOP-Bang score a prompt rather than a diagnosis?

It was designed for high sensitivity, so few patients with significant sleep apnoea are missed. The price is that many people who score high do not have it. A high score means: assume OSA, plan opioid-sparing anaesthesia and monitored recovery, and consider referral. It does not confirm the diagnosis.

>Drug dosing scalars

Dosing by total body weight risks overdose, while dosing by ideal body weight can under-dose. Ingrande and Lemmens
Drug dosing scalars
Dosing by total body weight risks overdose, while dosing by ideal body weight can under-dose.

Ingrande and Lemmens' review concluded that, "with the exception of neuromuscular antagonists, lean body weight is the optimal dosing scalar for most drugs used in anaesthesia including opioids and anaesthetic induction agents".
They also highlight that obstructive sleep apnoea and fat around the pharynx and chest wall make these patients more sensitive to the respiratory effects of anaesthetic drugs.
with the exception of neuromuscular antagonists, lean body weight is the optimal dosing scalar for most drugs used in anaesthesia including opioids and anaesthetic induction agents

Learning check: which weight would you use for a propofol induction dose in a 160 kg patient?

Lean body weight, titrated to effect. Total body weight would give a large overdose and severe hypotension. A maintenance infusion is a different question: it is often based on an adjusted weight, because clearance is higher. Always state the drug, and whether you mean induction or maintenance, before naming a scalar.

>Ramped positioning with a videolaryngoscope

Ramping (ear level with the sternal notch) is recommended mainly for direct laryngoscopy, and to improve oxygen reserve and the time before desaturation.

A 2025 meta-analysis of four RCTs (341 adults) compared ramped and sniffing positions when using a videolaryngoscope. It found no significant difference in intubation time, first-attempt success (RR 1.03) or glottic view.

Because head-up, ramped positioning improves functional residual capacity and slows desaturation. It also helps mask ventilation and makes rescue with direct laryngoscopy or front-of-neck access easier. What BMI is acceptable for day-case surgery?

There is no absolute BMI cutoff. BADS guidance is to assess functional capacity, comorbidity (especially OSA), and surgical complexity rather than weight alone. Many UK units accept BMI up to 50 for appropriate procedures, provided the patient meets all other day-case criteria and a suitable airway plan is in place.
When is voiding mandatory before day-case discharge?

After spinal/epidural anaesthesia, inguinal/femoral hernia repair, and perianal/urological surgery — because of the risk of urinary retention. For most other day-case procedures, voiding is not required as long as the patient is well, drinking, and has clear instructions on when to seek help if retention develops.
How should a patient with STOP-BANG ≥5 be managed for day surgery?

Stratify as high OSA risk. Use opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, prefer regional techniques, avoid long-acting sedatives, and monitor for ≥3 h post-op with continuous SpO₂. CPAP-dependent patients should bring their device. Many units admit STOP-BANG ≥5 patients overnight after general anaesthesia.

STOP-BANG ≥5 indicates high OSA risk. With good CPAP compliance and a short, predominantly regional/local anaesthetic technique (femoral block ± light sedation), day-case surgery is feasible.

Key precautions: avoid long-acting opioids and benzodiazepines; multimodal analgesia (paracetamol + NSAID + local infiltration); patient brings own CPAP; assess ≥4 h postoperatively; clear instructions for resuming CPAP at home.

Yes, with caveats. Use a regional-led technique to avoid airway manipulation and systemic opioids, ensure CPAP availability at home, and apply extended postoperative monitoring (≥4 h) to detect respiratory depression before discharge. Document an explicit unplanned-admission threshold.

Voiding is a discharge requirement after spinal/epidural anaesthesia, perianal surgery and inguinal hernia repair due to risk of post-op urinary retention. Bladder ultrasound to quantify volume; if >600 mL or unable to void, single in-out catheterisation and arrange community follow-up.

No — voiding is mandatory in this patient group. Confirm with bladder scan, catheterise (in-out) if >600 mL, and arrange follow-up before discharge. Failure to void is one of the commonest reasons for unplanned overnight admission in day-surgery units.

How does AAGBI guidance grade inter-hospital transfers?

How Often Transfers Go Wrong, and What Reduces the Risk

AAGBI 2009 grades the patient, not the transfer: critical-care dependency Levels 0–3. Level 2 and 3 patients (organ support, advanced respiratory support) must be escorted by competent, trained and experienced personnel — usually a doctor and a nurse or paramedic.

Three timed phases of transport ventilation: (1) brief bag-valve hand-ventilation while moving between machines, (2) switch to a turbine-driven transport ventilator that replicates ICU settings (mode, TV, PEEP, FiO₂) — observe ≥15 min before departure with continuous ETCO₂, and (3) O₂ cylinder/FiO₂ planning plus disconnection prevention.

The checklists and staffing rules on this page come from studies of how often, and how, things go wrong during transfers. This lesson sets out the numbers and how strong the evidence behind each preventive measure is.
The decision to transfer is made consultant-to-consultant; a consultant is not required to travel on every transfer. Staffing, monitoring and vehicle choice escalate with dependency.

the joint Association of Anaesthetists/SIVA guideline notes that volatile maintenance remains commonest in the UK and Ireland, but an inhalational technique is sometimes not possible or is contraindicated. It therefore states that all anaesthetists should be able to deliver TIVA competently and safely.

the guideline covers safe practice when TIVA is used, including mixed infusion and volatile techniques. It deliberately does not judge whether TIVA is better than volatile anaesthesia when both are possible.
Emergency gap:
a 2026 narrative review notes TIVA is well established electively but its use remains limited in emergencies, particularly for rapid sequence induction.

No. It sets safe-practice standards and says all anaesthetists should be competent in TIVA, but explicitly does not review TIVA versus volatile where both are possible.
Absolute pressure overcalls:

in the first 12 hours, 53 patients had absolute pressures over 30 mmHg. A 30 mmHg threshold would have meant fasciotomy for 50 patients (43%); a 40 mmHg threshold would have considered 27 (23%) for an unnecessary fasciotomy.
Differential pressure:

only the three patients whose differential pressure (diastolic minus compartment pressure) fell below 30 mmHg had fasciotomy. No case was missed and none of the 116 had sequelae at six months or later.
Anaesthetic relevance:

differential pressure depends on diastolic pressure, so hypotension under anaesthesia lowers it. Read pressures alongside the current blood pressure, and agree monitoring with the surgeons when the patient is obtunded or blocked.
>Limits: a single-centre study of tibial fractures with only three cases; it cannot define the threshold precisely for other limbs or injuries.
a single-centre study of tibial fractures with only three cases; it cannot define the threshold precisely for other limbs or injuries.

NCEPOD immediate intervention is life-, limb- or organ-saving, normally within minutes, with simultaneous resuscitation. Urgent intervention is normally within hours for acute or deteriorating potentially life-threatening conditions.

In septic shock from perforation or ischaemic bowel, antibiotics and circulatory support cannot replace source control. SSC recommends intervention as soon as medically and logistically practical after identifying an amenable source.

Its discussion of benefit within 6–12 hours is based on limited studies, not a licence to wait until that deadline. Establish the least invasive effective intervention with the surgeon and radiologist, and resuscitate in parallel rather than repeatedly postponing treatment for normal laboratory values.

>The pre-induction briefing should expose the competing risks. Discuss aspiration, difficult airway, shock, blood availability, antibiotic administration, anticipated operation and the postoperative destination. Decompression and resuscitation can reduce risk without eliminating it.

No. Ongoing infection may prevent normalisation. Resuscitate and arrange effective source control together, with senior surgical, anaesthetic and critical-care agreement. A suggested observational time window is not a reason to delay an immediately necessary intervention.

Obstructive failure needs a different emphasis

In severe asthma, extra external PEEP may worsen total PEEP and gas trapping. The priority is treating obstruction, limiting minute ventilation and allowing exhalation while monitoring circulation and gas exchange.
The severe-asthma review advises careful monitoring whenever external PEEP is added; there is no universally safe fraction of measured auto-PEEP for every patient.

New shock during ventilation requires immediate senior assessment for hyperinflation, pneumothorax, airway/circuit problems and other causes—not an assumption that more PEEP will help. Severe hyperinflation can impair venous return and cause barotrauma.
Stather 2005 harms

for the full intrinsic-PEEP lesson and emergency context.
does ATS's higher-PEEP recommendation justify routine prolonged recruitment inflations?
s higher-PEEP recommendation justify routine prolonged recruitment inflations?

No. Higher PEEP without recruitment is conditionally suggested for moderate-to-severe ARDS, whereas prolonged recruitment manoeuvres are strongly recommended against. These are different interventions with different evidence.
Stather 2005 measurement
PEEP can stabilise recruitable lung units and limit repeated closure and reopening. It can also overdistend already open units, impair venous return and increase right-ventricular afterload.
The effect depends on lung recruitability, chest-wall mechanics and circulation: the same increase can improve one patient's mechanics and harm another's.
ATS 2024 balance
Measure rather than infer from one pressure

>End-expiratory hold: measure total PEEP only when the patient is relaxed without active expiratory muscle effort. Effort can falsely elevate the result; airway closure can conceal trapped pressure in poorly communicating lung regions.
End-expiratory hold:

measure total PEEP only when the patient is relaxed without active expiratory muscle effort. Effort can falsely elevate the result; airway closure can conceal trapped pressure in poorly communicating lung regions.
>End-inspiratory hold: at zero flow, plateau pressure reflects static respiratory-system pressure, not peak resistive pressure. Inspiratory effort invalidates a passive interpretation.
A rising plateau in obstruction needs assessment for worsening hyperinflation and other causes, including pneumothorax and reduced compliance.<R label=

at zero flow, plateau pressure reflects static respiratory-system pressure, not peak resistive pressure. Inspiratory effort invalidates a passive interpretation. >Flow–time waveform: expiratory flow still continuing when the next breath starts suggests incomplete exhalation. Flow reaching zero does not prove every obstructed region is empty; combine it with holds and clinical assessment.
Flow–time waveform:

expiratory flow still continuing when the next breath starts suggests incomplete exhalation. Flow reaching zero does not prove every obstructed region is empty; combine it with holds and clinical assessment.
Stather 2005 occult
set PEEP is 5 and a valid expiratory hold reads 13 cmH₂O. What is intrinsic PEEP?

13 − 5 = 8 cmH₂O. The patient is ventilating above a total end-expiratory pressure of 13, not simply the set 5. Check for expiratory effort and hidden regional trapping before treating the number as exact.
Case 1 — severe asthma: high peak pressure, trapped gas and hypotension

A 34-year-old with severe asthma is intubated after exhaustion despite medical treatment. Predicted body weight (PBW) is 70 kg. During passive volume-controlled ventilation, expiration is still flowing when the next breath begins; peak pressure is 55 cmH₂O and blood pressure falls.

A high peak pressure includes airway resistance: measure plateau and total PEEP rather than equating peak with alveolar pressure. Urgently assess hyperinflation, pneumothorax, tube obstruction, circuit problems and other causes of shock.
Illustrative observed sequence: passive volume control
Less trapping and improved circulation in this fictional case

The team continues treatment of obstruction, reduces volume and rate, shortens inspiration and removes the routine inspiratory pause. At constant flow, 420 mL in 0.35 s corresponds to 72 L/min; the actual device waveform and timing must be checked.

A short diagnostic plateau hold is different from leaving a routine pause on every breath. Reducing minute ventilation is the central intervention; changing flow alone cannot compensate for excessive ventilation.

Lower ventilation can raise PaCO₂. Follow gases, pH, oxygenation and circulation, and assess whether hypercapnia is tolerable in this individual; it is not permission to ignore severe acidaemia or conditions in which hypercapnia is hazardous. These example volumes and pressures are not a universal asthma protocol.
If ARDS also exists, apply its PBW-volume and plateau-pressure guidance while still addressing obstruction.

PEEP; it changes only slightly here despite less hyperinflation. Raising external PEEP simply because auto-PEEP is high can worsen passive severe asthma; no fixed fraction is automatically safe.
does a peak pressure of 55 prove a plateau of 55, or require a switch to pressure control?

No. Resistive pressure can make peak much higher than plateau. Obtain valid measurements and assess delivered volume, expiration and circulation. A mode switch does not itself remove trapped gas; either controlled mode requires suitable timing and close monitoring.

> Case 2 — pressure control: the same setting delivers more volume as bronchospasm resolves

A 61-year-old with COPD and acute bronchospasm is receiving passive pressure-controlled ventilation. PBW is 70 kg.
The team uses a set inspiratory time of 0.7 s and rate of 12/min (4.3 s available for expiration), and checks whether the displayed inspiratory pressure is above PEEP or an absolute pressure.

>Total PEEP is the actual end-expiratory alveolar pressure. Intrinsic PEEP is the difference: total PEEP minus set PEEP. The ventilator
Total PEEP

is the actual end-expiratory alveolar pressure. Intrinsic PEEP is the difference: total PEEP minus set PEEP. The ventilator's normal pressure display cannot show it, because during expiration the gauge reads circuit pressure, not alveolar pressure, while gas is still flowing out.
Keller ATS Scholar 2022

>Why it builds up in bronchospasm: time constants

Passive expiration empties the lung exponentially. The rate is set by the expiratory time constant (τ), the product of resistance and compliance. After one τ about 37% of the tidal volume remains, after two τ 14%, and after three τ 5%.

A patient therefore needs an expiratory time longer than about three time constants to exhale the breath before the next one starts. Bronchospasm greatly raises resistance, lengthens τ and makes the available expiratory time too short at normal rates.
Each breath then leaves a little more gas behind, until a new, higher steady state is reached.<R label=
Why it builds up in bronchospasm: time constants

Passive expiration empties the lung exponentially. The rate is set by the expiratory time constant (τ), the product of resistance and compliance. After one τ about 37% of the tidal volume remains, after two τ 14%, and after three τ 5%.
Each breath then leaves a little more gas behind, until a new, higher steady state is reached.

Because τ calculated at the bedside uses resistance measured during inspiration, it may underestimate the true expiratory time constant when airway resistance is higher in expiration, as it is in asthma.
How to detect and measure it
>Flow–time waveform: if expiratory flow has not returned to zero when the next inspiration starts, gas is trapped. This is the quickest bedside sign.
Flow–time waveform:
if expiratory flow has not returned to zero when the next inspiration starts, gas is trapped. This is the quickest bedside sign.

>End-expiratory hold: occluding the expiratory port at end-expiration lets proximal airway pressure equilibrate with alveolar pressure, so the plateau reached is total PEEP, and the amount above set PEEP is intrinsic PEEP.
The patient must be relaxed, because active expiratory muscle contraction raises the reading without adding hyperinflation.<R label=

occluding the expiratory port at end-expiration lets proximal airway pressure equilibrate with alveolar pressure, so the plateau reached is total PEEP, and the amount above set PEEP is intrinsic PEEP.
The patient must be relaxed, because active expiratory muscle contraction raises the reading without adding hyperinflation.
Only lung units still connected to the airway equilibrate, so when airways close during expiration the hold can
intrinsic PEEP.
Treat a low value with suspicion if the plateau pressure is rising without another explanation.
>Trapped volume (VEI): the volume exhaled during 20–60 seconds of apnoea in a paralysed patient is the volume above functional residual capacity at end-inspiration. In Tuxen and Lane
Trapped volume (VEI):

the volume exhaled during 20–60 seconds of apnoea in a paralysed patient is the volume above functional residual capacity at end-inspiration. In Tuxen and Lane's work, a VEI above 20 ml/kg predicted hypotension and barotrauma in ventilated severe asthma.
Why it matters

SSC 2021 MAP 65
65 trial (age ≥65): permissive MAP 60–65 gave 41.0% vs 43.8% 90-day mortality, not significant.
65 trial 2020
Start at 65; in older vasodilated patients, chasing higher numbers adds vasopressor without proven benefit. Individualise for chronic hypertension or raised intracranial pressure.
Which vasopressor first?
>SOAP II: no mortality difference, but arrhythmias 24.1% with dopamine vs 12.4% with noradrenaline.<R label=

SOAP II 2010
Noradrenaline is the default first agent; dopamine has fallen out of use.
What resuscitation endpoint?
>ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: capillary refill-targeted 34.9% vs lactate-targeted 43.4% 28-day mortality (P = .06), less organ dysfunction at 72 h.<R label=
