ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 2019
Capillary refill time is a valid, fast, repeatable target; lactate falls slowly and is not only a perfusion marker.
Routine VA-ECMO in infarct shock?
>ECLS-SHOCK: 47.8% vs 49.0% 30-day mortality; more bleeding and vascular complications.<R label=
ECLS-SHOCK: 47.8% vs 49.0% 30-day mortality; more bleeding and vascular complications.
ECLS-SHOCK 2023
Do not use VA-ECMO routinely; reserve it for selected patients in experienced centres.
Microaxial pump (Impella CP)?
>DanGer Shock (STEMI shock, selected, no coma): 45.8% vs 58.5% mortality at 180 days<R label=
DanGer Shock (STEMI shock, selected, no coma): 45.8% vs 58.5% mortality at 180 days
DanGer Shock 2024
, but safety events 24.0% vs 6.2%.
DanGer Shock 2024 harms
The first device trial to show a survival benefit, in a narrow group; limb ischaemia, bleeding and renal replacement were more common.
>Bedside checklist: the first hour
Bedside checklist: the first hour

>
  • Call for help. Airway, breathing, two large-bore cannulas, bloods with lactate and a blood gas.
  • Look: mottling, capillary refill (press 10 s on the finger pad; normal ≤3 s), conscious level, urine output.
Call for help. Airway, breathing, two large-bore cannulas, bloods with lactate and a blood gas.
Look: mottling, capillary refill (press 10 s on the finger pad; normal ≤3 s), conscious level, urine output.
Point-of-care ultrasound: big or small heart, poor or good function, pericardial fluid, right heart strain, free abdominal fluid, lung B-lines.

Treat the type you find: fluid or blood for hypovolaemia; antibiotics and source control for sepsis; reperfusion and inotropes for cardiogenic; decompress for tension pneumothorax or tamponade; thrombolysis for massive pulmonary embolism.
Start noradrenaline early if MAP stays below 65 — peripherally through a good cannula while central access is arranged.
Insert an arterial line; non-invasive cuffs are unreliable in shock.
Reassess every 15–30 minutes. Stop fluids when the patient no longer responds or develops lung water.
In cardiogenic shock from a heart attack, call cardiology for the catheter lab early and discuss mechanical support only in a shock centre.

>Worked case (fictional)

A 71-year-old woman is cold and confused 6 hours after an anterior heart attack. HR 115, BP 82/58, lactate 5.2, capillary refill 6 s. Calculated MAP is about 66 and the shock index 1.4.

Ultrasound shows a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle and B-lines, so this is cardiogenic, not hypovolaemic: the team gives no fluid bolus. Noradrenaline holds the MAP at 65, an arterial line goes in and she goes straight to the catheter lab.

Cardiac output by thermodilution is 2.8 L/min, giving a cardiac power output of about 0.41 W. The shock team discusses a microaxial pump, weighing the DanGer Shock survival benefit against the limb and bleeding risks.

These are symptom-screen estimates, not the proportion with a diagnosis confirmed by a clinical interview. Do not confuse the original IES thresholds with IES-Revised thresholds used elsewhere.

The very high heterogeneity (I² 98.67% for prevalence) means the pooled estimate is a broad signal of burden, not “six in ten of every UK ICU population”. Timing, baseline function, screening cutoffs, diagnosis, geography and who survives or attends follow-up change the result.
Dasta analysed 51,009 adult ICU patients in 253 US hospitals in late 2002, converting billed charges to costs with hospital cost-to-charge ratios.
APACHE IV predicts ICU stay from day-1 data with admission diagnosis among its inputs, and it matched observed group means for 93% of 116 diagnoses.

every figure above is quoted word for word from the public summary of the ICNARC Case Mix Programme (CMP) Public Report 2024-25, the national clinical audit of admissions to adult critical care in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, covering April 2024 to March 2025 across 286 participating units.

a long ICU stay is a marker of severe illness and a cause of muscle wasting, weakness and lost weight. Length of stay is not a quality measure on its own: it reflects case mix, ward capacity and delayed discharge as well as care (teaching summary).
NICE CG50 night transfer
combined with an accurate description of disease
; the more severely impaired group overlaps the broader group, so do not add the percentages. These are follow-up participants, not 34% and 24% of all original admissions.

The CMP is observational audit data, not a trial: the 11.5% critical care mortality and 15% acute hospital mortality are raw, unadjusted figures for a very mixed case mix, and they describe populations, not individual risk.
Individual units are compared using risk-adjusted (not raw) mortality through the ICNARC model (teaching summary).

the 2024–25 report was released in 2026. It includes 209,047 patients but 222,377 admissions: a patient can have more than one admission. Scotland is not included in this CMP summary.
Do not apply the national averages to sepsis, ARDS, elective postoperative care or another specific diagnosis without examining the relevant case mix.
Public rounding versus the clinical summary
ICNARC CMP 2024-25 clinical outcomes

The clinical summary reports hospital survival as 84.6%, rounded to 85% in the public version; critical care survival is 88.5% in both. Its mean stays are 5.9 days in critical care and 20.4 days in acute hospital (public version: 6 and 20). Means are not medians: a minority of long stays can raise the average.

Hospital length of stay includes the hospital episode, not simply time on the ward after ICU. The public chart gives 7 critical care days and 16 hospital days for critical care non-survivors; its survivor/non-survivor grouping is by critical care outcome.
Denominator caution:

ICU survival, hospital survival, unique patients and admissions are different measures. The reports' rounded headline percentages do not establish a ward-only death rate: outcome follow-up, transfers, repeat admissions and eligible denominators must be checked first.

The percentage-point difference is not the percentage of ICU survivors who died on a ward. ICNARC is an audit of acute outcomes; it does not supply a national return-to-work or PTSD rate in this summary.
In the ICNARC CMP 2024-25 public summary, what proportion of admissions died in critical care and in acute hospital?
11.5% died in critical care; 15% died in acute hospital (85% survived to hospital discharge).
Long stays are one of the NICE CG83 rehabilitation risk factors, covered on

Five years on
PICS & follow-up
Five years on
Herridge 2011 five-year function
Herridge 2011 conclusion
the lungs largely recover, but physical function does not return to normal even at five years, and the burden extends to family caregivers.
Both Herridge cohorts were small Canadian ARDS groups of relatively young patients, so they show the pattern of recovery rather than the figures for every ICU survivor (teaching summary).
NICE CG83 review
Disability is broader than lung function
Hodgson 2017 disability

In this five-centre Australian cohort of hospital survivors ventilated for more than 24 hours, 65 of 262 followed-up survivors (25%) reported moderate or severe disability at six months using the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0. This is not a UK all-admission rate or simply a measurement of muscle strength.

Function includes mobility, self-care, cognition, relationships, usual activities and participation. Compare with the patient's pre-illness baseline: discharge home, normal spirometry and independence in daily life are not interchangeable endpoints.
What did Herridge find was the main reason for disability one year after ARDS?
Extrapulmonary problems, most prominently muscle wasting and weakness — lung volumes and spirometry were normal by 6 months, though gas transfer stayed low.
At 5 years in Herridge 2011, what was the median 6-minute walk distance?
436 m, 76% of predicted; neither younger nor older patients returned to normal predicted physical function.
Current UK audit versus historical all-readmission estimates:

ICNARC 2024–25 reports 1.1% unplanned readmissions within 48 hours. Rosenberg's approximately 7% concerns broader readmission definitions in older studies. Different time windows and planned/unplanned classifications explain why these figures cannot be used as competing estimates of the same outcome.

An early return may reflect deterioration, premature transfer or unavoidable disease progression; a low rate may also reflect limits on readmission. Interpret alongside case mix and mortality, not as an isolated quality score.
readmitted patients do much worse, but the review warns that readmission rates are not yet proven to measure quality of care.

Unstable vital signs at discharge are the most consistent warning sign, and night-time discharge was an independent predictor of death in one Australian cohort — consistent with NICE advice to avoid it.
These are associations from observational studies, not proof that changing discharge timing alone saves lives (teaching summary).
According to Rosenberg & Watts, what is the average ICU readmission rate and the most consistent predictor?
About 7% (range 4–14%); unstable vital signs at the time of ICU discharge.
What does APACHE II combine to give its severity score, and what is its range?
Initial values of 12 routine physiological measurements, age and previous health status; range 0 to 71.
Why compare units using risk-adjusted rather than raw mortality?
Because units admit different case mixes; adjustment compares observed deaths with those expected for that severity of illness.
Difficulty remembering instructions, managing medicines, planning a task or sustaining concentration can persist despite good physical recovery, including in younger survivors.

Longer delirium duration was independently associated with worse later cognition, but observational association does not prove that a particular delirium intervention prevents this disability. Pre-existing impairment, deaths and loss to follow-up affect estimates.
A review should distinguish new problems from baseline impairment and arrange assessment when daily function is affected; see
>PICS follow-up.
PICS follow-up
Do the BRAIN-ICU test comparisons mean survivors developed Alzheimer's disease?
No. They describe the severity of cognitive test scores, not a new neurological diagnosis; the two percentages overlap and apply to assessed survivors.
Kamdar 2020 employment change

Returning to any job is not returning to the same duties, hours or sustained employment. The reported ranges for subsequent job loss, occupation change and worse employment come from individual studies, not pooled risks to add together.
Physical fatigue, cognitive difficulty and psychological symptoms may all limit work; job demands, employer flexibility and the welfare system also matter.
The evidence search ended in February 2018 and between-study heterogeneity was high (I² 87%), so this 2020 review is a useful benchmark, not a current UK national statistic.

Ask about previous work, caring responsibilities, driving, finances and the tasks the person now finds difficult. A supported graded return and occupational-health input may be appropriate, but an ICU discharge date or a normal lung test alone cannot certify readiness for a safety-critical job.
Practical rehabilitation and information about work and benefits are covered in
>ICU Discharge Planning.
What is the denominator for the 60% return-to-work estimate at 12 months?
Previously employed survivors in the included follow-up studies, not all ICU admissions; return to work does not guarantee the same hours or lasting employment.

s general-ICU meta-analysis found clinically important PTSD symptoms in 25% at 1–6 months using an Impact of Event Scale threshold ≥35, versus 44% with the less restrictive ≥20 threshold. At 7–12 months the respective estimates were 17% and 34%. Thus “the PTSD rate” needs a time point, instrument and threshold.

These are symptom-screen estimates, not the proportion with a diagnosis confirmed by a clinical interview. Do not confuse the original IES thresholds with IES-Revised thresholds used elsewhere.

Depression and anxiety can persist as well
Depression and anxiety can persist as well
Rabiee 2016 depression
Nikayin 2016 anxiety

With Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale subscale thresholds ≥8, pooled depressive symptoms were 29%, 34% and 29% at 2–3, 6 and 12–14 months; anxiety symptoms were 32%, 40% and 34% at the same intervals. These older systematic reviews are reference estimates rather than a present-day UK audit.

PTSD, depression and anxiety overlap: adding them gives an invalid overall morbidity rate. A positive screen warrants clinical assessment; it does not establish a psychiatric diagnosis or show that ICU alone caused the symptoms.

Explore intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance, hyperarousal, low mood, loss of interest, anxiety and sleep problems alongside physical and cognitive recovery. Pre-existing mental ill health and frightening or delusional ICU memories can influence later symptoms.

Persistent distress or impaired daily function should prompt appropriate psychological assessment; urgent concerns about self-harm need immediate clinical help, not a routine follow-up appointment. The
>PICS Follow-Up Plan covers the assessment pathway and conflicting diary trials.
PICS Follow-Up Plan
covers the assessment pathway and conflicting diary trials.
Why can two studies report 17% and 34% PTSD symptoms at the same follow-up interval?
Different screening thresholds identify different groups. Neither symptom percentage is automatically a clinician-confirmed PTSD diagnosis.

Report the outcome domain and its definition alongside any percentage. Family members can also experience psychological and practical consequences; patient percentages should not be repurposed as family prevalence.
Latest psychological-intervention review
Cesari 2026 psychological interventions

Cesari's review, published online in June 2026, included 39 studies of ICU or post-ICU interventions. Evidence remained heterogeneous: 14 studies found improvement in at least one psychological outcome, 23 found no benefit and two evaluative interventions were associated with worse outcomes.

Counting positive studies does not establish a pooled treatment effect; narrative and multimodal approaches had signals of benefit but methodological limitations. Screening and referral are important, but neither follow-up attendance nor an ICU diary guarantees prevention of PTSD, depression or anxiety.

At the recommended 2–3 month review for patients with rehabilitation needs, document survival status, mobility and self-care, cognition, psychological symptoms, work/usual activities and progress against the person's goals. Use baseline-aware reassessment rather than a percentage to decide the next step.

It explained only 21.5% of variation between individual patients (62% between ICUs); the authors state its accuracy and utility are limited for individuals.
Oeyen 2010 quality of life
Oeyen 2010 study quality

Survivors report lower quality of life than matched populations, and it varies by diagnosis, with severe ARDS, prolonged ventilation, severe trauma and severe sepsis faring worst. Only 8% of studies met the review's quality criteria — notably, few measured quality of life
admission. Without a baseline, a low score may reflect pre-existing illness rather than harm from the ICU stay.
A UK five-year cohort using EQ-5D

In 300 level 3 patients from one Scottish university hospital (median stay 6.7 days), physical quality of life dipped, recovered by a year, then fell again, while mental scores reached population norms after six months.

An EQ-5D utility of 0.677 at five years means survivors valued their health state at roughly two-thirds of full health on that scale; it is a group mean, not an individual's score. Scores are only available from survivors who respond, so non-responders and deaths can bias averages upwards.
Physical, mental and utility measures can move in different directions — report which one is meant (teaching summary). Function and disability measures are in lessons 3 and 6–8.
What five dimensions does the EQ-5D cover, and what does a utility of 1 represent?
Mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression; 1 represents full health (0 equivalent to death).
In Cuthbertson 2010, what was the EQ-5D utility at 5 years?
0.677; physical scores were below population norms at all time points, while mental scores were similar to norms after 6 months.

ICU mortality, hospital mortality and long-term mortality are different numbers and must not be mixed. Some deaths happen on the ward after ICU discharge, and survivors who needed mechanical ventilation keep an excess risk for months afterwards.
Wunsch studied elderly US Medicare patients, so the absolute figures do not transfer directly to younger or UK populations (teaching summary). UK national figures are in the ICNARC lesson below.
UK survival after hospital discharge
Lone 2016 five-year survival

Lone used Scottish linked national registries: adult general ICU admissions in 2005 who survived hospital discharge, compared with matched hospital controls. Five-year mortality was 32.3% versus 22.7%; equivalently, survival was 67.7% versus 77.3% (arithmetic complements, not a new estimate).

The clock starts at hospital discharge, so these percentages exclude deaths during the index admission. This is useful long-term UK evidence, but it is a historical cohort, not the 2024–25 ICNARC population or a prediction for a present-day patient.
Comorbidity, pre-illness function, age and diagnosis matter; association with ICU admission does not establish that ICU care caused the excess deaths.
In Wunsch 2010, when was the excess mortality in ventilated ICU survivors concentrated?
In the first 6 months after hospital discharge.

Rivers 2001 EGDT
It was a single-centre trial with a very high control-group mortality, and it shaped the early Surviving Sepsis bundles.
The three multicentre trials and PRISM

ProCESS (USA, 2014), ARISE (Australasia, 2014) and ProMISe (England, 2015) each compared EGDT with usual care and found no mortality benefit. The PRISM meta-analysis pooled their individual patient data:
PRISM 2017 EGDT meta-analysis
PRISM 2017 subgroups

Why the difference? Usual care had improved: by 2014 patients already received early antibiotics and substantial fluid before randomisation, and control mortality was far lower than in Rivers. This explanation is teaching synthesis.
What replaced EGDT

The lasting lessons are early recognition, early antibiotics and source control, and prompt resuscitation with frequent reassessment, rather than fixed CVP or ScvO₂ targets. Current guidance uses lactate and capillary refill as perfusion markers:

Sepsis-3 dropped SIRS from the definition and removed the term "severe sepsis". Sepsis now means infection with a rise in SOFA of 2 or more; it is a definition of organ dysfunction, not of inflammation.

Hypotension alone, or a raised lactate alone, does not meet the definition. Both must persist after adequate volume resuscitation.
Screening is not diagnosis
SSC 2021 qSOFA screening

qSOFA (respiratory rate ≥22, altered mentation, systolic BP ≤100 mm Hg) identifies patients at risk of a poor outcome, but is too insensitive to rule sepsis out. No. Sepsis-3 requires both vasopressor-dependent hypotension and lactate above 2 mmol/L after adequate fluid. This is sepsis with hypotension needing vasopressors; treat it with the same urgency.

>Normal gap does not mean normal acid–base balance

In the simplified normal-gap model, a bicarbonate fall is accompanied by a chloride rise, keeping the sum of measured anions, and therefore AG, approximately unchanged.

>What is actually being compared?

The commonly named osmolar gap compares measured serum osmolality, preferably by freezing-point depression, with an estimate from sodium, urea and glucose. Osmolality is per kilogram of water; osmolarity is per litre of solution.

>Three independent variables within a chemical model

The Stewart model applies electroneutrality, mass conservation and dissociation equilibria. Its independent variables are PaCO₂, strong ion difference (SID) and total non-volatile weak acids (Atot, principally albumin and phosphate).

>Circuit anticoagulation is not systemic calcium control

Pre-filter citrate binds ionised calcium to inhibit circuit coagulation. Some calcium–citrate complex leaves in the effluent; the remainder returns to the patient. Calcium replacement compensates for losses.

>Acidosis is a process; acidaemia is a pH finding

High anion gap metabolic acidosis means a metabolic acidifying process accompanied by excess unmeasured anions. A low pH is common but not essential: concurrent respiratory or metabolic alkalosis can leave the pH normal or raised.

>Who BICAR-ICU studied

BICAR-ICU enrolled adults within 48 hours of ICU admission with severe metabolic acidaemia: pH 7.20 or lower, PaCO₂ 45 mmHg or lower and bicarbonate 20 mmol/L or lower, plus a SOFA score of 4 or more or lactate of 2 mmol/L or more.

>Chemistry is settled; outcome is not

In Stewart terms, 0.9% sodium chloride contains equal sodium and chloride, so large volumes lower plasma strong ion difference and produce a hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap acidosis. That is a predictable effect on the blood gas.

RTA: combine potassium, urine findings and renal function
Type 1, distal:

impaired distal acid secretion; urine remains inappropriately alkaline, typically above pH 5.5 during systemic metabolic acidosis. Hypokalaemia, hypocitraturia, nephrocalcinosis and calcium phosphate stones are clues. Autoimmune disease, inherited defects and amphotericin exposure are examples.
Urine pH alone is not diagnostic: exclude infection and other confounders.
Berend 2017 RTA
Type 2, proximal:

bicarbonate wasting until plasma bicarbonate reaches a lower renal threshold. Urine is alkaline during bicarbonaturia but can become acidic below pH 5.5 once that threshold is reached. Hypokalaemia is common. Look for Fanconi features: renal glycosuria despite normal blood glucose, phosphate and amino-acid loss.
Acetazolamide and proximal tubular injury are causes.
Type 4:
hypoaldosteronism or resistance, with hyperkalaemia and impaired ammonium excretion. Urine can still be acidic below pH 5.5, because low urine pH does not establish adequate total acid excretion.
Diabetes-related kidney disease, renin–angiotensin blockers, potassium-sparing diuretics and trimethoprim are relevant clues. Renal impairment may coexist; RTA does not require completely normal GFR.
Urinary anion gap: a conditional ammonium surrogate
UAG = urine Na⁺ + urine K⁺ − urine Cl⁻.

If ammonium is excreted mainly with chloride, a negative UAG suggests an appropriate ammonium response, as in diarrhoea; a positive value suggests reduced ammonium excretion, as in distal or type 4 RTA.
Proximal RTA can have a negative UAG
because distal ammonium excretion is preserved. A positive UAG therefore does not diagnose every RTA, and a negative one does not exclude all renal causes.
Berend 2017 urine gap

Use it only when the cause remains unclear. Polyuria, urine pH above 6.5, low urine sodium (below 20 mmol/L) and ammonium excreted with non-chloride anions such as ketoanions make it unreliable. Consider measured urinary ammonium where available, or the urinary osmolal gap with its own limitations.
Interpret fresh urine pH with potassium, volume status and culture findings rather than in isolation.

Can urine pH 5.0 and a negative UAG rule out RTA?
No. Proximal RTA can acidify urine once plasma bicarbonate falls below the reduced reabsorptive threshold, and its ammonium response can remain intact.

The commonly named osmolar gap compares measured serum osmolality, preferably by freezing-point depression, with an estimate from sodium, urea and glucose. Osmolality is per kilogram of water; osmolarity is per litre of solution.

The Stewart model applies electroneutrality, mass conservation and dissociation equilibria. Its independent variables are PaCO₂, strong ion difference (SID) and total non-volatile weak acids (A

Effective SID estimates bicarbonate plus albumin and phosphate charge; SIG = SIDa − SIDe estimates residual unmeasured strong-ion charge, not the identity of a toxin.

In the worked septic-patient example, Na 140, K 4.5, ionised Ca 1.1, Mg 0.9, Cl 115 and lactate 3.5 give SIDa = 30 mEq/L. Omitting the divalent valence factors incorrectly gives 28. The hypoalbuminaemia can offset acidosis on pH, while corrected AG or SIG still indicates unmeasured charge.

Story's simplified sodium–chloride contribution is Na − Cl − 38 mEq/L; the albumin contribution is 0.25 × (42 − albumin g/L). For Na 138, Cl 112 and albumin 20: −12 and +5.5 mEq/L respectively. This is an approximate partition, not a new measured quantity.

Does albumin loss cause alkalosis by raising SID?
No. It lowers total weak acids, a separate model variable. A patient can have low SID acidosis and low-albumin alkalosis simultaneously.
Circuit anticoagulation is not systemic calcium control

Pre-filter citrate binds ionised calcium to inhibit circuit coagulation. Some calcium–citrate complex leaves in the effluent; the remainder returns to the patient. Calcium replacement compensates for losses.

Post-filter ionised calcium assesses circuit anticoagulation, while a separately obtained systemic ionised calcium assesses the patient: do not confuse the sampling sites or contaminate samples with the calcium infusion.

The review describes a post-filter target of 0.2–0.35 mmol/L depending on protocol, and systemic replacement to the physiological range.

Recognise the process, not just the pH
BJA 2023 definition
Metabolic alkalosis is the non-respiratory alkalinising process. Read pH, bicarbonate and PaCO₂ together: a raised bicarbonate may instead be compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis.
Mixed disorders can leave the measured pH normal or low; compare previous gases and assess the anion gap, albumin and clinical history rather than excluding alkalosis from pH alone.
BJA 2023 mixed disorders
Separate generation from maintenance
BJA 2023 maintenance
Vomiting or gastric drainage removes acid and chloride; diuretics promote renal electrolyte losses; bicarbonate or metabolised precursors can add alkali.

Ask separately why the kidney has not removed it: volume/chloride depletion, potassium deficiency and impaired renal function can maintain the disturbance after the original cause stops. Volume depletion activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS), favouring sodium retention and hydrogen/potassium loss.

Review gastric losses, diuretic and alkali exposure, volume status, blood pressure, chloride, potassium, magnesium and kidney function. Urine chloride can help classify the mechanism, but active diuretics and the examination matter; it is not an automatic instruction to give fluid.

Establish pH, PaCO₂ and bicarbonate, then assess whether the respiratory response fits the metabolic process. Hypoventilation can compensate for metabolic alkalosis, but lung disease, respiratory muscle dysfunction and controlled ventilation can limit that response.

>Vomiting and gastric drainage: acid and chloride loss generate the disorder, while volume contraction and potassium depletion can maintain it. Quantify ongoing losses and consider why drainage remains necessary.

The review prioritises identifying the mechanism and stopping the precipitant. Address ongoing gastric losses, unnecessary alkali administration and diuretic exposure where clinically appropriate, while correcting the associated electrolyte/volume problem.

Alkalaemia increases calcium binding to albumin, reducing ionised calcium. The review associates this with neuromuscular excitability and impaired cardiac function; accompanying hypokalaemia can further increase arrhythmia risk. Total calcium alone may therefore miss the physiologically important reduction.

Metabolic alkalosis is an acid–base process that tends to increase pH through a non-respiratory mechanism. Alkalaemia means the measured blood pH is above 7.45. These are not interchangeable: metabolic alkalosis can coexist with metabolic or respiratory acidosis, leaving the final pH normal or even low.

BJA 2023 alkali gain
For the separate problem of citrate accumulation and its monitoring, see the
citrate anticoagulation lesson
>Hypoalbuminaemia: reduced weak-acid content creates an alkalinising component even when chloride is not low. Consider what other acidifying processes it may be concealing.
reduced weak-acid content creates an alkalinising component even when chloride is not low. Consider what other acidifying processes it may be concealing.
Post-hypercapnic alkalosis after ventilation starts

In chronic respiratory acidosis, renal adaptation raises bicarbonate and alters chloride handling. When ventilation lowers PaCO₂, the respiratory component changes faster than the renal adaptation reverses.
Persistent metabolic alkalosis can therefore become apparent, sometimes with severe alkalaemia; the BJA review describes renal resolution over
>3–5 days. Concurrent diuretic use and chloride/potassium depletion can prolong the problem.
3–5 days
. Concurrent diuretic use and chloride/potassium depletion can prolong the problem.
BJA 2023 posthypercapnia

Compare the previous PaCO₂/bicarbonate pattern with the current gas and review the ventilation goals and electrolyte/volume deficits. The interval is a physiological description, not a reason to wait passively when the patient is deteriorating, or an instruction to deliberately create hypoventilation.
This is bedside teaching synthesis.
bicarbonate remains high after PaCO₂ falls rapidly during ventilation of a chronically hypercapnic patient. What mechanism should you consider?

>Post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis: the renal adaptation outlasts the fall in PaCO₂. Also look for concurrent diuretics, chloride depletion and potassium deficiency rather than assuming a single cause.</Check> <LessonSources topicId={T} labels={[

Post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis: the renal adaptation outlasts the fall in PaCO₂. Also look for concurrent diuretics, chloride depletion and potassium deficiency rather than assuming a single cause.
Reassess perfusion, fluid balance, renal function and electrolyte response rather than prescribing a fixed volume for every patient.
BJA 2023 chloride
BJA 2023 potassium

Potassium replacement requires an approved local protocol, consideration of renal function and repeat measurements. Intravenous concentration, rate, access and monitoring requirements are safety-critical; this lesson intentionally does not convert the review's monitored example into a universal infusion prescription.
Check magnesium alongside potassium and the wider biochemical profile.
Volume expansion, endocrine disease or continued need for diuresis

A patient with volume expansion or excess mineralocorticoid activity is less likely to benefit from chloride-rich fluid alone. The BJA review discusses acetazolamide and potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone.

Choose an approach that addresses the underlying disease, potassium status, renal function and continuing fluid-management needs; do not infer that all patients labelled “chloride resistant” need the same drug or saline in addition.
BJA 2023 volume expansion
Biochemical improvement is not proof of faster liberation from ventilation

Acetazolamide promotes renal bicarbonate loss and can improve the biochemical alkalosis. However, the BJA review reports that the cited clinical trial in mechanically ventilated hypercapnic respiratory failure
>did not show a shorter duration of mechanical ventilation. Do not promise a weaning benefit merely because bicarbonate falls.
did not show a shorter duration of mechanical ventilation
. Do not promise a weaning benefit merely because bicarbonate falls.
BJA 2023 acetazolamide
a fluid-overloaded patient has alkalosis during necessary diuresis. Should every low chloride result trigger saline?

No. Determine the circulating-volume context and cause. Consider the need for continued diuresis, potassium/chloride replacement and clinician-selected alternatives; biochemical correction and weaning outcomes are separate questions.
Marked or worsening alkalaemia with arrhythmia, altered consciousness, neuromuscular symptoms, respiratory compromise or major electrolyte disturbance requires urgent senior assessment.

Review the gas trend, ECG, potassium, magnesium, ionised calcium, renal function and volume status; reassess delivered ventilation when mechanically ventilated. This is a practical safety synthesis, not a trial-derived escalation threshold.

Refractory cases need critical-care/nephrology input to address ongoing losses, renal limitations and competing fluid goals. The BJA review notes reports of hydrochloric acid use but explicitly says it is
>not recommended routinely. This page provides no acid-infusion recipe or automatic dialysis trigger; specialist therapies require an established protocol and close monitoring.
not recommended routinely
. This page provides no acid-infusion recipe or automatic dialysis trigger; specialist therapies require an established protocol and close monitoring.
BJA 2023 acid caution
Rehabilitation of the physiology needs repeated reassessment

Confirm whether pH and bicarbonate improve alongside correction of potassium/chloride deficits, cessation of losses and an appropriate fluid balance. A repeat gas must still be interpreted for mixed disorders: resolving one alkalinising process may expose an underlying acidosis previously hidden by it.
total calcium is normal but a severely alkalaemic patient develops tetany. Which calcium measurement matters?

Measure ionised calcium. Increased albumin binding in alkalaemia can lower ionised calcium despite a normal total calcium concentration; assess the patient and accompanying electrolyte abnormalities urgently.

asks why the kidneys have not excreted the excess bicarbonate. Volume depletion, chloride deficiency, potassium deficiency and impaired filtration may prevent correction even after vomiting or diuretic administration has stopped.

Volume depletion activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, encouraging sodium retention and distal potassium/hydrogen-ion loss. Chloride depletion limits bicarbonate secretion through the collecting-duct chloride–bicarbonate exchanger, pendrin.
Potassium deficiency promotes renal ammonium production and bicarbonate retention: hypokalaemia is not merely a coincidental blood-test abnormality, but a mechanism sustaining the alkalosis.
The Stewart description identifies the same clinical problems

A relative chloride deficit compared with sodium increases the strong ion difference and has an alkalinising effect. Reduced total weak acids, particularly hypoalbuminaemia, also produce an alkalinising component. This can conceal the pH effect of concurrent lactate or other unmeasured-anion acidosis.
A low albumin level is not, by itself, an indication to give albumin solely to correct pH.
The last sentence is clinical interpretation, not a treatment recommendation quoted from the review.
vomiting has stopped, but bicarbonate remains high with low chloride and potassium. Why?

>The generating event has ended, but chloride/potassium depletion and volume-related renal retention can maintain the disorder. Treating the precipitant alone may therefore be insufficient.</Check> <LessonSources topicId={T} labels={[

What GPICS is
— something all UK ICUs are expected to meet.
UK critical care is organised around the Intensive Care Society levels of care. The 2021 second edition is explicit about what the levels mean:

The Guidelines for the Provision of Intensive Care Services (GPICS) are the joint FICM/Intensive Care Society standards for how UK intensive care is organised and staffed:
Under the ICS 2021 levels, a patient who needs invasive ventilation alone is which level?
Levels of Adult Critical Care Second Edition, as in the original guidance, describes the care a patient requires, not where they are receiving it, nor does it measure the actual care being delivered.
The daytime consultant in ICM to patient ratio must not normally exceed a range between 1:8 and 1:12.

At baseline, less than 10% of residents and nurses understood the goals of care for the day. After implementing the daily goals form, greater than 95% of nurses and residents understood the goals of care for the day.
GPICS V3 (2026) is the definitive reference source for the planning, commissioning and delivery of adult intensive care services in the UK.

this was a before-and-after study in a single unit, so it shows that teams understood the plan better. It does not prove patients did better. In practice, finish each patient’s review by stating the goals out loud: what must happen today, what would trigger a call, and who is doing each task.
This latest version is broken down into five sections covering intensive care structure, workforce, clinical care, service development and preparedness.

It merges the pre-existing level 0 and level 1 into ward care. This frees up ‘level 1’ of critical care to represent the emerging Enhanced Care, with Level 2 and 3 remaining.
What changed from V2.1:

The best multicentre evidence for structured handover comes from I-PASS, a programme for resident doctors in children’s hospitals. It used a memory aid, training, observation of handovers and a standard written document:
Standards versus recommendations
As urgently as the clinical state dictates, and always within 14 hours of admission (V2.1 said 12 hours).
ICS Levels 2021 enhanced care
the 1:8 ratio for the on-site resident rota (doctors and ACCPs) was a daytime “should”; V3 makes it a 24/7 minimum standard. The consultant range of 1:8 to 1:12 is unchanged.

In 10,740 patient admissions, the medical-error rate decreased by 23% from the preintervention period to the postintervention period (24.5 vs. 18.8 per 100 admissions, P<0.001), and the rate of preventable adverse events decreased by 30% (4.7 vs. 3.3 events per 100 admissions, P<0.001).
GPICS grades its advice. In V3 the two tiers were renamed to make the distinction clearer:
What is the GPICS minimum registered nurse ratio for a level 2 patient?

So the current scheme is: ward care; level 1 (enhanced care, for example single-organ basic support or step-down patients); level 2; and level 3. Two of the level 2 descriptors are worth learning word for word:

The reason for intensivist-led care comes mainly from observational data. A systematic review compared “high-intensity” staffing (mandatory intensivist input or a closed unit) with “low-intensity” staffing:
Starmer 2014 I-PASS
For V3, the previously named ‘standards’ have been renamed ‘minimum standards’ and are defined as something we expect all ICUs in the UK to be able to meet.
Patients needing one organ systems monitored and supported at an advanced level (other than advanced respiratory support).

High-intensity staffing was associated with lower hospital mortality in 16 of 17 studies (94%) and with a pooled estimate of the relative risk for hospital mortality of 0.71 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.62-0.82).
Discharge from ICU is a handover between teams too, and GPICS requires both spoken and written handover:
GPICS V3 minimum standards
Level 3 needs at least 1:1; level 2 needs at least 1:2, plus a clinical shift leader who is not allocated a patient.
ICS Levels 2021 level 2
Pronovost 2002 staffing
The receiving (ward) team responsible for ongoing care need to be directly involved in this process and there should be a verbal as well as written handover.
‘Recommendations’ are now ‘recommendations for a quality service’ and are intended to act as markers for a high quality intensive care service.
What did the 2013 randomised trial of overnight in-house intensivists find?
Level 3 starts with the ventilated patient:
More is not always better. When one US academic unit randomised days to having an in-house intensivist overnight, on top of daytime intensivist care and resident cover:
GPICS V3 discharge handover
GPICS V3 quality recommendations
Patients needing advanced respiratory monitoring and support alone. Patients requiring monitoring and support for two or more organ systems at an advanced level.
In an academic medical ICU in the United States, nighttime in-hospital intensivist staffing did not improve patient outcomes.

I-PASS was a package tested in children’s wards, not adult ICUs, and it was not randomised. Its message is that a memory aid only works alongside training and a standard document. SBAR, call-outs and check-back for urgent escalation are taught on the
ICS Levels 2021 level 3
Delirium was added as a reason to step up a level, because an agitated patient needs more nursing to stay safe:
Patients who experience delirium and agitation in addition to requiring level 2 care.
ICS Levels 2021 delirium
Getting in and getting out: UK time standards
The Guidelines for the Provision of Intensive Care Services (GPICS V3, 2026) set time standards around admission and discharge:
Unplanned admissions to the ICU must occur within four hours of making the decision to admit and the completion of the essential resuscitation and imaging.
GPICS V3 admission timing
Patients must be reviewed, in person, by a consultant responsible for the ICU as urgently as the clinical state dictates, and always within 14 hours of admission to intensive care.
GPICS V3 consultant review
Discharge from intensive care to a general ward must occur only between 0700hrs and 2159hrs, except for reasons of surge.
GPICS V3 discharge
Discharge from intensive care to a general ward should occur within four hours of the decision.
GPICS V3 discharge four hours

the consultant review limit moved from 12 to 14 hours and now refers to “a consultant responsible for the ICU”; the four-hour admission clock now starts once essential resuscitation and imaging are complete; and four-hour discharge dropped from a minimum standard to a recommendation for a quality service, while the 07:00–21:59 window stays a minimum standard (with a surge exception).

the 14-hour standard is a maximum, not a target. A deteriorating patient needs consultant review as soon as their condition demands. Night-time discharges are avoided because ward staffing and senior cover are thinner then, so problems are less likely to be picked up.

the observational studies compared having intensivists with not having them, and could not fully adjust for differences between hospitals. The randomised trial added overnight presence to a unit already run by intensivists. The lesson is that intensivists direct care.
It is not that every extra consultant hour saves lives.
Nurses: the core of the unit
Level 3 patients must have a minimum registered nurse:patient ratio of 1:1 to deliver direct care. Level 2 patients must have a minimum registered nurse:patient ratio of 1:2 to deliver direct care.
GPICS V3 nurse ratios
There must be a clinical shift leader, who is not allocated a patient, on duty 24/7 in all ICUs.
GPICS V3 coordinator

the 1:1 and 1:2 ratios are unchanged from V2.1; V3 renames the supernumerary coordinator the clinical shift leader. The shift leader has no patients of their own so that they can cover breaks, run emergencies, manage beds and spot problems across the unit.
If they have to take a patient, that whole safety layer is lost.
The wider team on the ward round
V3 keeps twice-daily consultant rounds but now specifies that one must be in person:
A consultant in ICM must undertake ward rounds twice a day, one of which will be face-to-face, 7 days a week.
GPICS V3 ward round

V3 sets separate staffing chapters for pharmacists, physiotherapists, dietitians, speech and language therapists, occupational therapists and psychologists. Each role covers a different risk. Pharmacists catch drug doses and interactions, especially in kidney failure.

Physiotherapists help clear secretions and start rehabilitation early. Dietitians plan feeding. Speech and language therapists assess swallowing after a breathing tube or tracheostomy. Psychologists support recovery from distressing ICU experiences.
Advanced critical care practitioners increasingly fill resident-grade roles. Recovery after discharge is covered in
PICS Follow-up

11 (1:1 for level 3) + 2 (1:2 for three level 2 patients, rounded up) = 13 bedside nurses, plus a clinical shift leader, who must not take a patient. The unit also has more than ten beds, and GPICS V3 requires at least one additional enhanced critical care nurse who is not allocated a patient.

On day 90, the 56 participants in the intervention group who responded to the telephone interview had a significantly lower median IES score than the 52 participants in the control group (27 vs. 39, P=0.02) and a lower prevalence of PTSD-related symptoms (45% vs. 69%, P=0.01).

in the trial, relatives in the intervention group talked for more of the meeting. Listening is part of the treatment. Detailed family-meeting technique is covered in

(24.5 − 18.8) ÷ 24.5 ≈ 0.23, a relative reduction of 23%. The absolute reduction is 5.7 errors per 100 admissions. Because the study compared periods before and after the programme rather than randomising, other changes over the same period could explain some of the difference.
It was also done in children’s hospitals rather than adult ICUs.

when you read a GPICS statement, check which tier it is. A minimum standard is a commissioning floor every unit should meet; a quality recommendation marks out a high-quality service.
The time standards and staffing ratios quoted in the other lessons on this page have been re-checked word for word against GPICS V3 (2026). Where V3 changed a V2.1 standard, the lesson says so.
Editions and who uses it

The first version of GPICS was published in 2015. In 2016, GPICS Edition 1 was subject to a review. Edition 2 began in Summer 2017 and was published Summer 2019. Edition 2.1 was published in Summer 2022.
GPICS editions

Groups that check hospital quality, such as the Care Quality Commission (CQC) in England, also use GPICS. In Scotland, Scottish Intensive Care Society Audit Group (SICSAG) uses GPICS to help check how well intensive care units are working.

How to apply this in ICU:

obtain time-critical diagnostic imaging while resuscitation, medication review and renal monitoring proceed as clinically indicated. “Do not delay” does not mean “no renal risk”, that fluids are never needed, or that metformin must always be continued during AKI or shock.

Creatinine is a delayed functional marker, affected by muscle mass, fluid dilution and changing production. Calculated eGFR assumes steady-state creatinine and can be misleading during evolving AKI: a displayed eGFR above a threshold is not reassuring if creatinine is rapidly rising. Oliguria may appear earlier.
No routinely available biomarker, urinary cast or fractional-excretion result uniquely identifies CI-AKI.

The usual described creatinine course begins within 24 hours, peaks within about 4 days and often returns towards baseline in 7–10 days; severe or persistent AKI requires reassessment rather than an assumption of inevitable recovery

>Exam answer: the restrictive 70 g/L default from general ICU trials should not be assumed safe after acute brain injury. A higher threshold, such as the trials
Exam answer:

the restrictive 70 g/L default from general ICU trials should not be assumed safe after acute brain injury. A higher threshold, such as the trials' liberal arm (TRAIN: 90 g/L; HEMOTION: 100 g/L), is now evidence-informed. Weigh it against transfusion risks and local guidance.
>Limits: neither trial could blind clinicians. Outcomes were functional scales, and the trials used different populations and outcome timings, so they should not simply be pooled.

TRAIN (all acute brain injury). HEMOTION (TBI only) showed a similar direction of effect but was not statistically significant.

OPTIMISE II was designed to settle the question. It randomised 2,498 patients aged 65 or over at 55 hospitals worldwide, using cardiac output-guided fluid with low-dose inotrope during surgery and for 4 hours afterwards. Postoperative infection was not reduced (23.2% vs 22.7%; adjusted OR 1.03).
Acute cardiac events within 24 hours were more common in the intervention group (3.0% vs 1.7%), mainly arrhythmias.
OPTIMISE II 2024
cursor-pointer font-semibold text-foreground
Learning check: does goal-directed therapy reduce complications after major surgery?

The best current evidence says no, at least for older patients having elective GI surgery within modern enhanced-recovery care. The positive trend in OPTIMISE was not confirmed by the larger OPTIMISE II, which also found more early arrhythmias with inotrope.
Cardiac output monitoring still has a place in unstable patients, but a protocol with routine inotrope should not be presented as proven.

>Does routine critical-care admission improve survival? (Kahan 2017, ISOS)

This planned analysis of the International Surgical Outcomes Study included 44,814 elective surgical patients from 474 hospitals in 27 countries.
Patients admitted straight to critical care after surgery died more often (2% vs 0.3%; adjusted OR 3.01). This probably reflects their higher risk at baseline.

At hospital level, mortality was not associated with direct critical-care admission, with admission to treat complications, or with how many critical-care beds a hospital had. The result was the same when only high-risk patients were analysed.<R label=
Does routine critical-care admission improve survival? (Kahan 2017, ISOS)

This planned analysis of the International Surgical Outcomes Study included 44,814 elective surgical patients from 474 hospitals in 27 countries. Patients admitted straight to critical care after surgery died more often (2% vs 0.3%; adjusted OR 3.01). This probably reflects their higher risk at baseline.

At hospital level, mortality was not associated with direct critical-care admission, with admission to treat complications, or with how many critical-care beds a hospital had. The result was the same when only high-risk patients were analysed.
Kahan 2017 ISOS

This is observational data, so it cannot show that critical care makes no difference to individual patients. Its message is that routinely admitting patients to critical care is not, on its own, a proven way to save lives.
Recognising deterioration on the ward and escalating care quickly when complications develop (failure to rescue) may matter as much as where a patient goes first.
Learning check: how would you reconcile ISOS with UK advice to admit patients with predicted mortality ≥5%?

UK advice (NCEPOD, NELA) is based on the observed harm of under-provision and of late escalation for patients who are clearly high-risk. ISOS shows that blanket admission after elective surgery has not been proven to improve survival.
Both point the same way: target admission to risk, and make sure the ward can spot and rescue complications.

>Prophylactic CPAP after major abdominal surgery (PRISM 2021)

PRISM randomised 4,806 patients aged 50 or over having elective major open abdominal surgery at 70 hospitals in six countries. Patients received either CPAP within 4 hours of the end of surgery or usual care.
Pneumonia, re-intubation or death within 30 days occurred in 8.1% vs 8.2% (adjusted OR 1.01). Adverse events occurred in 8.9% of patients who received CPAP, most often claustrophobia.<R label=
Prophylactic CPAP after major abdominal surgery (PRISM 2021)

PRISM randomised 4,806 patients aged 50 or over having elective major open abdominal surgery at 70 hospitals in six countries. Patients received either CPAP within 4 hours of the end of surgery or usual care. Pneumonia, re-intubation or death within 30 days occurred in 8.1% vs 8.2% (adjusted OR 1.01).
Adverse events occurred in 8.9% of patients who received CPAP, most often claustrophobia.
PRISM 2021
Learning check: should every patient get CPAP after open abdominal surgery?

No. PRISM found no reduction in pneumonia, re-intubation or death with routine prophylactic CPAP. CPAP remains a treatment for established hypoxaemia or atelectasis, and for patients who already use it for obstructive sleep apnoea. It is not a routine preventive measure.

>Acute physiology (APS)
Physical: the legacy can last years
Recognise Post-Intensive Care Syndrome (PICS) — physical, cognitive, and psychological — and the role of the ABCDEF bundle in prevention.
Acute physiology (APS)
Herridge's cohort followed 109 survivors of ARDS for five years. At 5 years the median 6-minute walk distance was
436 m, 76% of predicted
. Younger patients recovered faster, but
neither younger nor older patients returned to normal predicted physical function
, even though lung function was normal or near-normal. Other physical and psychological problems persisted in patients
and family caregivers
for up to five years.
Herridge 2011
The limitation is therefore mainly outside the lung: muscle weakness, poor exercise tolerance and reduced physical quality of life.
Cognitive: comparable to brain injury or early dementia
BRAIN-ICU enrolled 821 adults with respiratory failure or shock; only 6% had cognitive impairment at baseline, and 74% developed delirium in hospital.
BRAIN-ICU 2013 sedatives
At 3 months, 40% had global cognition scores similar to moderate traumatic brain injury and 26% similar to mild Alzheimer's disease.
Deficits affected younger as well as older patients and persisted to 12 months.
Longer delirium was independently associated with worse cognition and executive function at 3 and 12 months.
BRAIN-ICU 2013
Sedative and analgesic use was
consistently associated with long-term cognitive impairment.
The modifiable target the trial points to is delirium duration, not one drug class. That is an association, not proof that shortening delirium prevents impairment.
Psychological: common, overlapping and linked to mortality
A UK-wide cohort of 21,633 ICU admissions sent questionnaires to 13,155 survivors; 38% replied.
Of the respondents, 55% passed the threshold for anxiety, depression or PTSD at 3 or 12 months
: anxiety 46%, depression 40% and PTSD 22%. Patients with depression symptoms were
47% more likely to die in the first 2 years
after ICU discharge (HR 1.47).
Hatch 2018
With only 38% responding, the true prevalence in all survivors may be lower or higher; non-responders are a known source of bias in postal surveys.
Prevention in the ICU: the ABCDEF bundle
The bundle is:
ssess, prevent and manage pain;
oth spontaneous awakening and breathing trials;
hoice of analgesia and sedation;
elirium assessment and management;
arly mobility and exercise;

amily engagement. In the ICU Liberation Collaborative (over 15,000 adults), complete bundle performance was associated with lower delirium (AOR 0.60), coma (AOR 0.35), next-day ventilation (AOR 0.28), physical restraint (AOR 0.37), ICU readmission (AOR 0.54) and discharge somewhere other than home (AOR 0.64).
ICU Liberation 2019
This was an observational quality-improvement study, so it shows association, not that the bundle prevents PICS itself.
After the ICU: what NICE asks for
For the full step-by-step plan, see the
PICS Follow-Up Plan
During the ICU stay:
a short clinical assessment as early as possible to find patients at risk of physical and non-physical morbidity, followed by a comprehensive assessment of rehabilitation needs for those at risk.
NICE CG83 recs
2–3 months after critical care discharge:
review patients with rehabilitation needs, with a face-to-face functional reassessment of health and social care needs.
Do follow-up clinics and diaries work?
ICU diaries:
in a randomised trial of 352 patients with ICU stays over 72 hours, receiving a diary of their stay 1 month after discharge reduced new PTSD at 3 months from 13% to 5%.
Jones 2010 (ICU diaries)
Nurse-led follow-up clinics:

the UK PRaCTICaL trial (286 patients, three hospitals) found no evidence that a nurse-led follow-up programme improved quality of life at 12 months, and it cost more. The authors suggested future work should focus on early physical rehabilitation, delirium, cognitive dysfunction and relatives.
PRaCTICaL 2009
So "follow-up clinics reduce PTSD" is not supported as a general statement; the evidence is specific to the intervention.

An operational debrief is an after-action conversation about how the team worked: what happened, what helped, what obstructed care and what should change next time. It is not a retrospective test of the most junior clinician, a substitute for incident investigation, or a treatment for traumatic stress.

Speaking up in a crisis means making a safety concern audible, understandable and actionable, then checking that it has been addressed. Merely thinking that the leader must have noticed is not communication.

>TeamSTEPPS means Team Strategies and Tools to Enhance Performance and Patient Safety. The AHRQ framework organises teachable teamwork behaviours around communication, team leadership, situation monitoring and mutual support, with team structure at the centre.

Set the purpose.

Explain that the aim is to understand team performance, not allocate blame. Invite contributions across roles, including people who observed rather than performed the main procedure. Ask whether anyone has an immediate safety concern.
Reconstruct the shared facts.

Recap the intended plan, key changes and actions. Separate observations from assumptions: “the request was not acknowledged” is more useful than “nobody cared”. Where recollections differ, record the uncertainty rather than forcing agreement.
Explore work as it actually happened.

Ask what information each person had at the time, whether roles were clear, whether requests were heard and what equipment or workload constraints shaped decisions. Avoid judging earlier choices solely using facts learned afterwards.
