Obstetric

A supporting suture is placed around the cervix during pregnancy in selected patients at risk of preterm birth. History-, ultrasound- and examination-indicated procedures differ: rescue cerclage with exposed membranes is not equivalent to an elective stitch.
This entry illustrates a transvaginal McDonald-type stitch; Shirodkar and transabdominal techniques differ.
Lithotomy with supported legs; avoid sustained aortocaval compression as gestation advances and coordinate any head-down tilt with the obstetric team.
Confirm gestation, indication, cervical findings and suitability, including assessment for labour, infection, bleeding and ruptured membranes.

Agree maternal assessment, fasting/aspiration strategy and appropriate fetal assessment. Rescue cases may be urgent and have a greater risk of membrane rupture and pregnancy loss; anaesthesia cannot make an unsuitable cerclage safe.
Establish regional or general anaesthesia, position and expose the cervix with vaginal instruments.

Check neuraxial contraindications and adequate block before instrumentation. Treat maternal hypotension promptly; general anaesthesia requires a pregnancy-appropriate airway plan. Cervical traction can provoke a vagal response.
Identify the cervix and, if necessary, carefully reduce exposed membranes; pass a circumferential cervical suture.
Maintain immobility and communicate any bleeding or suspected membrane rupture. Reduction of membranes and needle placement are surgical decisions; the drawing is not a guide to needle depth.
Tie the suture to support the cervix without occluding its canal; inspect the operative field and trim the ends.
Reassess blood loss and comfort. Unexpected pain, bleeding or cardiorespiratory change warrants reassessment rather than assuming a short procedure is risk-free.
Remove instruments, complete maternal and appropriate fetal checks, and document follow-up and stitch-removal plans.

Confirm block recovery, analgesia and discharge suitability. Give a clear handover for contractions, bleeding, fluid loss or fever. Labour with a stitch in situ requires urgent obstetric review to prevent cervical injury.
Suitability for rescue cerclage
Maternal hypotension and positioning
Membrane rupture during cervical instrumentation
Labour with the stitch in situ
Regional or general anaesthesia may be appropriate; the choice depends on urgency, gestation, patient preference, contraindications and local expertise.

A cervical stitch reduces risk in selected patients but does not guarantee a term birth. Antibiotics, tocolysis and fetal monitoring follow the indication and local obstetric plan, not a universal anaesthetic prescription.
Transabdominal cerclage is a separate abdominal operation and has different future delivery/removal implications.

Removal of the uterus at or after delivery for uncontrollable haemorrhage or planned treatment of placenta accreta spectrum (PAS). Planned PAS surgery with a specialist multidisciplinary team differs from emergency hysterectomy for refractory postpartum bleeding.
A total or subtotal procedure may be chosen according to pathology, bleeding and anatomy; the diagram illustrates total hysterectomy after caesarean delivery.
Usually supine with uterine displacement before delivery; possible lithotomy for vaginal access. Maintain access to the airway, vascular lines and blood-product delivery.
Agree specialist surgical, anaesthetic, neonatal and blood-bank plans, or activate the emergency haemorrhage pathway.

Prepare reliable large-bore access, monitoring, warming, rapid transfusion and a critical-care destination. In planned PAS, review imaging, anticipated bladder involvement and conversion to general anaesthesia if starting neuraxially; in an emergency, resuscitation and source control run together.
Expose the uterus and deliver the baby if still pregnant, with the uterine incision selected to avoid the placenta where possible.

Coordinate delivery with the neonatal team and reassess haemodynamics immediately. For planned caesarean hysterectomy in PAS, leave the placenta in situ rather than attempting separation, which may trigger massive bleeding.
Develop distorted pelvic planes, identify ureters and bladder, and control vascular pedicles.

Bleeding may be sudden and extreme, especially with invasion near the bladder. Follow physiological response, measured losses, haemoglobin/coagulation and local major-haemorrhage guidance; correct hypothermia and monitor ionised calcium during transfusion.
Remove the uterus using the selected total or subtotal technique and repair associated injury if required.

Communicate ongoing bleeding, acidosis and vasoactive requirements. Pelvic vascular-control adjuncts are selected specialist measures, not guaranteed prevention of haemorrhage; their risks and monitoring needs should be discussed before use.
Secure haemostasis, close the vault or cervical stump as appropriate and transfer with an explicit organ-support plan.

Reassess coagulation, temperature, fluid balance and ventilation before extubation. Ongoing shock, large transfusion or organ injury may require critical care. Arrange thromboprophylaxis when safe, pain relief and sensitive follow-up after fertility loss and difficult birth.
Emergency induction in haemorrhagic shock
Placental separation in suspected PAS
Pelvic/bladder dissection and major haemorrhage
Transfusion-related hypocalcaemia and coagulopathy
Postoperative organ support

The recommendation to leave the placenta in situ concerns the caesarean-hysterectomy approach to PAS; it is not a instruction to leave every retained placenta untreated. Conservative PAS approaches are separate selected specialist pathways.
Neuraxial, general or combined strategies depend on anticipated bleeding, urgency and patient factors. No technique guarantees haemodynamic stability.
Total and subtotal hysterectomy have different distal anatomy. Quantified blood loss and repeated physiological assessment matter more than the qualitative High badge.
Gynaecology

Laparoscopic removal of an ovarian cyst while aiming to preserve viable ovarian tissue. Management depends on symptoms, imaging, fertility wishes and malignancy risk; not every cyst needs surgery. The operation may change to oophorectomy, laparotomy or an oncology pathway if anatomy or findings require it.
An emergency torsion pathway is not identical to elective cyst removal.
Supine or modified lithotomy with Trendelenburg as needed; secure the patient, protect pressure points and move both legs together.
Confirm imaging, pregnancy assessment where appropriate, malignancy-risk assessment and consent for possible change of approach or ovarian removal.

Review anaemia, pain, comorbidity and urgency. Vomiting or an acute abdomen changes aspiration risk; choose monitoring and blood availability from the patient and expected dissection rather than a routine day-case label.
Establish laparoscopic ports and pneumoperitoneum, position and inspect the pelvis.

Recheck tube, lines and ventilation after tilt. Insufflation may cause bradycardia, raised airway pressures or hypercapnia; severe instability also requires assessment for entry-related vascular injury.
Open the ovarian surface and develop the plane between the cyst wall and healthy ovarian tissue.

Maintain appropriate relaxation and perfusion while tracking bleeding. Adhesions and endometriosis may extend dissection close to bowel, ureter or vessels. Avoid assuming cyst rupture is benign: contents and malignancy risk matter.
Separate the cyst, retrieve it in a suitable bag, manage spillage if present and secure ovarian haemostasis.

Communicate blood loss and operative extension. Irrigation and specimen retrieval can prolong surgery; haemostasis must balance bleeding control with preservation of ovarian tissue. Conversion or oophorectomy is a surgical decision.
Reinspect the pelvis, remove ports and close; agree recovery and follow-up for histology.

Use multimodal analgesia and PONV prevention and assess bleeding and recovery before discharge. Worsening abdominal pain, fever, dizziness or instability warrants assessment for haemorrhage, visceral injury or other complications.
Laparoscopic entry injury
Pneumoperitoneum and head-down positioning
Cyst dissection and ovarian bleeding
Spillage or unexpected malignant features
The diagram shows local coronal anatomy and one preserved ovary; it is not a guarantee of ovarian preservation or a prediction of fertility.
Dermoid spillage can provoke chemical peritonitis; suspected malignancy requires appropriate specialist planning, not indiscriminate drainage.
Apply procedure-appropriate multimodal analgesia, nausea prevention and risk-based VTE prophylaxis. Emergency torsion or haemorrhage can invalidate an elective recovery pathway.

Removal of the uterus through the vagina for suitable benign disease, often alongside prolapse repair. The cervix is removed in a total vaginal hysterectomy; ovary/tube removal and pelvic-floor reconstruction are separate decisions.
Vaginal access avoids abdominal ports but does not eliminate bleeding, visceral injury or postoperative urinary problems.
Lithotomy with carefully supported legs and access for vaginal surgery; protect pressure points and avoid excessive hip flexion/abduction.
Confirm the indication, uterine size, prolapse and intended adnexal or pelvic-floor procedures; catheterise and expose the cervix.
Review anaemia, frailty, cardiopulmonary reserve and anticoagulants. Agree general versus regional anaesthesia, expected duration, blood availability and postoperative bladder-care needs.
Incise around the cervix, mobilise the bladder and enter the appropriate peritoneal planes.
Ensure adequate block/anaesthetic depth before traction; a vagal response is possible. Scarring from previous surgery can make bladder dissection difficult and increase injury risk.
Sequentially divide and secure supporting ligaments and uterine vascular pedicles.

Bleeding from deep pedicles can be concealed from direct anaesthetic view. Communicate suction/swab loss and haemodynamics; the ureters lie close to the operative field and require surgical protection.
Deliver and remove the uterus vaginally, completing any separately agreed adnexal procedure or prolapse repair.

Unexpected uterine size, adhesions or bleeding can prolong surgery or require another approach. Reassess position and block duration rather than assuming the original anaesthetic will remain adequate.
Check haemostasis, provide appropriate apical support and close the vaginal vault; confirm packs and postoperative drainage plans.

Record any vaginal pack and its removal plan. Provide multimodal analgesia, antiemesis and risk-based thromboprophylaxis; postoperative bleeding or urinary retention needs assessment before discharge.
Lithotomy-related pressure/nerve injury
Bladder mobilisation
Uterine pedicle bleeding and ureteric injury
Pack accounting and urinary recovery
Vaginal hysterectomy is not the same as vaginal prolapse repair alone, and the ovaries are not routinely removed solely because the uterus is removed.
Regional anaesthesia is an option when suitable, not a requirement. A more extensive repair or change of approach alters duration and recovery.
Support early mobilisation and oral intake as appropriate; escalating pain, bleeding, fever or oliguria warrants evaluation for complications.
Dermatology

Excision of a skin lesion for diagnosis or treatment, with closure selected for the defect: primary suture, local flap or graft. Margin and depth depend on diagnosis, site and oncological guidance; an ellipse in the diagram is not a universal cancer margin.
Most small procedures use local anaesthesia; larger, sensitive-site or complex reconstructions may require additional anaesthetic support.
Determined by lesion and reconstruction site; supine, lateral or prone. Plan airway access and pressure protection before draping.
Confirm lesion, site, consent and the intended excision/reconstruction, including histology and anticoagulant plans.

Assess comorbidity, anxiety, ability to remain still and whether sedation is really needed. Review bleeding and thrombosis risks individually; do not automatically stop prescribed antithrombotic treatment.
Mark the lesion and planned margins, prepare the field and infiltrate local anaesthetic or establish another agreed technique.

Reconcile local-anaesthetic type and cumulative dose from every operator/site. Inject incrementally with appropriate precautions and be ready to recognise systemic toxicity; sedation does not replace effective local analgesia.
Excise the lesion to the selected plane, orient the specimen and send it for histology.

Facial/scalp fields may bleed more than the Low badge suggests. Maintain verbal contact if awake and protect airway access when face drapes restrict visibility. The excision plane must follow pathology, not the schematic.
Achieve haemostasis and assess defect size, tension and the choice of primary closure, local flap or skin graft.
Electrosurgery requires fire precautions, especially with oxygen near the face. Larger reconstruction may need more infiltration, time or a change of anaesthetic plan; record every additional dose.
Complete reconstruction and dress the wound; provide bleeding, wound-care and pathology follow-up plans.

Confirm recovery after any sedation and appropriate escort/discharge arrangements. Give instructions for persistent bleeding, expanding haematoma, infection or compromised flap/graft; histology may require further treatment.
Correct-site marking and pathology-dependent margins
Cumulative local-anaesthetic exposure
Facial oxygen/electrosurgery fire risk
Postoperative bleeding and reconstruction viability
The illustration shows primary closure of one small defect; it does not prescribe a melanoma margin or cover every flap/graft technique.
Small skin surgery usually does not need general anaesthesia. Sedation requires monitoring and rescue capability appropriate to its depth, particularly when airway access is limited.
Larger oncological resections and complex reconstruction can have materially greater bleeding and physiological risk than a minor lesion excision.

Staged skin-cancer excision with mapped microscopic assessment of peripheral and deep margins, aiming to conserve uninvolved tissue. Further tissue is removed from mapped positive areas until clearance, then reconstruction is planned.
Used for selected cancers and sites; it is not interchangeable with a routine excision or an automatic indication for every skin cancer.
Usually awake with local anaesthesia, positioned for the lesion site and repeated access. Allow comfort and pressure protection during waiting periods.
Confirm the diagnosis, lesion/site and appropriateness for Mohs; explain repeated stages, waiting periods and reconstruction options.

Review ability to tolerate a potentially lengthy awake procedure, anxiety and comorbidity. Make an individual antithrombotic plan; medically necessary treatment is not routinely stopped simply because skin surgery is planned.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic, debulk as appropriate and remove the first thin layer with orientation and mapping.

Account for all local-anaesthetic doses, including any later reconstruction. Assess analgesia before cutting; communicate vasoconstrictor use and watch for toxicity rather than relying on a single injection being small.
Process and examine mapped peripheral/deep margins microscopically while protecting the wound.

Maintain comfort, hydration appropriate to the planned anaesthetic and clear communication during waiting. If sedation is used, monitoring continues during processing; its risks do not disappear when surgery pauses.
Excise further tissue only from mapped positive regions and repeat microscopy until margins are clear.

Duration and final defect size are unpredictable. Reconcile additional infiltration, bleeding and patient tolerance at each pass; a new anaesthetic plan may be required for extended or complex reconstruction.
After clearance, reconstruct by the selected closure/flap/graft or arrange delayed repair; dress and plan follow-up.

Agree whether reconstruction stays under local anaesthesia or needs theatre support. With facial surgery, manage oxygen/electrosurgery fire risk and airway access. Give bleeding and wound-care advice and reassess discharge after sedation.
Mapped specimen orientation and margin assessment
Repeated infiltration and cumulative local-anaesthetic dose
Unpredictable duration/defect size
Facial reconstruction and airway/fire precautions
Five teaching stages do not mean five excision passes. The fourth stage may repeat; the positive sector shown in the diagram is illustrative, not a patient result.
Microscopic margin control conserves tissue but does not promise freedom from recurrence. Diagnosis, histology, site and patient factors determine the treatment pathway.
Most Mohs procedures use local anaesthesia without an anaesthetist; anaesthetic input is particularly relevant to sedation, difficult positioning, severe comorbidity or substantial reconstruction.
General & GI

Removal of the rectum, anal canal and sphincter complex with an end colostomy, usually for low rectal cancer when sphincter preservation is unsuitable. Unlike anterior resection, there is no colorectal anastomosis and the colostomy is permanent.
Open, laparoscopic and robotic abdominal approaches and conventional or extralevator perineal excision vary by tumour and team.
Abdominal phase supine or Lloyd-Davies/lithotomy; perineal phase in lithotomy or prone jackknife. Two-team simultaneous surgery or repositioning may be used.
Confirm operative extent, marked colostomy site and perineal positioning; establish abdominal access and explore.

Assess anaemia, nutrition, frailty and effects of neoadjuvant treatment. Agree blood availability, analgesia, monitoring and postoperative destination. Secure the airway and lines before head-down tilt or a later prone turn.
Mobilise the sigmoid/left colon and divide selected mesenteric vessels, protecting the ureters and autonomic nerves.

Pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg affect ventilation and venous return. Titrate fluids and vasoactive support to perfusion, avoiding both overload and hypovolaemia; watch for vascular or splenic injury during mobilisation.
Dissect the rectum and mesorectum through the pelvis to meet the planned perineal plane.

Deep pelvic and presacral venous bleeding can be abrupt. Communicate suction loss and haemodynamics; prolonged lithotomy requires careful leg support, pressure protection and vigilance for well-leg compartment syndrome.
Perform perineal excision of anus and sphincters, with levator excision where indicated; remove the specimen.

If turning prone, coordinate the turn, recheck tube, ventilation, eyes and lines, and keep the abdomen free of compression. Perineal dissection adds bleeding and pain; flap reconstruction, if needed, extends the operation.
Close or reconstruct the perineal defect, mature the end colostomy and close the abdomen.

Provide analgesia for both abdominal and perineal wounds. Reassess temperature, haemostasis and airway oedema before extubation; arrange stoma support, VTE prevention and an appropriate recovery/critical-care plan.
Presacral or pelvic haemorrhage
Lithotomy-related nerve injury and well-leg compartment syndrome
Airway/line security during prone repositioning
Two operative wounds and possible flap reconstruction
Elective enhanced recovery includes nutritional/anaemia optimisation, multimodal analgesia, individualised fluids and early mobilisation; emergency obstruction or sepsis changes this plan.
APR permanently separates stool passage from the perineum: there is no colorectal join to leak, but pelvic collections, wound breakdown, urinary dysfunction and stoma complications remain possible.
Neuraxial analgesia depends on surgical approach, coagulation, anticoagulants and local expertise; it is not mandatory for every APR.
Resection of the caecum, ascending colon and a variable portion of transverse colon with terminal ileum, commonly for cancer. Continuity is usually restored with an ileocolic anastomosis.
Extended resections remove more transverse colon; emergency ischaemia, obstruction or perforation may require a stoma or staged reconstruction instead.
Usually supine, with tilt adjusted for laparoscopic/robotic exposure; open surgery uses a suitable abdominal incision.
Explore the abdomen and establish open or minimally invasive access.

Assess anaemia, bowel preparation-related dehydration and obstruction. Decide aspiration precautions from the clinical state; pneumoperitoneum can cause bradycardia, raised airway pressures and hypercapnia.
Mobilise the right colon and hepatic flexure, protecting the duodenum, right ureter and retroperitoneal structures.

Maintain relaxation and reassess ventilation after tilt. Mobilisation can injure adjacent structures; unexpected blood loss or instability needs immediate discussion rather than assuming an insufflation effect.
Divide the ileocolic pedicle and other vessels required by the planned resection; complete mesenteric division.
Dissection is close to major mesenteric veins, so bleeding may be sudden. Monitor perfusion and temperature and communicate significant haemodynamic changes during vessel division.
Divide terminal ileum and colon, remove the specimen and form an ileocolic anastomosis when appropriate.

Assess blood loss and perfusion before reconstruction; avoid both excessive fluids and undue restriction. A stapled or sutured, intracorporeal or extracorporeal join may be used; unstable emergency patients may need a different strategy.
Inspect haemostasis and bowel viability, close incisions and agree postoperative care.

Use approach-appropriate multimodal analgesia and PONV prevention. Plan early feeding/mobilisation as tolerated; escalating pain, tachycardia, fever or organ dysfunction warrants assessment for leak, bleeding or sepsis.
Aspiration risk in obstructed patients
Mesenteric vascular bleeding
Pneumoperitoneum and tilt
Physiological suitability for anastomosis
Right hemicolectomy usually joins ileum to colon, not colon to rectum. Resection extent and vessel ligation depend on pathology and anatomy.

Elective ERAS principles include optimisation, opioid-sparing analgesia, individualised balanced fluids and early recovery; invasive monitoring and critical care depend on risk rather than the operation name.
Open surgery may benefit from thoracic epidural where appropriate; routine epidural use is not recommended for laparoscopic colorectal surgery.

Removal of the descending colon with variable distal transverse/sigmoid colon, commonly for cancer. Reconstruction may be colocolic or colorectal depending on the remaining bowel; the diagram shows one colorectal reconstruction.
This is not synonymous with low anterior resection, and it does not necessarily involve total mesorectal excision.
Supine or modified lithotomy, with tilt adjusted for minimally invasive exposure and access needed for reconstruction.
Explore and establish open, laparoscopic or robotic access; assess disease and planned resection.
Assess hydration, anaemia and cardiorespiratory reserve. Use aspiration precautions where obstruction is present; secure the patient and airway before tilt.
Mobilise descending colon and, where needed, splenic flexure, protecting the left ureter and spleen.
Splenic capsular injury can produce unexpected bleeding. Adjust ventilation for pneumoperitoneum/tilt and protect pressure points; track lithotomy duration when legs are elevated.
Divide the required vascular pedicles and mesentery, preserving adequate supply to the retained bowel.

Vessel division may cause significant blood loss. Support systemic perfusion without fluid overload; surgical assessment of bowel viability remains essential and cannot be inferred from normal blood pressure alone.
Divide and remove affected colon; construct a tension-free colocolic or colorectal join if clinically suitable.
Communicate hypothermia, acidosis, vasopressor needs and bleeding before reconstruction. Anastomotic assessment and any protective stoma are surgical decisions based on local and systemic risk.
Assess haemostasis and anastomosis as appropriate, close and implement the postoperative plan.

Tailor analgesia to incision and approach, minimise opioid-related ileus, and monitor recovery for bleeding, ileus, anastomotic leak and sepsis. Critical-care admission depends on physiology and risk.
Splenic injury during flexure mobilisation
Mesenteric bleeding
Positioning injury during prolonged surgery
Anastomotic perfusion and tension
The retained bowel determines whether the join is colocolic or colorectal; the illustrated configuration is not universal.
Apply elective colorectal enhanced recovery where appropriate, including early feeding and mobilisation, VTE prevention and tailored fluids; emergency contamination or shock changes priorities.
Distinguish left hemicolectomy from Hartmann's procedure: Hartmann leaves a closed distal stump and end colostomy rather than a primary join.

Resection of diseased sigmoid/rectosigmoid colon, closure of the distal rectal stump and formation of an end colostomy without a primary anastomosis. Often used for perforated diverticulitis or other high-risk emergency colorectal disease, but not the default for every perforation.
Restoration of continuity is a separate later operation and is not guaranteed.
Supine or modified lithotomy; often open abdominal access in unstable patients, with minimally invasive approaches in selected cases.
Resuscitate and prepare for source control; explore the abdomen and identify perforation, contamination or obstruction.

Give indicated antibiotics promptly and manage hypovolaemia/sepsis alongside urgent surgery. Plan induction for aspiration risk and possible cardiovascular collapse, including appropriate monitoring and vasoactive support.
Mobilise affected sigmoid/rectosigmoid bowel and identify/protect ureters within inflamed tissue.
Inflammation distorts tissue planes and may increase blood loss. Track haemodynamics, temperature, urine output and acid-base trends, interpreting them together rather than using one target alone.
Control mesenteric vessels and resect the diseased bowel to suitable margins.
Communicate escalating vasopressor needs, coagulopathy, acidosis and hypothermia. In extreme instability, abbreviated damage-control surgery may supersede completing the planned procedure.
Close the distal rectal stump and bring viable proximal colon to an end-colostomy site; do not form a primary join.
Maintain perfusion and reassess losses. A closed rectal stump can still leak and cause pelvic sepsis; absence of an anastomosis does not eliminate postoperative intra-abdominal complications.
Complete source control, mature the colostomy, close when appropriate and transfer with a clear postoperative plan.

Reassess ventilation, perfusion and organ support before deciding on extubation. High-risk septic patients may require ongoing critical care; hand over antibiotics, fluid balance, vasoactive drugs and concerns about source-control adequacy.
Induction in shock or bowel obstruction
Dissection through inflamed planes and bleeding
Adequacy of source control

WSES 2020 recommends Hartmann for diffuse diverticular peritonitis in critically ill patients and selected patients with multiple comorbidities; the recommendation is strong but based on low-quality evidence. Selected stable patients may instead undergo primary anastomosis with or without diversion.
A later reversal requires reassessment of fitness and pelvic anatomy; many patients retain a permanent stoma. Do not promise reversal.

Balance rapid source control with resuscitation, multimodal analgesia, VTE prevention and stoma care. Elective fasting/carbohydrate pathways are not automatically appropriate for obstructed or septic emergency patients.

A hysteroscope passes through the cervix into a fluid-distended uterine cavity. Polyps or selected submucosal fibroids are removed using mechanical or electrosurgical instruments. Larger/deeper fibroids may need staged treatment; a diagnostic outpatient hysteroscopy is a different procedure.
Lithotomy, with both legs moved together; protect pressure points and allow continuous access to fluid-balance monitoring.
Assess the lesion, bleeding/anaemia, pregnancy exclusion, comorbidities and intended distension medium; agree fluid-deficit stop limits.

Distinguish saline used with bipolar/mechanical systems from electrolyte-free media used with some monopolar systems. Tailor limits to cardiac/renal reserve; the surgeon and anaesthetist must agree them before starting.
Establish the agreed anaesthesia, position in lithotomy, dilate the cervix if required and introduce the hysteroscope.
General, regional or selected local techniques depend on procedure and patient. Cervical manipulation can cause vagal bradycardia; perforation can occur during dilation or insertion.
Distend and inspect the uterine cavity, identifying the lesion and tubal ostia.
Track inflow minus recovered outflow continuously, including spillage. A measured deficit is not identical to intravascular absorption. Use the lowest distension pressure compatible with visibility.
Resect the polyp or fibroid under direct vision and retrieve tissue for histology.

Opened venous channels allow intravasation. Saline overload can cause pulmonary oedema; hypotonic media can also cause hyponatraemia. Suspect perforation or vascular gas embolism with sudden hypotension, hypoxaemia or an abrupt capnography change.
Check haemostasis and final fluid deficit, withdraw instruments and plan recovery or escalation.

Communicate the medium, deficit and any suspected injury. New breathlessness, confusion, hypoxaemia or instability requires assessment for overload, electrolyte disturbance, haemorrhage or perforation rather than routine discharge.
Cervical entry — perforation or vagal response
Intravasation through opened uterine vessels
Abrupt cardiorespiratory deterioration — gas embolism or bleeding
Final fluid reconciliation and recovery assessment
Fluid-deficit limits are stop/escalation safeguards, not quantities known to be safe for an individual patient. Avoid treating every recorded deficit as absorbed fluid.
This entry covers transcervical intrauterine surgery, not laparoscopic hysterectomy. Confirm equipment, electrosurgical mode, medium and local emergency pathway at the brief.
Urology

A resectoscope enters through the urethra and removes visible bladder tumour with tissue for pathological staging, often including detrusor muscle where appropriate. Lateral-wall electrosurgery can stimulate the obturator nerve and cause an abrupt adductor contraction.
Tumour burden and repeat/re-staging procedures vary.
Lithotomy with protected legs and pressure points; urinary drainage and irrigation remain accessible.
Review tumour site/size, haematuria, anaemia, anticoagulants, infection and the resection plan.
Identify a lateral-wall tumour before choosing anaesthesia. Agree how to prevent obturator-mediated leg movement; neuraxial anaesthesia alone does not reliably block this reflex.
Establish anaesthesia, position and insert the resectoscope through the urethra.

General anaesthesia with adequate neuromuscular block or regional anaesthesia with selected obturator nerve block may be used according to the plan. Avoid assuming immobility because the patient is unconscious.
Survey the bladder under irrigation, locating tumour, ureteric orifices and the intended resection margins.
Avoid overdistension and track irrigation losses. Bipolar saline avoids the classic hypotonic-medium mechanism but does not eliminate fluid overload or extravasation.
Resect tumour and obtain appropriate base/deep tissue for staging, then coagulate bleeding points.

An obturator jerk can drive the loop through the bladder wall. Stop and reassess sudden leg movement, abdominal distension, pain in an awake patient, or unexplained instability; perforation may be intraperitoneal or extraperitoneal.
Confirm haemostasis, retrieve specimens and establish drainage; decide whether immediate intravesical treatment is appropriate.

Suspected perforation or bleeding requiring irrigation changes the postoperative plan and can contraindicate immediate intravesical chemotherapy. Handover haematuria, catheter/irrigation requirements and any suspected injury.
Lateral-wall resection — obturator jerk
Bladder perforation and irrigation extravasation
Haemostasis and postoperative clot retention
Low blood-loss risk is a qualitative badge: large, vascular or extensive tumours can bleed substantially. Differentiate TURBT from prostate resection rather than copying a TURP plan.
Coordinate analgesia, nausea prevention and monitoring with the intended day-case or inpatient pathway; persistent bleeding, pain or physiological change needs reassessment.
Breast & Plastics

Non-viable burned tissue is excised to a suitable wound bed and covered with a thin autologous skin graft, often meshed. The donor retains part of its dermis so it can heal. Large burns commonly need staged operations; temporary coverage may be used when definitive autograft is not yet feasible.
Depends on burn and donor sites; supine, lateral or prone. Plan turning, pressure protection and secure airway/vascular access before draping.
Review burn extent/depth, time since injury, inhalation injury, resuscitation, organ function, infection and donor sites.

The early shock phase and later hypermetabolic phase differ. Assess airway oedema or contracture, available access, haemoglobin and blood availability; small grafts do not share the risk of extensive excision.
Establish anaesthesia, position and warm the patient; prepare recipient and donor sites.

Large exposed surfaces create substantial heat loss. Warm fluids and theatre measures must remain compatible with skin injury and fire safety. Altered drug responses and repeated anaesthetics require individual assessment.
Excise eschar tangentially or to the selected deeper plane; achieve haemostasis.

Diffuse wound bleeding can be rapid and underestimated in soaked swabs/drapes. Reconcile losses, perfusion, haemoglobin and coagulation with the team; local adrenaline or tourniquet measures do not replace monitoring.
Harvest partial-thickness donor skin, mesh if selected, and apply/fix the graft to the prepared bed.
The donor site adds pain and bleeding. Maintain perfusion and temperature without indiscriminate fluid loading; consider appropriate regional/local analgesia as part of a multimodal plan.
Dress graft and donor sites, protect immobilisation and transfer with a recovery/critical-care plan.

Handover blood products, fluid balance, temperature, analgesia and graft positioning. Major burns, inhalation injury or ongoing instability may require continued ventilation and critical care rather than immediate extubation.
Airway control with inhalation injury or contracture
Excision — deceptively rapid blood loss
Extensive exposure — hypothermia
Transfer and dressing-related positioning requirements
Burn resuscitation formulae are starting guides, not automatic intraoperative replacement prescriptions; use measured physiological endpoints and the burns-team plan.

Suxamethonium can cause dangerous hyperkalaemia after burn-related receptor upregulation; avoid its use outside the immediate acute window and follow specialist guidance. Resistance to non-depolarising relaxants may develop; use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring.
Graft and donor-site pain are distinct from background burn pain. Agree dressing-change analgesia, nutrition and rehabilitation with the specialist team.
Oral & Maxillofacial

Planned osteotomies reposition the maxilla and mandible to correct skeletal jaw relationships. A Le Fort I mobilises the maxilla; bilateral sagittal splits mobilise the tooth-bearing mandible. Splints/temporary fixation establish occlusion before plates secure the new position. Jaw order, movements and additions vary.
Supine with supported head and agreed head-up tilt; protect eyes, teeth and nerves. The surgeon shares the airway and needs dental occlusion.
Review airway, jaw anatomy, OSA, nasal patency, imaging, orthodontic plan and anticipated blood loss.

Agree nasal versus alternative airway access and postoperative fixation/rescue plans. Restricted oral opening or abnormal craniofacial anatomy may alter airway strategy; elective nasal intubation is not automatically safe in every patient.
Secure the agreed airway, protect pressure points and expose intraoral tissues.

Fix the tube away from the operative field and recheck it after movement. A throat pack is not routine; if selected, record insertion/removal. Local vasoconstrictors require dose communication and haemodynamic observation.
Perform Le Fort I maxillary mobilisation and bilateral sagittal mandibular splits in the planned order.

Maxillary/pterygoid bleeding can be brisk. Monitor blood loss and be ready for trigeminocardiac bradycardia during manipulation. A field-quality strategy must not compromise cerebral or systemic perfusion.
Reposition the jaw segments using the occlusal splint; apply temporary intermaxillary fixation and secure plates/screws.
Dental fixation removes oral airway access. Know how fixation will be released in an emergency; coordinate tube position and any release before extubation.
Check haemostasis and occlusion, remove any pack, suction under direct vision and implement the agreed extubation plan.

Blood, facial swelling, nasal obstruction and residual sedation can compromise breathing. Selected high-risk patients need delayed extubation. Ensure fixation-release equipment, antiemesis and trained postoperative staff.
Shared-airway access and tube protection
Maxillary mobilisation — bleeding or trigeminocardiac reflex
Intermaxillary fixation — loss of oral access
Extubation with swelling and altered jaw anatomy
The diagram is a local lateral teaching view, not a blueprint for osteotomy angles or a complete vascular map. Genioplasty and other adjuncts alter the sequence.

Use multimodal analgesia and nausea prevention, especially if elastics/fixation remain. Postoperative airway strategy must account for OSA and the direction of jaw movement, not just procedure duration.
ENT & Head and Neck

Removal of the entire larynx, usually for cancer, permanently separates the trachea from the pharynx. The trachea is sutured to the neck skin as an end stoma; the pharynx is closed for swallowing. Neck dissection or flap reconstruction may be added.
Partial laryngectomy preserves different anatomy and is not covered by this sequence.
Supine, head supported with agreed neck extension; protect irradiated or restricted cervical tissues and maintain access to the airway and lines.
Review endoscopy/imaging, tumour obstruction, prior radiotherapy, nutrition and the resection/reconstruction plan; agree primary and rescue airway strategies.

Stridor, a friable tumour or restricted neck/mouth opening can make induction hazardous. An awake approach or awake surgical airway may be appropriate after specialist assessment; avoid assuming a standard asleep oral intubation will be safe.
Establish anaesthesia and the agreed airway; expose the neck and perform neck dissection if indicated.

Secure the tube away from the field and keep rescue access available. Assess access/arterial monitoring and blood availability by anticipated extent; previous radiotherapy increases technical difficulty.
Mobilise the larynx, divide the trachea and transfer ventilation to a sterile cuffed tube through the distal trachea.

Explicitly coordinate the airway handover. Protect the cuff from cutting instruments; use airway-fire precautions around an open oxygenated trachea. Confirm sustained waveform capnography, depth and fixation before abandoning the previous airway.
Remove the larynx, close or reconstruct the pharyngeal defect, and mature the permanent tracheal end stoma; a voice prosthesis may be placed.

After separation, mouth/nose oxygen and oral intubation cannot reach the lungs. Check stomal-tube depth to avoid endobronchial placement; flap reconstruction adds prolonged surgery, perfusion and donor-site considerations.
Complete haemostasis, drains and airway checks; transfer with a laryngectomy-specific handover and bedhead sign.

Oxygenation, suction and any ventilation are through the stoma. Ensure humidification, suitable emergency equipment and trained staff. Monitor bleeding, plugging and swelling; do not remove a TEP voice prosthesis during routine airway troubleshooting.
Induction with a potentially obstructed tumour airway
Tracheal division and transfer of ventilation
Permanent loss of mouth-to-lung connection
Postoperative stoma obstruction or bleeding
A total laryngectomy is not a tracheostomy: the upper airway no longer connects to the lungs. If anatomy is uncertain in an emergency, oxygenate face and stoma until clarified.
Plan multimodal analgesia, nutrition, communication support and postoperative care with the head-and-neck team. Pharyngocutaneous fistula and wound problems are later surgical concerns.
These are typical high-level stages, not a dissection guide; combined neck dissection/flap work changes duration and blood-loss risk. Emergency recommendations follow NTSP.
Resection of part or all of the tongue for cancer. A small accessible defect may be closed directly; larger defects can need regional or free-flap reconstruction, sometimes with neck dissection.
The extent and location of resection determine airway, swallowing and speech consequences; total tongue resection is not equivalent to a small partial glossectomy.
Supine with head supported; oral access and tube route agreed before draping. A flap donor site may need simultaneous access and careful limb positioning.
Review tumour site/extent, mouth opening, endoscopy/imaging, bleeding, swallowing, aspiration risk, nutrition and prior radiotherapy.

Agree the primary airway and rescue plan with the surgeon. Large tongue/base-of-tongue lesions can obstruct ventilation and be damaged by instrumentation; consider awake airway management in an at-risk patient.
Secure the airway using the agreed route and expose the oral cavity; elective tracheostomy may be performed for extensive surgery.
Nasal intubation can improve oral access when appropriate, but is not mandatory or suitable for every case. Plan postoperative airway protection before resection, not after swelling appears.
Resect the involved tongue with oncological margins; control lingual vessels and perform neck dissection if indicated.

Bleeding can be brisk and enter the shared airway. Track suction losses and haemoglobin by clinical need; recheck the tube after retractors or head movements. Margins and resection extent are surgical decisions.
Close the defect or reconstruct with a flap; free-flap vessels are joined to recipient neck vessels and perfusion assessed.

Maintain temperature, oxygenation and adequate perfusion without indiscriminate fluid loading. Goal-directed fluids and judicious vasopressors may be appropriate; protect donor-site pressure points and communicate perfusion concerns.
Check haemostasis and the reconstructed airway; recover with planned tracheostomy care, delayed extubation or selected immediate extubation.

Tongue/floor-of-mouth oedema, flap bulk and haematoma can obstruct the airway and make reintubation difficult. Extubation requires an assessed rescue plan and appropriate monitoring; no single strategy suits all resections.
Initial airway control with a friable or obstructing tumour
Lingual vessel bleeding in a shared airway
Flap reperfusion and prolonged reconstruction
Postoperative obstruction from oedema, flap bulk or haematoma

Tracheostomy is not routine for every small partial glossectomy, but may be essential for extensive or high-risk resections; evidence from selected reconstruction cohorts cannot override individual assessment.
Plan opioid-sparing analgesia, aspiration precautions, enteral nutrition and speech/swallow rehabilitation with the multidisciplinary team.
Blood loss and care requirements rise with neck dissection, extensive resection and free-flap reconstruction; the moderate-risk badge is qualitative, not a predicted volume.

A rigid suspension laryngoscope exposes the larynx for magnified inspection, biopsy or treatment of vocal-fold lesions. Cold instruments or a laser may be used. The surgeon and anaesthetist share the same narrow airway; stenosis or an obstructing lesion can make a short procedure high risk.
Supine in an individually suitable laryngoscopy position; protect teeth, lips, eyes and cervical spine. Suspension limits airway access.
Review airway symptoms, endoscopy, lesion/stenosis, respiratory reserve and cervical/dental issues; agree surgical and ventilation plans.

Stridor and severe obstruction demand specialist planning, including rescue access and whether spontaneous breathing should initially be preserved. Select a small tube or a specialist tubeless technique according to lesion, access and team expertise.
Induce anaesthesia using the agreed approach and establish ventilation; protect teeth and insert the suspension laryngoscope.

Insertion is strongly stimulating. TIVA is often useful for open-airway techniques; muscle relaxation depends on the strategy. Reassess ventilation and tube/catheter position after suspension rather than assuming the airway is unchanged.
Inspect the larynx under magnification and perform biopsy or the planned lesion treatment.

A small tracheal tube may restrict surgical access and increase resistance. Tubeless approaches need explicit oxygenation, ventilation and rescue plans; oxygen insufflation alone does not guarantee carbon-dioxide clearance.
If jet ventilation or laser treatment is selected, apply its dedicated safety plan throughout treatment.
Jet ventilation requires unobstructed expiration: impaired egress can cause gas trapping and barotrauma. Monitor oxygenation and CO2 by methods appropriate to the technique.

For laser use, choose wavelength-appropriate laser-resistant equipment when a tube is used, minimise oxidiser enrichment as safely feasible, avoid nitrous oxide and coordinate ignition/oxygen delivery. Tubeless oxygen also carries fire risk.
Secure haemostasis, remove instruments and reassess the airway before emergence and recovery.

Look for bleeding, oedema or residual obstruction; suction appropriately and agree extubation or continued airway support. Watch for laryngospasm, stridor, hypoventilation and barotrauma; recovery/discharge depends on airway status, not just procedure length.
Induction with laryngeal obstruction
Suspension — restricted access or displaced tube
Jet ventilation — inadequate expiration and barotrauma
Laser activation — airway fire
Emergence — laryngospasm or oedema
Small-tube ventilation, intermittent apnoea, spontaneous ventilation and jet ventilation are alternatives with different limitations; none is a default for all lesions.
Jet pressures, frequencies and apnoea intervals require specialist equipment and patient-specific protocols, not values inferred from this summary.

For suspected airway fire, stop surgery and oxidiser delivery, remove burning airway material and extinguish with saline/water, then re-establish ventilation and assess injury according to the local emergency protocol.
Paediatric
Removal of diseased teeth, sometimes alongside restorations, during one general anaesthetic. The dental team and anaesthetist share the airway; the extent of treatment is agreed before starting.
Supine with head supported; dental access, tube route and table rotation agreed with the team.
Review the dental plan, consent, medical history, fasting and airway; agree recovery and discharge arrangements.
Assess age, respiratory illness, obstructive sleep apnoea and comorbidities. Complex or high-risk children need an appropriate paediatric service, not simply a longer routine day-case slot.
Induce anaesthesia and secure an airway compatible with the dental work; nasal tracheal intubation is common when suitable.
The airway is shared and may become inaccessible. Confirm tube position, fixation and the rescue plan; nasal instrumentation can itself cause bleeding.
Examine the teeth; extract the planned teeth, with local anaesthetic and restorative treatment where indicated.
Record all local anaesthetic administered by both teams to avoid cumulative toxicity. Suction blood and debris; communicate before moving the head or applying instruments near the tube.
Achieve socket haemostasis and clear the mouth; confirm removal of any throat pack used.
A throat pack is not automatically required. If used, its insertion and removal must be explicitly recorded and checked; do not rely on a pack to replace airway protection or suction.
Recover the airway and observe until appropriate for discharge.
Anticipate laryngospasm, obstruction, pain, nausea and bleeding. Choose the extubation strategy by aspiration and airway risk; give carers clear bleeding, hydration and analgesia advice.
Airway instrumentation and restricted access
Blood/debris during extraction
Pack-removal check if used
Emergence — laryngospasm or obstruction
Blood loss is usually small but must be judged against the child's size and extent of surgery.
Coordinate multimodal analgesia and antiemetics without duplicating drugs given by the dental team.
Service guidance supports the care setting; it does not prescribe the extraction technique.

Removal of the foreskin for an agreed indication. This entry concerns hospital surgery in children, not neonatal bedside device circumcision; technique and anaesthesia depend on age and clinical circumstances.
Supine, with warming and modesty maintained; local access without excessive leg abduction.
Confirm indication, consent and operative plan, including anatomical abnormalities and bleeding history.
Assess age, prematurity, respiratory illness and day-case suitability; postoperative respiratory observation is individualised.
Provide anaesthesia and analgesia: commonly general anaesthesia with a penile/ring block or another agreed regional technique.
Selected infants may have spinal anaesthesia in experienced services. Track total local anaesthetic across all injections; a block does not remove the need for respiratory monitoring.
Prepare the field, release adhesions as required and excise the foreskin using the planned technique.
Check that analgesia is adequate before incision. Surgical methods vary; this is not a cutting or block-placement guide.
Control bleeding, suture skin edges and apply the planned dressing.
Persistent bleeding warrants surgical reassessment, even when the expected blood loss is low. Avoid assuming a distressed child only has pain.
Recover and provide wound, pain and urinary advice.
Plan opioid-sparing analgesia; review bleeding and ability to pass urine according to the service's discharge pathway. Former preterm infants may need extended observation.
Regional/local injection — cumulative dose
Incision before block onset
Bleeding and postoperative urinary problems
General, local and neuraxial approaches are not interchangeable in every child.
Use age- and risk-appropriate recovery arrangements; no universal discharge time is set here.

Closure of a patent processus vaginalis causing an indirect hernia. Open herniotomy or laparoscopic closure may be used; routine childhood repair usually does not require the mesh reinforcement used in adults.
Supine; open groin exposure or laparoscopic abdominal ports.
Confirm side, reducibility, urgency and evidence of incarceration or compromised bowel.
An incarcerated hernia can bring dehydration, obstruction and aspiration risk; it is not equivalent to a well elective infant. Assess prematurity and respiratory risk.
Induce anaesthesia or establish an agreed regional technique in a selected infant.
An awake spinal approach can reduce some early respiratory events but does not abolish postoperative apnoea risk; sedation and conversion plans matter.
Open approach: expose and separate the sac from cord structures. Laparoscopic approach: inspect the internal ring and hernia contents.
Maintain warmth. Laparoscopic insufflation affects ventilation and venous return; communicate pressure and positioning concerns rather than applying adult assumptions.
Reduce contents and close the sac neck/internal ring while protecting adjacent structures.
If bowel is compromised, the operation and postoperative needs may expand. Contralateral inspection or repair is an individual surgical decision, not automatic.
Close and recover with a risk-based respiratory and analgesia plan.
Former preterm and young infants may need monitored admission. Observe for apnoea irrespective of apparently uncomplicated surgery or the anaesthetic technique.
Incarceration — possible obstruction
Infant induction or regional conversion
Pneumoperitoneum if laparoscopic
Postoperative apnoea risk
Adult hernia guidance and routine mesh repair should not be transferred to infants.
Regional analgesia and local infiltration can reduce opioid requirements; discharge depends on infant risk and local policy.
Cardiothoracic

Repair of native valve leaflets/chordae and often the annulus, or replacement with a prosthesis. Sternotomy and minimally invasive approaches differ; this entry does not cover transcatheter edge-to-edge repair.
Supine for sternotomy; modified supine for right mini-thoracotomy, with peripheral cannulation access if planned.
Review lesion, ventricular and right-heart function, pulmonary pressures and the operative approach; establish monitoring and anaesthesia.
Mitral stenosis and regurgitation have different haemodynamic priorities. Avoid generic valve targets; assess rhythm, filling and cardiac output using the actual lesion and physiology.
Expose the heart, anticoagulate and cannulate for cardiopulmonary bypass; clamp the aorta and give cardioplegia.
Confirm anticoagulation and bypass readiness. Peripheral cannulation adds limb/vascular risks; minimally invasive work may require lung isolation and makes airway access harder.
Open the left atrium and repair or replace the valve.
Coordinate perfusion, temperature and blood conservation. Repair may use a ring and leaflet/chordal techniques; the chosen repair is not represented by one universal sequence.
Close, de-air, release the clamp and separate from bypass with transoesophageal echocardiographic assessment.

Assess residual regurgitation/gradient, ventricular function and complications such as systolic anterior motion after repair. Troubleshoot low output with the surgeon and perfusionist rather than treating every cause alike.
Reverse anticoagulation when agreed, achieve haemostasis and transfer to cardiac critical care.
Plan bleeding surveillance, rhythm/pacing and ventilatory support. Postoperative antithrombotic treatment depends on repair versus prosthesis, rhythm and the cardiology/surgical plan.
Induction in severe valve disease
Cannulation and anticoagulation
De-airing and separation from bypass
Residual valve dysfunction or low output
High bleeding risk reflects bypass and major cardiac surgery, not a predicted transfusion requirement.
TOE use requires expertise and assessment of contraindications; minimally invasive and sternotomy pathways differ.

Removal of an entire lung, usually for malignancy. This is more physiologically demanding than lobectomy; postoperative reserve, right-heart load and protection of the remaining lung dominate planning.
Lateral decubitus with the operative side uppermost; approach may be open or minimally invasive.
Confirm resection extent and cardiopulmonary fitness, including predicted postoperative lung function and exercise assessment when indicated.
Review right ventricular function, pulmonary hypertension and previous treatment; a completion pneumonectomy can be especially complex. Agree analgesia and postoperative care before induction.
Induce anaesthesia, establish lung isolation and position laterally.
Confirm device position bronchoscopically and recheck after positioning. Protect dependent pressure points and ensure access to the airway and vascular lines.
Enter the chest and dissect the hilum, dividing pulmonary vessels and the main bronchus in the surgeon's chosen sequence.
Anticipate major vascular bleeding and hypoxaemia during one-lung ventilation. Communicate before vessel occlusion; protect the ventilated lung and investigate sudden haemodynamic change.
Remove the lung and check bronchial stump closure, haemostasis and the surgical drainage plan.
Stump tests require coordinated ventilation. Drain management after pneumonectomy is procedure-specific; do not automatically apply lobectomy suction practices.
Close, restore two-airway communication as appropriate and recover for close respiratory/cardiac surveillance.
Use careful, individualised fluid management to avoid both hypoperfusion and remaining-lung oedema. Watch for respiratory deterioration, arrhythmias and right-heart dysfunction.
One-lung ventilation — hypoxaemia
Hilar vessel division — major bleeding
Bronchial stump and drainage plan
Remaining-lung injury and postoperative arrhythmia
Avoid fluid overload; a rigid fluid volume is not prescribed by this summary.
Analgesia must allow effective breathing and coughing without excessive sedation. Planned recovery location reflects physiological risk, not operation name alone.

A small gastric pouch is joined to a Roux limb of jejunum; a second bowel join reunites it with the biliopancreatic limb. The excluded stomach usually remains in situ. This differs from sleeve gastrectomy and one-anastomosis bypass.
Supine, usually head-up during laparoscopy; secure against sliding and protect pressure points.
Review bariatric assessment, obstructive sleep apnoea, cardiometabolic disease, airway and thromboprophylaxis plans.
Plan preoxygenation, airway equipment and postoperative respiratory support; obesity does not itself justify treating all patients as having identical aspiration or airway risk.
Induce anaesthesia, position and establish laparoscopic ports/pneumoperitoneum.
Rapid desaturation and difficult mask ventilation may occur. Reassess tube position, ventilation and haemodynamics after insufflation and head-up positioning.
Create the small gastric pouch and divide the jejunum to form the Roux and biliopancreatic limbs.
Stapling/dissection can cause bleeding. Coordinate any gastric tube positioning or withdrawal before stapling; prevent accidental incorporation of the tube.
Construct the gastrojejunostomy and jejunojejunostomy, in the surgeon's chosen order; close relevant mesenteric defects.
Maintain stable perfusion and ventilation through a potentially prolonged operation; technique and limb lengths vary and are not prescribed here.
Check the joins as planned, remove instruments and recover through the bariatric pathway.
Use multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, PONV prevention and risk-based respiratory support. Unexplained tachycardia, pain or deterioration may indicate bleeding or leak and warrants urgent review.
Induction — limited oxygen reserve
Insufflation and head-up
Stapling near gastric tube
Postoperative bleeding, leak or respiratory compromise
VTE prevention, early mobilisation and safe nutrition follow the bariatric programme.
Sleep-apnoea support is individualised; do not replace the patient's established plan with a blanket rule.
Ophthalmic

Removal of vitreous through small scleral ports, followed by treatment of retinal pathology. Laser, membrane peeling and gas or silicone-oil tamponade may be used; external scleral buckling is a different or additional technique.
Supine with head still under ophthalmic drapes; postoperative posture depends on the repair.
Confirm eye, indication, previous ocular gas and choice of local/regional anaesthesia with monitored care or general anaesthesia.
Assess ability to lie still and tolerate duration/drapes. Check block risks and cardiopulmonary disease; general anaesthesia may be appropriate when cooperation or airway safety is uncertain.
Prepare the eye and insert pars plana ports with an infusion system.
Prevent coughing, movement and straining during intraocular work. Sedation must not compromise ventilation under restricted-access drapes.
Remove vitreous and perform the indicated retinal repair, such as membrane peeling or laser.
Ocular manipulation, particularly accompanying scleral buckle work, can trigger bradycardia. Alert the surgeon, stop the stimulus and assess oxygenation/ventilation before further treatment.
Use gas or oil tamponade if needed; close the ports.

Do not use nitrous oxide when intraocular gas is present: bubble expansion can raise intraocular pressure and cause permanent visual loss. This also applies to later anaesthetics and nitrous-oxide analgesia while gas remains.
Recover with antiemetic/analgesic treatment and explicit gas/posture instructions.
Record the gas and ophthalmic restrictions. Air travel, altitude and future anaesthesia advice lasts until ophthalmology confirms gas resolution, not a universal number of days.
Ocular block and immobility
Oculocardiac reflex
Gas tamponade — nitrous oxide exclusion
Postoperative posture and future anaesthesia advice
A Low blood-loss category does not mean low consequence from ocular haemorrhage.
Gas and silicone oil are not interchangeable; nitrous oxide restrictions specifically concern gas.
Orthopaedic & Spine
Removal of a herniated lumbar disc fragment compressing a nerve root, through open microscopic or minimally invasive access. It is not a spinal fusion; exposure and extent of disc removal vary.
Usually prone on supports that avoid abdominal compression, with eyes and pressure points protected.
Confirm symptoms, baseline neurology, level, imaging and consent; identify urgent deficits or cauda equina features.
Record neurological deficits before anaesthesia. Agree any neuromonitoring, positioning limitations and postoperative neurological review.
Provide anaesthesia and turn prone with a secured airway and coordinated team.
Recheck tube, ventilation, lines, eyes and pressure areas after turning. The abdomen should not be compressed; prone positioning reduces access for airway rescue.
Confirm the level with imaging, expose the operative area and perform limited bony/ligamentous access as required.
Wrong-level prevention is a team check. Monitor haemodynamics and blood loss; an apparently small operation can still cause a vascular or dural injury.
Identify/protect the nerve root and remove the compressing fragment under magnification.
Communicate unexpected bleeding or physiological change. A dural tear may change the surgical closure and postoperative mobilisation plan.
Check decompression/haemostasis, close, turn supine and recover.

Check limb movement and symptoms against baseline once assessable. New weakness, worsening pain or bladder dysfunction needs urgent surgical assessment rather than attribution to residual anaesthesia.
Turning prone — airway/eye/line protection
Level confirmation
Disc removal — neural or dural injury
New postoperative neurological deficit
Multimodal analgesia and early mobilisation are individualised to the procedure and any complication.
Fusion-specific blood-loss estimates and protocols do not automatically apply to microdiscectomy.

Manual separation and removal of a retained placenta after vaginal birth under appropriate anaesthesia. Bleeding and haemodynamic state determine urgency; suspected placenta accreta spectrum requires senior obstetric planning, not forced separation.
Lithotomy in theatre, with safe supports and access for haemorrhage resuscitation.
Assess retention, blood loss, uterine tone and haemodynamic state; escalate and prepare theatre.
Visible bleeding may underestimate total loss. Activate the obstetric haemorrhage pathway when indicated, obtain access and prepare blood products according to the clinical situation.
Establish regional or general anaesthesia appropriate to urgency, circulating volume and any existing epidural.
Neuraxial extension is not automatically safe in major hypovolaemia. General anaesthesia needs an obstetric airway and aspiration-risk plan; communicate the resuscitation priorities.
Support the uterus externally and pass a hand through the cervix to locate the placental separation plane.
Ensure adequate anaesthesia and monitor continuing blood loss; uterine manipulation is painful and may provoke rapid physiological change.
Separate and remove the placenta if a safe plane exists; assess completeness and uterine cavity.
If no plane can be found, stop and seek senior help for possible accreta. Do not force detachment; haemorrhage may escalate and require a different operative strategy.
Treat uterine atony/haemorrhage, give prophylactic antibiotics per the adopted protocol and arrange recovery.
Reassess haemostasis, perfusion, coagulation and analgesia. Uterotonic choice and drug doses follow the local obstetric pathway; continue surveillance for bleeding and infection.
Haemorrhage and anaesthetic choice
Painful uterine exploration
No separation plane — possible accreta
Persistent atony or bleeding after removal
High risk describes the potential for major postpartum haemorrhage, not a prediction that every patient will bleed heavily.
This summary deliberately does not set a universal time-to-removal or drug regimen.
Vascular

Endovascular treatment of selected carotid stenoses with a stent. This is not carotid endarterectomy: plaque remains in place, and patient selection, embolic protection and antiplatelet planning are central.
Supine on a radiolucent table; access may be femoral, radial or a selected direct carotid approach.
Confirm the planned access, antiplatelet preparation and baseline neurological examination; obtain arterial access, commonly under local anaesthesia.
Preserve communication for neurological assessment where feasible. Sedation must not obscure a new deficit or compromise ventilation; establish access to the patient despite the imaging equipment.
Navigate catheters and perform angiography to define the lesion.
Review renal function, contrast exposure and allergy history. Access injury may cause groin or concealed retroperitoneal bleeding despite an apparently low-blood-loss procedure.
Administer procedural heparin before crossing the lesion and establish the chosen embolic protection strategy.
Document heparin and anticoagulation monitoring with the operator. Distal filters and proximal flow reversal are different techniques; protection choice is not universal.
Selective predilatation, self-expanding stent deployment and selective postdilatation.
Carotid sinus stimulation can cause bradycardia, hypotension or asystole. Agree anticholinergic preparation and haemodynamic support before balloon inflation; report neurological change immediately.
Completion angiography, removal of protection devices and access closure.

Reassess neurology, blood pressure and the access site. Persistent haemodynamic depression or new headache, seizure or deficit needs urgent assessment; plan observation and the prescribed antiplatelet course.
Lesion crossing — cerebral embolisation
Balloon inflation — bradycardia and hypotension
New neurological deficit
Access bleeding and postprocedural blood-pressure disturbance
CIRSE 2024 provides technical standards of practice, not a substitute for individual treatment selection or local emergency pathways.
GALA studied endarterectomy, not stenting: do not transfer its general-versus-local trial result to this procedure.
A qualitative Low blood-loss category does not exclude catastrophic vascular injury. Assess antithrombotic and access-related bleeding risk individually.

Open removal of obstructing plaque at the common femoral artery, sometimes extending into its branches. A patch may widen the repair; additional angioplasty or stenting makes this a hybrid procedure rather than a bypass.
Supine with the operative groin exposed; hybrid cases need imaging access and preparation for additional arterial access.
Confirm the revascularisation plan and expose the femoral artery through a groin incision.
General or spinal anaesthesia is selected by the patient and team. Review cardiovascular, renal and diabetic comorbidity and the antithrombotic plan before choosing a neuraxial technique.
Obtain vascular control and open the narrowed artery.
Agree and document the procedural anticoagulation plan; prepare for bleeding during arterial exposure. This is local arterial control, not an aortic cross-clamp.
Remove plaque from the common femoral artery and any involved branch origins.
Maintain stable physiology, warming and adequate analgesia during the period of interrupted limb flow; the extent and duration depend on the disease.
Close the arteriotomy, using a patch where appropriate; restore and check limb flow.
Communicate before restoration of flow and document the postoperative limb assessment. A cold, painful limb or new deficit requires prompt vascular review.
If planned, treat other stenoses with angioplasty or stenting; then close the groin wound.
Hybrid work adds procedure time, imaging and contrast exposure. Monitor the access site and arrange analgesia and observation appropriate to the patient's vascular risk.
Arterial exposure and anticoagulation — bleeding
Restoration of flow and limb assessment
Hybrid angioplasty — additional access and contrast
The NHS leaflet supports the broad sequence and anaesthetic options; GVG supplies the limb-revascularisation context, not fixed anaesthetic drug or pressure targets.
The choice of open, endovascular or hybrid treatment depends on disease distribution and patient risk. BASIL-2 is not a trial of anaesthesia for femoral endarterectomy.

Placement of a donor kidney in the recipient's lower abdomen, joining its artery, vein and ureter to the recipient. This entry covers implantation, not donor nephrectomy; native kidneys usually remain in place.
Supine; lower abdominal incision into the chosen iliac fossa, with access to the bladder.
Confirm the graft and recipient plan; induce anaesthesia and prepare the lower abdomen.
Check recent dialysis, potassium, acid-base balance, fluid status and cardiovascular disease. Preserve dialysis access; review aspiration risk and renal handling of drugs.
Expose recipient vessels and prepare the graft in the iliac fossa.
Maintain temperature, perfusion and access for resuscitation. Agree timing of locally prescribed immunosuppression and antimicrobial prophylaxis; infusions may have specific haemodynamic risks.
Join the graft vein and artery to recipient vessels under vascular control; the precise sequence varies.
Know when reperfusion is approaching. Use clinical assessment and, where appropriate, haemodynamic monitoring to guide volume rather than loading every patient to a fixed central venous pressure.
Release vascular control and assess graft perfusion.
Anticipate blood-pressure change and reassess potassium, acid-base status and volume. Maintain perfusion without fluid overload; titrated vasopressors may be needed despite adequate filling.
Join the donor ureter to the bladder, commonly with a temporary ureteric stent; achieve haemostasis and close.

Monitor urine output and postoperative renal biochemistry. Immediate urine production is not guaranteed and its absence alone does not establish graft failure; delayed graft function needs transplant-team assessment.
Induction in a dialysis patient with cardiovascular or electrolyte disturbance
Graft reperfusion
Balancing perfusion against pulmonary fluid overload
Postoperative oliguria or electrolyte disturbance
Renal clearance alters the duration of several drugs. Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and an appropriate reversal plan are important.
The 2024 anaesthesia review supports balanced crystalloids and assessment of fluid responsiveness; no single fluid volume or pressure target is appropriate for every recipient.
Postoperative analgesia and medication choices must account for changing graft function; follow the transplant service's monitoring and immunosuppression pathway.

Reduction of a groin hernia and reinforcement of the defect, commonly with mesh. Open anterior repair, totally extraperitoneal (TEP) and transabdominal preperitoneal (TAPP) repairs are distinct approaches; tissue repair is an alternative in selected circumstances.
Supine; laparoscopic repair may use head-down tilt. Agree unilateral or bilateral repair and the planned approach.
Open: groin incision with local, general or selected regional anaesthesia. Laparoscopic: ports and creation of the operative space, usually under general anaesthesia.
HerniaSurge recommends local anaesthesia for reducible open repair when the team is experienced. This recommendation is not for laparoscopic surgery or strangulated bowel.
Identify the sac and reduce its contents; assess bowel viability if incarcerated or strangulated.
An emergency obstruction is not an uncomplicated day-case hernia: assess aspiration, dehydration and sepsis risks and agree whether bowel resection may be necessary.
Reinforce the defect, usually with mesh in the tissue plane appropriate to the chosen approach.

During laparoscopy, monitor the effect of insufflation on airway pressures, oxygenation and carbon dioxide, and adjust ventilation. During awake open repair, respond to pain with supplementation rather than excessive sedation.
Complete haemostasis; release insufflation if used and close the wounds.
Use multimodal analgesia and nausea prevention to support mobilisation. Recovery and discharge depend on pain, physiology, social circumstances and any complications, not just the small incision.
Pain or movement during awake open repair
Laparoscopic insufflation
Unexpected ischaemic bowel in an emergency repair
HerniaSurge 2023 suggests general or local rather than regional anaesthesia for older patients, reflecting medical-complication risk; anaesthetic choice remains individualised.
These stages describe a broad repair pathway, not identical mesh placement for TEP, TAPP and open surgery.
The NHS patient information supports the operative overview; HerniaSurge provides the technique-specific anaesthetic recommendations.

Laparoscopic removal of the appendix for appendicitis. Perforation, abscess or peritonitis changes the source-control and postoperative plan; this entry describes surgery once that treatment has been selected.
Supine, with table tilt adjusted for exposure and pressure areas protected.
Induce general anaesthesia; establish laparoscopic access and CO₂ insufflation.
Assess aspiration risk, fasting, vomiting, ileus and physiological disturbance individually. Monitor respiratory mechanics and haemodynamics after insufflation.
Inspect the abdomen, identify the appendix and assess perforation or contamination.
Confirm antimicrobial prophylaxis and communicate any sepsis or hypovolaemia. The operative findings determine whether postoperative antibiotics and higher-acuity observation are needed.
Separate and control the mesoappendix, including its vessels.
Maintain stillness and adequate anaesthesia. Bleeding is usually limited but monitor both surgical bleeding and physiological deterioration.
Secure the appendiceal base, divide the appendix and retrieve it, usually in a bag.
Closure may use ligatures, clips or a stapler according to tissue condition and surgeon judgement; there is no universal device for every appendix.
Complete source control and haemostasis, desufflate and close.
Plan analgesia, nausea prevention and postoperative destination. Routine lavage or drains should not be assumed; the adopted guideline and intraoperative findings guide management.
Induction when aspiration or sepsis risk is present
Pneumoperitoneum — altered ventilation
Perforation or peritonitis — source control and postoperative planning

Plan postoperative breathing support jointly when sleep apnoea coexists with skull-base reconstruction, rather than assuming nasal positive-pressure treatment is automatically safe.

Systemic heparin before clamping.

The critical moment for the brain. Maintain blood pressure at or above the patient's baseline to support collateral flow. In an awake patient, test speech, contralateral hand grip and consciousness immediately and repeatedly; under general anaesthesia, cerebral monitoring (e.g.
stump pressure, near-infrared spectroscopy or transcranial Doppler) guides shunt use.
Arteriotomy and, if needed, insertion of a temporary shunt from the common to the internal carotid artery.

Plaque removal (endarterectomy), then closure of the arteriotomy, often with a patch.
Keep the patient still; coughing or movement is dangerous with an open artery.
Back-bleeding and flushing, then release of clamps (external carotid first, then internal).

GALA found no significant difference in the composite of stroke, myocardial infarction or death by 30 days (4.8% general vs 4.5% local); this does not prove equivalence. Choose by patient, surgeon and anaesthetist preference.

Regional technique: superficial (± intermediate) cervical plexus block with surgical local anaesthetic supplementation; deep cervical plexus block carries more risk (phrenic block, intravascular injection).
Arterial line before induction or block; measure blood pressure in both arms preoperatively and use the higher-reading arm.
Postoperative blood pressure control matters: hypertension raises the risk of hyperperfusion syndrome (headache, seizures, intracerebral haemorrhage) and haematoma.
Cranial nerve injury (hypoglossal, recurrent laryngeal, marginal mandibular) may affect swallowing or the airway after surgery.
Replacement of the aneurysmal infrarenal aorta with a synthetic tube or bifurcated graft through a laparotomy or retroperitoneal approach.
