Laparotomy, packing the bowel aside and opening the retroperitoneum over the aorta.
Large evaporative heat and fluid losses: active warming, warmed fluids and cell salvage should be running. Bowel handling can cause mesenteric traction syndrome (flushing, hypotension).
Dissection of the aneurysm neck below the renal arteries and of both iliac arteries.
Bleeding can be brisk, especially from the left renal vein and iliac veins; keep blood products available.
Systemic heparin, then clamping of the iliac arteries and the aorta below the renal arteries.

Cross-clamp raises afterload suddenly: hypertension and possible myocardial ischaemia or LV failure. Anticipate with deeper anaesthesia or vasodilators (e.g. GTN) just before clamping; the higher the clamp, the bigger the effect and the greater the kidney and gut ischaemia.
Opening of the aneurysm sac, removal of thrombus and oversewing of back-bleeding lumbar arteries.
Back-bleeding from lumbar and inferior mesenteric arteries can be significant; return salvaged blood.
Proximal then distal anastomosis of a tube or bifurcated graft.
Before declamping, assess volume status and cardiac function, correct hypovolaemia, acidosis, calcium and haemoglobin, and prepare titrated vasopressors — rather than giving a routine fluid load.
Sequential release of the clamps, one limb at a time.

Declamping causes hypotension: sudden fall in afterload, reactive hyperaemia and washout of acid, potassium and vasodilators from the ischaemic legs. Agree slow, staged release with the surgeon; give fluid and vasopressors; reclamp if pressure collapses.
Closure of the sac over the graft, retroperitoneum and abdomen; check leg and bowel perfusion.
Watch for colonic ischaemia, lower limb ischaemia (trash foot) and abdominal compartment syndrome after closure.

Coronary disease is common in this group; perioperative myocardial injury is a leading cause of death.

NICE NG156 recommends offering open repair (rather than EVAR) for unruptured infrarenal aneurysms unless there are anaesthetic or medical contraindications or a hostile abdomen — EVAR has lower early mortality but more long-term reintervention.
A covered stent graft is passed from the femoral arteries and deployed inside the aneurysm to exclude it from the circulation.
Supine on a radiolucent table with arms out of the X-ray field; often in an interventional suite or hybrid theatre.
Femoral artery access — open cut-down or percutaneous puncture with closure devices.
Can be done under general, regional or local anaesthesia with sedation; the patient must lie flat and still for a long time.
Heparin, then guidewires and sheaths passed into the aorta; angiography to mark the renal arteries.
Iodinated contrast: protect the kidneys with adequate hydration and avoid nephrotoxins. Breath-holding on request improves imaging.

Cannulation of the contralateral gate and deployment of the iliac limb(s).

Check distal leg perfusion; groin haematoma or access-vessel injury can cause concealed bleeding.

EVAR-1 showed lower 30-day mortality with EVAR than open repair (1.7% vs 4.7%), but this early advantage did not translate into long-term survival benefit and EVAR needs lifelong surveillance.
Radiation protection for staff; limited access to the patient once draped and under the C-arm.

Emergency control of haemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm, by open repair or emergency EVAR when anatomy allows.
Supine; patient fully prepped and draped before induction.
Rapid CT (if stable enough) to decide open versus endovascular repair; activation of major haemorrhage protocol.

Restricted resuscitation (permissive hypotension) before aortic control: ESVS suggests a systolic pressure of around 70–90 mmHg while the patient stays conscious; individualise (e.g. myocardial ischaemia) and avoid aggressive fluid that worsens bleeding.

Induction can cause cardiovascular collapse by losing sympathetic tone and the tamponading effect of abdominal muscle tone. Use cautious doses and have vasopressors and blood running. For EVAR, use local anaesthesia where tolerated and feasible, with a clear plan for conversion to general anaesthesia.
Open: immediate laparotomy and supracoeliac or infrarenal aortic clamp. EVAR: aortic occlusion balloon if needed, then stent graft deployment.

Closure (or temporary abdominal closure).

Removal of all or part of the thyroid gland through a transverse neck incision, preserving the recurrent laryngeal nerves and parathyroid glands.

Removal of the palatine tonsils, commonly in children for recurrent tonsillitis or obstructive sleep-disordered breathing.

Suction under direct vision and confirm haemostasis first. Choose deep or awake extubation by aspiration, obstruction and airway-rescue risk — favour awake extubation when these risks are higher (e.g. severe OSA, difficult airway, bleeding).

Children with obstructive sleep apnoea are more sensitive to opioids: use opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, avoid codeine, and plan postoperative monitoring or admission by OSA severity, age and comorbidity.
Return to theatre for bleeding: treat as a full stomach (swallowed blood), the patient may be hypovolaemic, and visualisation may be difficult.
Delivery of the baby through a lower segment uterine incision via a Pfannenstiel (transverse) abdominal incision.
Supine with left lateral tilt or uterine displacement to relieve aortocaval compression.
Pfannenstiel skin incision, division of rectus sheath and separation of rectus muscles.

Under spinal or epidural anaesthesia, confirm and document bilateral loss of light touch to T5 or higher with satisfactory motor block before incision (cold alone is unreliable). Confirm prophylactic antibiotics have been given before skin incision.
Opening of the peritoneum, bladder reflected, lower segment uterine incision.

Spinal hypotension: NICE recommends starting prophylactic phenylephrine immediately after the spinal, with crystalloid co-loading, aiming for systolic pressure at least 90% of baseline and avoiding below 80%.
Delivery of the baby (fundal pressure may be needed).

Fundal pressure and uterine exteriorisation are the most uncomfortable moments for the mother — take any reported pain seriously: ask the surgeon to pause when safe, assess and treat promptly, and offer conversion to general anaesthesia when appropriate.
Reassurance or sedation is not a substitute for adequate anaesthesia.
Delivery of the placenta and uterotonic given.

For routine haemorrhage prophylaxis follow current NICE NG192, which now links to its carbetocin recommendation (slow IV injection); oxytocin remains widely used for treatment. Rapid uterotonic boluses cause hypotension and tachycardia. Watch blood loss and uterine tone.
Uterine repair (NICE advises against routine exteriorisation or routine peritoneal closure), then sheath and skin closure.

NICE NG192 recommends regional anaesthesia for caesarean birth where possible.

General anaesthesia risks: difficult airway and aspiration — follow obstetric difficult airway guidance.
Stent-graft repair of descending thoracic aortic disease (aneurysm, dissection, traumatic transection or penetrating ulcer) delivered from the femoral artery under fluoroscopy.
Supine with arms out or tucked to allow C-arm access; left arm access may be needed for left subclavian work.
Femoral access (percutaneous or cut-down); large-bore sheath; systemic heparin.

General or local anaesthesia with sedation; arterial line (right radial is usual because the left subclavian origin may be covered). Large-bore IV access and cross-matched blood for access-vessel injury.
Angiography and measurement; the planned landing zone may mean covering the left subclavian artery (with or without prior bypass).
Covering the left subclavian reduces vertebral and spinal collateral flow: higher risk of stroke and spinal cord ischaemia.
Stent-graft advanced and deployed; blood pressure may be lowered briefly during deployment to prevent graft migration.
Agree the target pressure and the drug (e.g. short-acting vasodilator, or rapid ventricular pacing in some units) before deployment; restore pressure promptly afterwards.
Ballooning of seal zones and completion angiography for endoleak.
Ballooning briefly occludes the aorta, causing a pressure spike proximally.
Sheath removal and access closure.
Reverse heparin if asked; check distal limb perfusion.

ESVS guidance recommends measures to protect the spinal cord when extensive thoracic aortic coverage is planned, including cerebrospinal fluid drainage in selected high-risk patients and maintaining an adequate mean arterial pressure.
A lumbar CSF drain needs coagulation and anticoagulation planning; drain complications include headache, bleeding and infection.
Spinal cord ischaemia can be delayed: serial neurological checks after surgery; new weakness needs immediate pressure augmentation and CSF drainage if a drain is in place.

A 2023 meta-analysis found no clear reduction in spinal cord ischaemia with prophylactic drainage in TEVAR and a small risk of serious drain complications, so drainage is selective rather than routine.
Laparoscopic removal of most of the greater curve of the stomach, leaving a narrow tube, for severe obesity.
Supine, reverse Trendelenburg (head-up), often with legs apart; secure strapping and padding for a heavy patient.
Pneumoperitoneum and port placement; liver retractor inserted.
Ramped preoxygenation and head-up positioning; expect rapid desaturation at induction. Dose drugs by an appropriate weight scalar (lean or adjusted weight for most).
Greater curve mobilised from the omentum, dividing short gastric vessels.
Keep good muscle relaxation for workspace; recruitment and PEEP help oxygenation with pneumoperitoneum.
Bougie passed orally into the stomach along the lesser curve to size the sleeve.

The anaesthetist usually passes the bougie: remove any nasogastric or temperature probe first, and pass gently — oesophageal perforation is a recognised complication. Communicate clearly with the surgeon.
Stomach divided with sequential staple firings alongside the bougie; staple-line leak test (air or dye) may be done.
Withdraw the bougie before the final staple fire unless the surgeon asks otherwise, so it is not stapled in.
Specimen removed and ports closed.
Multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia and PONV prophylaxis; extubate awake, head-up, fully reversed.

Monitor neuromuscular block quantitatively and ensure full reversal before extubation.
Open or laparoscopic removal of part of the liver, usually for colorectal metastases or primary liver cancer.
Supine; arms out. Open surgery often uses a subcostal (rooftop or J-shaped) incision.
Laparotomy or laparoscopy; liver mobilised and intraoperative ultrasound to map lesions and vessels.
Arterial line; central venous access is common. Epidural, wound catheters or intrathecal morphine for analgesia, depending on coagulation and local practice.
Inflow control: hepatic artery and portal vein to the resected part divided; intermittent Pringle manoeuvre (clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament) may be used.
Pringle reduces bleeding; it causes a small rise in afterload and a fall in venous return. Record clamp times.
Parenchymal transection.

The main bleeding phase. A low central venous pressure strategy (restricting fluid, head-down, vasodilators) is often used to reduce back-bleeding from hepatic veins — balance against hypotension and air embolism risk.
Haemostasis and bile-leak check; once transection is complete, restore normovolaemia.
Give fluid back after transection; check lactate, glucose and coagulation.
Closure, with or without drain.

Have cell salvage available where appropriate (oncological use depends on local policy).

Removal of the bladder (with prostate in men, or uterus and anterior vaginal wall in women) and pelvic lymph nodes for muscle-invasive bladder cancer, with urine diverted through an ileal conduit or neobladder. Open or robotic.
Supine, or lithotomy with steep head-down for robotic surgery.
Access (laparotomy or robotic ports with pneumoperitoneum) and pelvic lymph node dissection.
Long case: careful pressure-point care, warming, arterial line. Steep head-down for robotic cases raises airway pressure and causes facial/airway swelling.
Bladder pedicles divided and bladder (with prostate or uterus) removed.
Major pelvic venous bleeding can be sudden; urine output cannot be measured once the ureters are divided.
Isolation of a segment of ileum; bowel continuity restored.

Ureters joined to the ileal conduit, which is brought out as a stoma (or a neobladder is made).

Supine, head extended and turned; two teams may work at once (head and donor site).
Airway secured — sometimes awake intubation or awake tracheostomy for obstructing tumours.
Plan the airway jointly with the surgeon; a shared, distorted airway is common. Avoid the flap donor arm for cannulas and blood pressure cuffs.
Tumour resection and neck dissection; tracheostomy if planned.
Carotid sinus handling can cause bradycardia. Swap to the tracheostomy tube with the surgeon in a planned, step-by-step way.
Flap raised at the donor site.
Long operation: warming, pressure care, urinary catheter, thromboprophylaxis.
Microvascular anastomosis of flap artery and vein to neck vessels; flap inset.
Flap perfusion depends on cardiac output and blood pressure: aim for normovolaemia, normothermia and an adequate mean pressure; avoid both under-filling and over-filling (oedema).
Closure; postoperative flap monitoring.
Smooth emergence; tracheostomy care. Avoid neck ties that compress the flap vessels.

Laparoscopic removal of the uterus (and often tubes and ovaries) for benign disease or early cancer.

Intraocular lens inserted; incisions self-seal.

Division of the hypertrophied pyloric muscle down to the mucosa in an infant with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. A medical, not surgical, emergency: fluid and electrolyte correction comes first.
Supine infant on a warmed table; open right upper quadrant/umbilical incision or laparoscopic ports.
Preoperative resuscitation and correction of the hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
Do not list the infant until electrolytes and acid-base status are corrected per local paediatric criteria; alkalosis is associated with delayed emergence and postoperative apnoea.

Access to the pylorus (open or laparoscopic) and delivery of the pyloric 'olive'.

Closure and local anaesthetic infiltration or block.

One or two burr holes are made over a chronic subdural collection, the membrane is opened, the liquefied haematoma is irrigated out and a drain is usually left. Patients are often elderly and anticoagulated.
Supine with the head turned and supported on a head ring; head-up tilt per surgeon.
Preoperative review: neurology, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use and reversal plan, comorbidities.
Agree reversal with the neurosurgical and haematology teams. Older patients with frailty and cardiac disease are common.
Anaesthesia: general anaesthesia or local anaesthesia with or without sedation, depending on patient and surgeon.
General anaesthesia allows ventilatory control; local techniques avoid airway instrumentation but require a cooperative, still patient. Avoid hypercapnia and hypotension.
Scalp incision and burr hole(s); dura and outer membrane opened.
Scalp infiltration helps analgesia; the release of a large collection may cause transient haemodynamic change.
Irrigation of the cavity with warm saline; drain placement (subdural or subperiosteal).
Surgeons may request a Valsalva manoeuvre to help expel fluid and air — coordinate with ventilation.
Closure; postoperative drain management and neurological observation.
Plan a smooth emergence with prompt neurological assessment; prevent PONV and screen for delirium.
Anticoagulation reversal before incision

Choice of anaesthesia depends on neurological status, haematoma size and location and surgical approach.
Recurrence is common; reoperation patients need the same review.
Local-versus-general comparisons are largely observational; do not treat them as proof of superiority.
Arthroscopic repair or decompression in the shoulder through several small portals with fluid distension of the joint. Pain can be severe; position carries haemodynamic and cerebral risks.
Beach chair (sitting) or lateral decubitus with arm traction.
Regional anaesthesia: interscalene brachial plexus block or a phrenic-sparing alternative (e.g. suprascapular plus axillary nerve blocks).
Interscalene block causes ipsilateral phrenic nerve palsy in most patients — caution in respiratory disease. Consider alternatives; check for Horner's, hoarseness and local anaesthetic toxicity.
Positioning in beach chair or lateral; head secured in neutral.
In beach chair, cerebral perfusion pressure is lower than arm BP suggests; correct BP measurement for height difference and avoid hypotension. Protect eyes, neck and pressure points.
Portal placement and joint distension with irrigation fluid; surgeon may request controlled hypotension for visibility.
Agree acceptable BP limits — deliberate hypotension in the sitting position risks cerebral ischaemia. Fluid can extravasate into neck tissues; check airway at the end.
Repair (anchors, sutures) or decompression; closure of portals.
Awake or sedated surgery under block is possible; otherwise GA with a secured airway accessible despite drapes.

Fracture fragments are reduced, the teeth placed in correct occlusion, and the bone fixed with miniplates through intraoral (or sometimes external) incisions. The surgeon needs the teeth to meet, which shapes airway choice.
Supine, head ring, shared airway with the surgeon; table often turned 90–180°.
Airway assessment: mouth opening (trismus from pain versus mechanical block), bleeding, associated head, cervical spine and midface injuries.
Plan the airway jointly. Options include videolaryngoscopy, awake tracheal intubation, nasal intubation, submental intubation or tracheostomy, depending on injuries and occlusion needs.
Intubation — commonly nasotracheal, so the teeth can be brought together.
Nasal intubation is avoided or approached cautiously if there are midface or skull-base fractures. Secure the tube well; throat pack per local safety checks.
Intermaxillary fixation (temporary or arch bars) to restore occlusion.
Once jaws are fixed, there is no oral access to the airway. Know how and who removes the fixation.
Fracture reduction and miniplate fixation through intraoral incisions; fixation released if not required postoperatively.
Ensure haemostasis and remove the throat pack before emergence; suction the pharynx.
Extubation fully awake, with postoperative airway plan.
If the jaws stay wired, wire cutters must accompany the patient and staff must know how to use them. Give antiemetics to reduce vomiting with fixed jaws.

Intermaxillary fixation — loss of oral airway access

Facial trauma may coexist with brain and cervical spine injury.

Staged reconstruction of the lip (typically in infancy) and palate (later in infancy) by a cleft team. The airway is shared with the surgeon, can be difficult, and is at risk of obstruction after palate repair.
Supine with head ring and shoulder roll (neck extended); table turned; patient fully draped.
Preoperative assessment for associated syndromes and congenital anomalies, feeding, weight and recent respiratory infection.
Cleft anomalies are associated with numerous congenital abnormalities; look specifically for features predicting difficult laryngoscopy and for cardiac disease.
Induction and oral intubation with a preformed south-facing RAE tube secured in the midline below the lower lip.
Laryngoscopy may be difficult (blade can fall into the cleft); confirm tube tip position visually and by auscultation, since the preformed curve may not fit the child.
Positioning with neck extension; throat pack; for palate surgery, insertion of the Dingman mouth gag.
Recheck the tube after every move. The gag can kink or displace the tube or raise airway pressures, and throat pack insertion/removal can cause accidental extubation.
Infiltration with local anaesthetic and adrenaline; lip or palate repair.
Infiltration reduces bleeding and adds analgesia. Use multimodal analgesia and titrate opioids carefully because of the risk of respiratory events.
Throat pack removal, suction under direct vision and awake extubation; postoperative airway monitoring.
Oropharyngeal/nasopharyngeal swelling in nasal-breathing infants can obstruct the airway; a nasopharyngeal airway or tongue suture may be placed. Monitor for obstruction throughout recovery.
Laryngoscopy and intubation
Mouth gag insertion and head movement — tube kinking or displacement
Extubation and recovery — airway obstruction
Effective communication with the surgeon about the shared airway is essential.
Timing of lip and palate surgery and analgesic doses follow the local cleft team protocol; this summary does not set them.

An opening is made in the anterior trachea (usually around the second to fourth rings) and a tracheostomy tube inserted, for prolonged ventilation, airway obstruction or head and neck surgery. The most dangerous moment is the handover from the tracheal tube to the tracheostomy tube.
Supine with shoulder roll and neck extended (if the cervical spine allows); head ring.
Planning: indication, airway plan if the tracheostomy fails, anticoagulation, and equipment (tube sizes, capnography).
Agree in advance who withdraws the tracheal tube and when; have a plan for re-intubation from above.
Neck incision, division of strap muscles and division or retraction of the thyroid isthmus.
Bleeding from the isthmus or anterior jugular veins is possible. Keep the patient deeply anaesthetised and paralysed.
Opening of the trachea (window or flap).
Reduce inspired oxygen as far as is safe and stop diathermy before the trachea is opened — airway fire risk. The cuff may be punctured if the tube is not withdrawn appropriately.
Withdrawal of the tracheal tube under direct vision until its tip is just above the stoma, then insertion of the tracheostomy tube.
Do not remove the tracheal tube fully until correct tracheostomy placement is confirmed by sustained capnography; then remove it.
Securing the tube (ties/sutures), chest auscultation and handover with bedhead signs.
Displacement in the early days is dangerous because the tract is not formed; follow National Tracheostomy Safety Project emergency algorithms.
Tracheal opening — airway fire and cuff damage
Tube exchange — loss of the airway
Early displacement after surgery
Confirm placement with waveform capnography every time.
Ensure the ward knows whether the upper airway is patent (tracheostomy) or not (laryngectomy).

Removal of the kidney with its fat and fascia, usually for renal cell carcinoma. Most cases are laparoscopic or robotic; tumour extending into the renal vein or inferior vena cava (IVC) turns it into a major open vascular operation.
Lateral (flank) with the table broken, or supine for open transperitoneal and IVC cases.
Preoperative staging including the level of any venous tumour thrombus; assessment of renal function and the remaining kidney.

Thrombus level dictates the plan: higher levels may need large-bore access, cell salvage discussion, transoesophageal echo and, rarely, cardiopulmonary bypass. Plan for reduced renal reserve afterwards.
Positioning in the lateral flank position with kidney rest and table break.
Lateral flexion can reduce venous return and cause hypotension; protect the dependent arm, eyes and brachial plexus, and check ventilation of the dependent lung.
Mobilisation of the kidney; control and division of the renal artery, then the renal vein.
Sudden bleeding from the renal vessels or IVC is the main intraoperative danger. Pneumothorax can follow pleural breach in flank approaches.
For IVC thrombus: clamping of the IVC above and below the thrombus, cavotomy and thrombus removal.
Caval clamping can sharply reduce venous return and cardiac output; the thrombus can embolise to the lungs — echo helps track it. Coordinate clamping with the surgeon.
Haemostasis and closure; postoperative analgesia and renal monitoring.
Epidural, wound catheters or multimodal analgesia depending on approach; avoid nephrotoxins and dose renally cleared drugs for the new renal function.
Renal hilum and IVC dissection — massive bleeding
Caval clamping — loss of venous return
Thrombus manipulation — tumour embolism
Most uncomplicated nephrectomies are low-to-moderate blood loss; IVC extension changes this fundamentally.
High-level thrombus cases belong in high-volume multidisciplinary centres.

Craniotomy during which the patient is awake for part of the operation, so speech or movement can be tested while the surgeon maps and removes tumour near eloquent cortex. Communication, comfort and airway access are central.
Supine or semi-lateral, head in pins; drapes arranged so the patient's face can be seen and the airway reached.
Patient selection and preparation: ability to cooperate, anxiety, airway, obesity and sleep apnoea; rehearsal of intraoperative tests.
Poor cooperation and difficult airway are relative contraindications; agree the technique (sedation/monitored care or asleep-awake-asleep) with the team.
Scalp block and pin-site infiltration; head fixation.
Effective local anaesthesia is essential whatever technique is used; respect maximum local anaesthetic doses.
Bone flap and dural opening under sedation or general anaesthesia (supraglottic airway in asleep-awake-asleep).
Avoid hypercapnia and airway obstruction with sedation; dural opening is painful unless infiltrated.
Awake phase: cortical stimulation mapping and tumour resection while the patient talks or moves.
Patient must be awake but comfortable. Seizures can be provoked by stimulation — have cold saline for the cortex and anticonvulsant drugs ready. Watch for nausea, pain and agitation.
Closure, often with sedation or general anaesthesia resumed; early neurological assessment.
Plan smooth emergence or deepening; continue PONV prophylaxis and pain control.
Airway obstruction or apnoea during sedation
Intraoperative seizure during stimulation
Loss of cooperation in the awake phase
No single technique is optimal; choose for the patient and surgeon.
A supraglottic airway, or conversion to general anaesthesia, must be immediately available.

Pedicle screws and rods are used to straighten and fuse a curved spine, usually in adolescents. Neuromuscular scoliosis (cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophies) carries much higher respiratory, cardiac and bleeding risk than idiopathic scoliosis.
Prone on a spinal frame with abdomen free; head in a pressure-relieving headrest.
Preoperative assessment: lung function, cardiac function (especially muscular dystrophies), nutrition, seizures and secretions; postoperative critical care bed.

Neuromuscular patients have a higher risk of perioperative complications; plan for postoperative ventilation or non-invasive support where reserve is poor. Avoid suxamethonium in muscular dystrophies.
Induction, large-bore access, arterial line; prone positioning.
Protect eyes, face, breasts/genitals and limbs; keep the abdomen free to lower venous pressure and bleeding.
Exposure and pedicle screw insertion across many levels.
Blood loss can be large: tranexamic acid and cell salvage are commonly used. Total intravenous anaesthesia suits motor evoked potential monitoring; avoid neuromuscular block after baseline.
Rod insertion and curve correction.

Highest risk of spinal cord injury. If neuromonitoring signals fall, raise blood pressure, correct anaemia and temperature, and agree with the surgeon whether to release correction or do a wake-up test.
Bone graft, closure and postoperative care.
Multimodal analgesia (often intrathecal morphine or PCA); monitor for respiratory depression, ileus and ongoing bleeding.
Correction manoeuvre — spinal cord ischaemia
Major blood loss during long instrumentation
Blood pressure, haemoglobin and anaesthetic depth all affect neuromonitoring — keep them stable.
Exact transfusion and tranexamic acid regimens follow local protocols; this summary does not set them.

The diseased liver is removed and a donor liver implanted, with vascular anastomoses (caval, portal, arterial) and biliary reconstruction. Three phases — dissection, anhepatic and neohepatic — each bring distinct anaesthetic problems, peaking at graft reperfusion.
Supine with arms out; access for large-bore lines, cell salvage and possible venovenous bypass.
Assessment of end-stage liver disease: coagulopathy, portopulmonary hypertension, hepatopulmonary syndrome, hepatorenal syndrome, cardiomyopathy and sarcopenia.
Portopulmonary hypertension and cardiac disease can make transplant unsafe; check echocardiography and right heart assessment per the transplant unit protocol.
Dissection (pre-anhepatic) phase: mobilisation of the native liver despite portal hypertension and collaterals.
Major bleeding is common: large-bore access, rapid infuser, cell salvage and point-of-care viscoelastic testing guide replacement. Monitor for hypocalcaemia from citrate.
Anhepatic phase: vascular clamping (caval or piggyback technique) and removal of the native liver.
Venous return falls with full caval clamping; no liver means no citrate or lactate clearance and worsening acidosis. Watch potassium.
Graft implantation and reperfusion through the portal vein.

Post-reperfusion syndrome: sudden hypotension, bradycardia, hyperkalaemia and pulmonary hypertension; intracardiac thrombus can occur. Prepare vasopressors, calcium and treatment for hyperkalaemia; transoesophageal echo helps.
Neohepatic phase: arterial and biliary anastomoses, haemostasis; transfer to critical care.
Graft function shows as falling lactate, improving coagulation and acid-base. Avoid fluid overload that congests the graft.
Dissection — massive haemorrhage
Reperfusion — post-reperfusion syndrome and hyperkalaemia
Specialist transplant anaesthesia team; protocols for transfusion and coagulation management are centre-specific.
Intracardiac thrombus and right heart failure may need advanced support including mechanical circulatory support.

Removal of a catecholamine-secreting adrenal tumour, usually laparoscopically. Tumour handling can cause severe hypertension and arrhythmias; after the adrenal vein is tied, blood pressure and glucose can fall sharply.
Lateral decubitus (transperitoneal) or prone (retroperitoneoscopic).
Preoperative preparation with an endocrinologist: biochemical confirmation, cardiac assessment and medical preparation (commonly α-blockade, then β-blockade if needed).
Practice varies: a 21-centre review found many patients had surgery without α-blockade with low complication rates, so follow the local multidisciplinary pathway.
Induction and arterial line before induction; vasodilators and short-acting β-blocker ready.
Avoid triggers of catecholamine release: light anaesthesia, hypoxia, hypercapnia, histamine-releasing drugs and metoclopramide.
Pneumoperitoneum and tumour mobilisation.
Insufflation and handling cause hypertensive surges and tachyarrhythmias; treat promptly (e.g. magnesium, phentolamine, nitroprusside or GTN, esmolol per local practice) and tell the surgeon.
Ligation of the adrenal vein.
Catecholamine levels fall: expect hypotension needing fluid and vasopressors. Stop vasodilators in advance.
Tumour removal, closure and postoperative monitoring in HDU.
Monitor for persistent hypotension and rebound hypoglycaemia; give steroid cover after bilateral adrenalectomy.
Tumour handling — hypertensive crisis
Adrenal vein ligation — sudden hypotension
Early postoperative — hypoglycaemia
Close surgeon–anaesthetist communication during handling is essential.
There are no randomised trials comparing preparation strategies.

Endoscopic clearance of diseased sinus tissue and polyps to restore drainage. Small amounts of bleeding ruin the endoscopic view, so the anaesthetic aim is a still patient and a dry surgical field. The orbit and skull base lie close by.
Supine, reverse Trendelenburg (head-up), head slightly turned towards the surgeon; table often turned.
Preoperative assessment: asthma, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, anticoagulants and obstructive sleep apnoea.
Nasal polyps often coexist with asthma and NSAID sensitivity — check before giving NSAIDs.
Topical vasoconstrictor to the nose; induction and airway (reinforced tracheal tube or reinforced supraglottic airway with throat pack).
Topical vasoconstrictors (e.g. cocaine or adrenaline preparations) can cause hypertension and arrhythmias.
Optimising the field: head-up tilt, controlled heart rate and blood pressure.
Evidence favours TIVA over volatile anaesthesia for a better surgical field with less blood loss; tranexamic acid is also used. Agree acceptable blood pressure limits.
Endoscopic uncinectomy, ethmoidectomy and opening of sinus ostia.
Orbital or skull-base injury can occur: watch for sudden eye swelling or CSF leak and tell the surgeon.
Haemostasis, packing, throat pack removal and smooth emergence.
Suction the pharynx under direct vision; avoid coughing and straining. Patients with nasal packs breathe through the mouth.
Topical vasoconstrictor — hypertension and arrhythmia
Bleeding obscuring the field
Orbital or skull-base injury
Very low blood pressure targets risk organ hypoperfusion; balance field quality with patient safety.
Throat pack removal must be part of the sign-out check.

An AT <11 mL/kg/min predicts increased postoperative cardiopulmonary morbidity and 30/90-day mortality after major non-cardiac surgery; 11–14 mL/kg/min is intermediate risk and >14 mL/kg/min low risk (Older 1993; POM-HR).

The V-slope plot is the primary method for determining the anaerobic threshold (AT). Below the AT, VCO₂ rises in a 1:1 ratio with VO₂. Above AT, the slope steepens as excess CO₂ is produced from bicarbonate buffering of lactic acid.
When should elective non-cardiac surgery be deferred after PCI?

Elective non-cardiac surgery should be delayed at least 1 month after PCI regardless of stent type. Beyond this, whether to continue or interrupt dual antiplatelet therapy is a multidisciplinary (heart team) decision balancing individual thrombotic risk against surgical bleeding risk (ESC Non-Cardiac Surgery 2022).

>PONV: current Fifth Consensus guidance (2025/2026)

The Fifth Consensus is the latest iteration located, published online November 2025 with a 2026 issue date. It recommends two prophylactic interventions in adults at any risk for PONV, rather than waiting for a very high score.

Evidence reviewed October 2026. The latest source available is not necessarily a newly collected dataset: NAP4 and NAP5 remain important historical national audits; NAP7 provides more recent arrest data.

>Consent for anaesthesia 2026 from the Association of Anaesthetists and the GMC’s Decision making and consent, updated in August 2026. The Association’s 2026 revision updates timing, mode, conduct and content of discussions and adds perioperative medicine.

Give an absolute frequency and a percentage, using a consistent denominator and time horizon. Say what the event actually means, how severe or lasting it can be, which population was studied and whether the estimate is historical, contemporary or individualised.

Risk is the combination of the patient, operation, anaesthetic technique and care pathway. Frailty, functional capacity, organ disease, urgency, sepsis, blood loss, duration and available postoperative support matter.
Older adults

General tools such as SORT and NSQIP work across many operations, but specialist scores are built on data from one type of surgery and are usually better calibrated for it. Each score predicts a defined outcome in the population it was built on; check that the patient and the outcome match before quoting it.

Most serious perioperative harm comes from the interaction of the patient’s illnesses with the stress of surgery, not from the anaesthetic drugs themselves. Conditions change the type of risk as well as the size, so state which outcome a figure describes.

An anaesthetised patient cannot report pain from pressure or stretch, and anaesthesia blunts the circulatory reflexes that normally protect against posture changes. Positioning harm is therefore shared by the whole team, and the risks are position-specific.

Regional anaesthesia changes the risk profile rather than removing risk. Discuss neuraxial and peripheral techniques on their own terms: the figures below come from different populations and cannot be merged into one “regional risk” number.

Reduce baseline risk with opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, appropriate regional techniques, propofol-based anaesthesia where suitable, avoiding volatile agents where appropriate, and adequate hydration.

RCoA patient leaflets are communication estimates, often for routine surgery, and are not patient-specific predictions. Their denominators below describe natural frequencies, not necessarily underlying study sample sizes.

“Rare” alone is ambiguous; “99% safe” omits which harm is being counted. Pair positive and negative framing and check understanding.

A healthy person having a short elective procedure and a critically ill person having emergency laparotomy cannot be assigned the same anaesthetic risk. A score complements assessment; it does not decide whether surgery should proceed.

In US Veterans Affairs hospitals, 30-day mortality after major non-cardiac surgery was 8% for patients aged 80 and over versus 3% for younger patients, but under 2% for many common operations such as hernia repair, knee replacement and carotid endarterectomy.

ASA physical status is a useful shared language, but it is subjective and is not a numerical prediction tool.
Most published figures come from single centres or closed-claims registries: they show which harms occur and which factors are associated with them, not a personal probability for a given patient.
NAP3 covers central neuraxial blocks; the RCoA peripheral-block leaflet and the Australian and New Zealand registry cover peripheral nerve blocks; none of them predicts an individual patient.

Use different pharmacological classes for combination prophylaxis, and a different class for rescue when prophylaxis fails. Review drug timing, prior doses, QT risk, sedation and other adverse effects, and look for causes such as hypotension or pain. Prevention lowers but does not eliminate risk.

>A risk-focused bedside checklist
A risk-focused bedside checklist
Before induction:

confirm identity, procedure, consent and treatment limits; allergies and previous events; airway/dental and aspiration assessment; monitoring, equipment and backup plan; needed blood and postoperative support.
During anaesthesia:

maintain reliable anaesthetic delivery, oxygenation, ventilation and circulation; assess neuromuscular function where relevant; protect eyes and pressure areas; track blood loss, temperature and emerging complications.
At emergence:

confirm airway strategy, neuromuscular recovery, analgesia and antiemetic plan; anticipate obstruction, respiratory depression and haemodynamic instability rather than treating extubation as a routine endpoint.
In recovery and handover:
specify actual intraoperative events, ongoing risks, escalation triggers, analgesic/sedative exposures, support and monitoring needs. A low score is not reassurance when the patient is deteriorating.
After harm:

stabilise and escalate, explain known facts and uncertainty honestly, document, arrange investigation and follow-up, and follow the applicable duty-of-candour process. Disclosure should not wait for certainty about blame.

NAP5 reported about 1 in 8,200 with neuromuscular blockade versus 1 in 135,900 without it. These observational subgroups differ in procedure and patient risk as well as paralysis; they are not proof of a simple causal multiplier.

>Anaphylaxis, airway events and arrest are different endpoints

NAP6 reviewed 266 Grade 3–5 reports, including 40 arrests and 10 deaths. The calculated 10/266 ≈3.8% case-fatality among reviewed severe reactions is not a 3.8% chance of death per anaesthetic.

Antibiotics, neuromuscular blockers, chlorhexidine and dyes may trigger reactions, so “allergic to the anaesthetic” can conceal the actual culprit. Clarify previous reactions, document suspect exposures, and ensure specialist investigation rather than assigning an unverified drug allergy.<R label=

NAP6 reviewed 266 Grade 3–5 reports, including 40 arrests and 10 deaths. The calculated 10/266 ≈3.8% case-fatality among reviewed severe reactions is not a 3.8% chance of death per anaesthetic.

Antibiotics, neuromuscular blockers, chlorhexidine and dyes may trigger reactions, so “allergic to the anaesthetic” can conceal the actual culprit. Clarify previous reactions, document suspect exposures, and ensure specialist investigation rather than assigning an unverified drug allergy.

NAP7’s mixed-population arrest rate reflects underlying disease, surgical and anaesthetic factors. Many arrests occur in non-elective and complex surgery; an arrest may be survived. NAP4’s 46-per-million major airway composite includes several outcomes.

Its airway-complication death estimate of 5.6 per million (about 1 in 180,000) is not the combined risk of death or brain injury. Reporting completeness limits both precision and comparison across eras.

>Regional and neuraxial techniques need their own discussion

Neuraxial and peripheral blocks have their own figures — NAP3 estimated permanent harm after central neuraxial block at 2.0–4.2 per 100,000, alternative case classifications rather than confidence limits — and should not borrow general anaesthetic rates.
Decision making and consent

Material risk is patient-centred, not a numerical cutoff
Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board

[2015] UKSC 11 requires reasonable care to make patients aware of material risks and reasonable alternative or variant treatments. A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient’s position would attach significance to it, or the clinician knows or should reasonably know this particular patient would.
A rare vocal injury can be highly material to a singer; persistent hand weakness may dominate a pianist’s decision. There is no universal “below 1% need not be discussed” rule.
Montgomery 2015
McCulloch v Forth Valley Health Board

[2023] UKSC 26 addresses whether an alternative is reasonable using the professional-practice test. It does not replace the patient-centred material-risk disclosure standard. Offer clinically reasonable options; a patient may refuse, but is not entitled to demand an unsafe or inappropriate anaesthetic technique.
McCulloch 2023
GMC refusal
The discussion: options, benefits, harms and values
Establish what matters:
previous distress, pain, nausea, being awake, cognitive recovery, occupation, independence, beliefs, blood products and postoperative ventilation. Ask rather than assume.
Describe reasonable options:

general anaesthesia, neuraxial or peripheral regional techniques, local anaesthesia, sedation or combinations where appropriate. Explain expected sensations, practical limits and possible conversion to general anaesthesia. Regional or sedation techniques are not inherently risk-free.
Individualise harms:

common temporary effects, serious uncommon harms, technique-specific risks and risks unusually important to this patient. Include block failure, nerve injury, headache or urinary retention when relevant; include airway/dental injury and awareness when relevant to general anaesthesia.
Discuss benefits and uncertainty:
analgesia, conditions for surgery and recovery, what prevention can and cannot achieve, likely postoperative care, and uncertainties in personalised estimates.
Include no action:
explain the consequences of declining anaesthesia or surgery with the treating team, without coercion. Risk of not treating may be high, but does not extinguish choice.
Support understanding:

qualified interpreter where needed, accessible information, time for questions and teach-back. Supply information before the day of elective surgery where practicable; confirm the agreed plan when circumstances change.
GMC patient priorities
Capacity, voluntariness and refusal

Presume adult capacity. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific; disability, communication difficulty, an unwise choice or disagreement is not proof of incapacity. Support decision-making and address reversible problems.

In England and Wales, the Mental Capacity Act framework asks whether an impairment or disturbance of mind/brain makes the person unable to understand, retain, use or weigh relevant information, or communicate the decision.
Apply the correct law for the jurisdiction: Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland do not have identical statutory arrangements.
GMC capacity
Mental Capacity Act

A capable adult can refuse a proposed technique or life-saving treatment. Explore reasons, understanding and alternatives without coercion, and document the limits and implications. Sedation, severe pain or shock may affect capacity but do not automatically remove it.
Avoid seeking a first meaningful elective consent discussion after premedication or during induction.

When capacity is lacking, identify valid applicable advance decisions and legally authorised decision-makers, and use the appropriate best-interests/overall-benefit framework. In England and Wales, “next of kin” has no automatic power to consent for an adult.

An odds ratio is not a risk ratio, and either needs a baseline risk before translating into a patient-facing absolute estimate. Confidence intervals and calibration uncertainty should temper precision.

A change in ascertainment is not automatically a change in underlying safety.

“Any sore throat” is not the same as persistent voice injury; temporary tingling is not permanent motor deficit; perioperative arrest is not death caused by anaesthesia.
A denominator of all anaesthetics differs from general anaesthetics with muscle relaxation, central neuraxial blocks or elderly patients after major inpatient surgery.
Older trials without prophylaxis describe baseline risk, not risk after current prevention. Audit year, case-mix, reporting completeness and confidence intervals matter.
Do not add complication percentages: outcomes overlap, are not independent, and may use different denominators. Do not subtract unrelated cohorts to claim benefit from a technique.
>The arithmetic above is educational, not a validated anaesthetic-risk calculator. Accurate arithmetic does not validate an input probability or make a treatment recommendation.
The arithmetic above is educational, not a validated anaesthetic-risk calculator. Accurate arithmetic does not validate an input probability or make a treatment recommendation.
Learning check: can a one-in-100,000 figure be irrelevant simply because it is very small?
No. Severity, alternatives and the patient’s own circumstances may make a rare harm material. Explain uncertainty without burying a risk the patient would reasonably find important.

>Postoperative mortality is not anaesthesia-attributable mortality. SORT, NELA and NSQIP estimate outcomes after surgery, reflecting illness, surgery and the whole perioperative course. They cannot tell you the probability of death caused solely by an anaesthetic.
Discuss survival, complications, function, loss of independence, prolonged recovery and the consequences of not operating as separate outcomes.<R label=
Postoperative mortality is not anaesthesia-attributable mortality.
SORT, NELA and NSQIP estimate outcomes after surgery, reflecting illness, surgery and the whole perioperative course. They cannot tell you the probability of death caused solely by an anaesthetic.
Discuss survival, complications, function, loss of independence, prolonged recovery and the consequences of not operating as separate outcomes.
NELA calculator
Tool selection and limitations
Inputs and intended outcome
Interpretation and limits
I–VI classification of preoperative systemic disease; E denotes emergency.
Not a calibrated probability. ASA III is not a fixed percentage risk; grading has inter-rater variation and does not describe operation severity.
Age, ASA, urgency, severity, high-risk specialty and cancer; 30-day postoperative mortality in adult inpatient surgery.
Original cohort excluded cardiac, neurosurgical, obstetric and transplant procedures. Check applicability rather than extrapolating to children or every specialty.
SORT v2
SORT clinical judgement 2020
Combines SORT with clinician-estimated risk; 2020 study of 22,631 patients at 274 hospitals.
Clinical judgement adds information, not certainty. In that validation study all evaluated approaches overpredicted risk. Identify version and local calibration.
Emergency abdominal surgery; 30-day death risk. Current parsimonious model uses audit data from December 2016–November 2019.
Not an elective-surgery score. Use alongside judgement, frailty and plans for senior care and postoperative support; never in isolation.
ACS NSQIP
Procedure/CPT code and patient factors; individual postoperative complications and death within 30 days, plus length of stay.
US surgical population. Verify operation coding and transportability to local practice; outcomes such as pneumonia and death are not interchangeable.
RCRI 1999
High-risk surgery, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin treatment, creatinine >2 mg/dL (about 177 µmol/L).
Major cardiac complications, not all-cause mortality. Original stable/nonurgent noncardiac cohort differs from modern troponin-defined injury cohorts; do not mix their percentage tables.
ARISCAT 2010
Age, oxygen saturation, recent respiratory infection, anaemia, surgical site, duration and emergency status; postoperative pulmonary complications.
A composite respiratory outcome, not simply pneumonia and not mortality. Performance depends on population and actual procedural details.
Female sex, nonsmoking, prior PONV/motion sickness, postoperative opioids; 24-hour PONV.
Original 0–4 factor risks: 10%, 21%, 39%, 61%, 79%, under inhalational anaesthesia without prophylaxis. These are not residual risks after modern prevention.
STOP-Bang
Snoring, tiredness, observed apnoea, pressure, BMI, age, neck circumference, sex; OSA screening.
Screening is not diagnosis or a direct probability of postoperative respiratory arrest. Positive findings inform airway, opioid and monitoring assessment.
Frailty and CPET
CPET limitations
Clinical Frailty Scale and comprehensive assessment; exercise physiology including oxygen uptake, anaerobic threshold and ventilatory efficiency.
Baseline function, reserve and independence matter. No universal CFS or CPET cutoff converts to a fixed anaesthetic death probability; interpret for the proposed operation and patient.
A practical preoperative sequence

>
  • Clarify the indication, urgency, alternatives and likely natural history without surgery with the surgical team.
  • Establish baseline function, frailty, cardiopulmonary reserve, renal disease, previous anaesthetic problems, allergies, airway, dentition, PONV and patient priorities.
  • Select an applicable tool and document its version, endpoint, time horizon and assumptions.
The lesson for consent is that age raises risk mostly by reducing the ability to survive a complication. Frailty, function and the type of operation matter more than the number of years.

common after major and emergency surgery in older people, and linked to longer stay and later cognitive decline. ESAIC 2024 recommends screening risk, avoiding unnecessary deep anaesthesia and drugs such as benzodiazepines, and using non-drug prevention.
Brain health:

ASA 2025 guidance covers perioperative care of older adults having inpatient surgery. It does not show that any particular anaesthetic technique prevents dementia, so avoid promising that one choice protects long-term brain health.
Loss of function:
for many older patients, being able to live at home matters more than survival figures. Ask about it and discuss it.
APRICOT studied 31,127 anaesthetics in children across 261 European hospitals.

Severe critical events occurred in 5.2% (95% CI 5.0–5.5), mostly respiratory (3.1%, such as laryngospasm and bronchospasm), with cardiovascular instability in 1.9%; 30-day in-hospital mortality was 10 per 10,000 and did not depend on the type of anaesthesia.
Younger age and poorer health were the main risk factors, and greater experience of the most senior anaesthetist was protective.
APRICOT 2017
For parents, explain that breathing problems during the anaesthetic are the most common serious event and that a recent cold increases them.
NELA risk calculator
30-day mortality, built from the UK National Emergency Laparotomy Audit. NELA states it must not be used alone, and its derivation data run from December 2016 to November 2019.
Cardiac surgery
EuroSCORE II

In-hospital mortality, built from 22,381 patients in 154 hospitals in 43 countries. In the test group, actual mortality was 4.18% and predicted 3.95%, with an area under the curve of 0.81; the original EuroSCORE over-predicted mortality.
EuroSCORE II 2012
Hip fracture
Nottingham Hip Fracture Score

30-day mortality from age, male sex, two or more other illnesses, abbreviated mental test ≤6/10, haemoglobin ≤10 g/dL, living in a care home and cancer. Area under the curve 0.72 — reasonable, not precise.
Nottingham Hip Fracture Score 2008
Major non-cardiac surgery
RCRI and ESC surgical risk categories
Major cardiac complications; combines patient factors with the risk category of the operation.
ESC non-cardiac surgery 2022
Operations with lung risk
Lung complications after surgery; upper-abdominal and chest operations score highest.

A score supports, not replaces, clinical judgement: in an international study of 22,631 patients, a model combining SORT with doctors’ estimates was developed, and all methods tested overpredicted risk.
Exercise testing can add information for major surgery but has its own limitations.
Learning check: can you use the NELA calculator to counsel a patient before elective bowel surgery?
No. It was built from emergency laparotomies and predicts emergency 30-day mortality; use a tool developed or validated for elective surgery instead.

the 2022 ESC guideline combines patient factors with the risk category of the operation (low <1%, intermediate 1–5%, high >5% 30-day cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction) and supports the RCRI as a simple bedside index.
Ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes and creatinine above 177 µmol/L are the RCRI patient factors; the sixth factor is high-risk surgery.
Respiratory disease:

lung complications depend on both patient and operation. ARISCAT combines age, oxygen saturation, recent chest infection, anaemia, upper-abdominal or chest incision, long surgery and emergency surgery.
Obstructive sleep apnoea:

often undiagnosed, and linked to difficult airways and breathing problems after surgery, particularly with opioids. In the STOP development study, 27.5% of 2,467 surgical patients screened as high risk; STOP-Bang adds BMI, age, neck size and sex to improve sensitivity. It is a screening tool, not a diagnosis.

CPOC guidance asks for HbA1c in the referral pathway and optimisation before elective surgery, because poor control is associated with infection, longer stay and other complications. An HbA1c threshold is a trigger for review, not a fixed risk number.
CPOC diabetes 2023
Frailty and cognitive impairment:
frailty predicts complications, longer stay and loss of independence better than age alone. Cognitive impairment raises delirium risk and affects consent.
Other conditions
— anaemia, kidney disease, liver disease, neuromuscular disease and previous airway difficulty — enter the scoring tools below or need specific planning rather than a separate generic number.
Ulnar neuropathy is the classic upper-limb injury and can occur despite correct padding; brachial plexus injury follows abduction, head rotation and shoulder braces.
ASA neuropathy advisory 2018
Skin and soft-tissue pressure injury rises with long procedures, low perfusion and immobility.
Prone position
Postoperative visual loss:
rare but devastating, most often ischaemic optic neuropathy after long spinal fusion.

In the ASA Postoperative Visual Loss Study Group case-control study (80 cases, 315 controls), independent risk factors were male sex (OR 2.53), obesity (OR 2.83), Wilson frame use (OR 4.30), anaesthesia duration (OR 1.39 per hour) and estimated blood loss (OR 1.34 per litre), while a higher colloid share of non-blood fluid was protective (OR 0.67 per 5%).

These odds ratios describe associations, not a personal risk. Direct globe pressure causes a different injury — central retinal artery occlusion — so the eyes must be free of pressure and checked regularly. For high-risk patients, discussing visual loss during consent and considering staged procedures are reasonable.
POVL study group 2012
Airway and lines:

the tube, lines and monitoring can be dislodged during turning or hidden under drapes; access is poor if the airway is lost. Plan the turn, secure the tube, and have a plan for supine return and resuscitation, including a prone CPR approach.
Edgcombe prone 2008
Circulation and ventilation:

abdominal compression raises intra-abdominal pressure, reducing venous return and increasing epidural venous bleeding; supports should leave the abdomen free. Oxygenation is usually preserved, but compression of chest or abdomen raises airway pressures.
Kwee prone 2015
Pressure points:
face, chin, breasts, genitalia, iliac crests and knees; facial oedema, tongue swelling and cervical injury from excessive neck rotation or extension.

In a prospective Mayo series of 991 adults under general anaesthesia in lithotomy, 15 (1.5%; 95% CI 0.8–2.5%) developed lower-limb neuropathy — obturator, lateral femoral cutaneous, sciatic and common peroneal nerves.
All were sensory, began within four hours, and 14 of 15 resolved within six months; time in lithotomy beyond 2 hours was a major risk factor.
Warner lithotomy 2000

Prolonged lithotomy, especially with head-down tilt and calf support, is also linked to well-leg compartment syndrome — the same complication discussed for long pelvic surgery in the Operations Library. Limit duration, use symmetrical, gradual leg movement, and lower the legs periodically in long cases.
Gill 2019 well-leg
Sitting and beach-chair positions

Upright positioning under anaesthesia lowers the blood pressure at the head relative to the arm cuff by roughly the hydrostatic column between them; uncorrected, a “normal” arm pressure can hide cerebral hypoperfusion, and catastrophic cerebral ischaemia has been reported in healthy patients after shoulder surgery with deliberate hypotension.
Reference blood pressure to the external auditory meatus or correct for the height difference.
Pohl beach chair 2005
The sitting craniotomy adds venous air embolism, because surgical veins sit above the heart, and paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale.
Lateral and steep head-down positions

dependent brachial plexus and axillary vessel compression (hence the chest roll below the axilla), dependent ear and eye pressure, peroneal nerve compression at the fibular head, and ventilation–perfusion mismatch between lungs.
Steep Trendelenburg (for example robotic prostatectomy):

raised intracranial and intraocular pressure, facial and airway oedema that can cause post-extubation stridor, endobronchial tube migration, and sliding with brachial plexus stretch from shoulder braces. Check cuff leak or airway swelling before extubation in long cases.
Consent and documentation

Positioning risks are often material: a spinal fusion patient may want to know about visual loss, and a musician about ulnar nerve symptoms. Discuss position-specific risks when they are relevant to that patient, document the position, padding and checks performed, and record any new deficit promptly.
not confidence limits

. Risk was not uniform: obstetric neuraxial blocks carried substantially lower risk than perioperative and chronic-pain settings, so do not quote the pooled figure unchanged to a labouring patient or an elderly patient having emergency hip surgery.
NAP3 neuraxial
Post-dural-puncture headache:

the RCoA patient leaflet gives a combined risk of 1 in 100 to 1 in 500 procedures after an epidural or spinal. Accidental dural puncture with a large epidural needle and headache after a fine spinal needle are different events; young patients and obstetric patients are more susceptible.
Describe the postural, severe nature of the headache and that treatment, including epidural blood patch, exists.
RCoA PDPH
Common, usually temporary effects:

hypotension from sympathetic block, urinary retention, itch from neuraxial opioids, shivering and incomplete or failed block with possible conversion to general anaesthesia. These are far more likely than permanent injury and belong in every consent discussion.
High or total spinal:

excessive cephalad spread can cause respiratory compromise and cardiovascular collapse; it is a recognised emergency of neuraxial and some peripheral techniques, not a reason to quote a fatality figure we do not have.
Vertebral canal haematoma and abscess:

rare but time-critical. New severe back pain, progressive leg weakness or bladder/bowel dysfunction after neuraxial block is a red flag needing urgent assessment and imaging, because delayed decompression worsens outcome.
Antithrombotic drugs, spinal pathology and sepsis modify risk; follow drug-specific timing guidance rather than memory.
ASRA anticoagulation 2018
Peripheral nerve blocks: nerve injury and local anaesthetic systemic toxicity

The RCoA 2024 leaflet reports that fewer than 10 in 100 patients notice temporary nerve symptoms after a peripheral block, about 1 in 100 still has symptoms a year later, and 2–5 in 10,000 have permanent nerve damage. Most temporary injuries recover within weeks to about three months.

These are communication estimates across block types; a specific block in a specific patient may differ, and surgery, positioning and tourniquets also injure nerves — not every post-block deficit is needle- or drug-caused.
RCoA PNB nerve damage

Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) is uncommon but life-threatening. In the Australian and New Zealand registry (25,336 peripheral blocks, 2007–2012), LAST occurred in 0.87 per 1,000 blocks (95% CI 0.54–1.3), and ultrasound guidance was associated with a lower incidence.
Presentation can be delayed and may begin with neurological symptoms — perioral tingling, metallic taste, agitation, seizure — before cardiovascular collapse.

Management follows the ASRA 2020 checklist: call for help, give 20% lipid emulsion early, treat seizures with a benzodiazepine, use smaller-than-normal adrenaline doses (start <1 microgram/kg), avoid vasopressin, calcium-channel blockers and beta-blockers, and observe after stabilisation.
LAST resuscitation differs from standard ALS.
LAST registry 2013
ASRA LAST checklist 2020
Wrong-site block:

a never event. The Stop Before You Block campaign requires a site check immediately before needle insertion with the team; voluntary registries do not reliably capture it, so no trustworthy incidence figure is quoted here.
RA-UK Stop Before You Block
Block-specific harms:

pneumothorax with blocks near the pleura, phrenic nerve involvement and dyspnoea with interscalene approaches, Horner syndrome, vascular puncture and haematoma. Name the harms of the actual block planned rather than reciting a generic list.
Block failure:
partial or failed blocks are common enough that every plan needs an agreed fallback — supplementation, repeat block or conversion to general anaesthesia — discussed in advance.
Consent for regional techniques

Apply the same material-risk standard as for general anaesthesia: explain benefits, common temporary effects, serious rare harms, the possibility of failure and conversion, and reasonable alternatives including no regional technique.

Patient education, optimisation of comorbidities (anaemia, smoking, nutrition), avoidance of prolonged fasting with carbohydrate loading up to 2 hours before induction, and avoidance of routine mechanical bowel preparation in colorectal surgery.
Why is goal-directed fluid therapy preferred over fixed-volume regimens in ERAS?

Stroke-volume optimisation with small balanced crystalloid boluses titrated to dynamic indices reduces postoperative complications and length of stay compared with both liberal and overly restrictive fixed regimens (POM-O, OPTIMISE).
How does opioid-sparing analgesia fit into ERAS?

A multimodal regimen — paracetamol, NSAIDs (where safe), regional or neuraxial blocks, dexamethasone and adjuncts such as lidocaine or ketamine — reduces opioid requirements, postoperative ileus and PONV, supporting earlier mobilisation and oral intake.

mild, treated hypothyroidism rarely delays surgery. Severe untreated disease brings reduced cardiac output, blunted response to hypoxia and hypercapnia, hypothermia, hyponatraemia and slow drug clearance, so sedatives and opioids last longer.

TSH drives follicular cells to trap iodide, which thyroid peroxidase oxidises and attaches to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin (organification), forming MIT and DIT. Coupling gives T4 (DIT + DIT) and T3 (MIT + DIT).
Low T3 with normal or low TSH is common in critical illness and is not treated with thyroid hormone (teaching synthesis).

The goitre and the airway

venous congestion and laryngeal oedema, not just direct compression, cause the obstruction, so the airway may stay swollen after evacuation. Give oxygen, call for senior surgical and anaesthetic help, and prepare for a difficult intubation and front-of-neck access.

The gland secretes mostly T4; most circulating T3, the more active hormone, is made in peripheral tissues by deiodinase enzymes. Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase, which is why they stop new hormone synthesis but not release of stored hormone.

CPOC (2023) and NATA (2017) recommend identifying anaemia at the point of listing for major elective surgery, allowing at least 6 weeks for investigation and treatment.
A full blood count, ferritin, transferrin saturation, B12, folate and renal function form the minimum panel; CRP is needed to interpret ferritin in inflammation (functional iron deficiency).
What is the safe platelet count for spinal or epidural anaesthesia?

AAGBI (2013) and BSH (2017) support neuraxial blockade with a platelet count ≥80 ×10⁹/L provided the count is stable and the cause of thrombocytopenia is benign. Counts of 50–80 ×10⁹/L require an explicit risk–benefit assessment; below 50 ×10⁹/L neuraxial techniques are generally avoided.
Never transfuse platelets in HIT, TTP or ITP without specialist advice.
How do you manage a patient presenting for emergency surgery with severe thrombocytopenia of unknown cause?

Discuss with haematology before transfusing. Avoid platelets in TTP/HIT (may worsen thrombosis). For life-threatening bleeding, give platelets to a target of >50 ×10⁹/L (>100 for CNS/eye), correct fibrinogen (>1.5 g/L), and consider TXA 1 g.
Use general rather than neuraxial anaesthesia and minimise invasive lines where possible.
What antibiotic should be given for suspected neutropenic sepsis?

Per NICE neutropenic-sepsis guidance, empirical piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV (or meropenem if previous resistance / β-lactam allergy with cross-reactivity assessment) within 1 hour of recognition, after blood cultures. Add vancomycin or teicoplanin only for suspected line infection, MRSA risk or severe mucositis.
What HbS target is needed before major surgery in sickle cell disease?
A simple top-up transfusion to Hb ~100 g/L is usually sufficient for most surgery and is as effective as exchange transfusion at preventing perioperative complications.

This section concerns a patient with an established kidney transplant undergoing another operation. Immediate care after the transplant operation itself is a separate specialist pathway: do not import a urine-for-urine replacement regimen or a transplant-centre pressure target into every non-transplant operation.

Document a plan for periods when oral dosing is impossible, rather than allowing “nil by mouth” to omit essential medicines.

Protect any functioning dialysis fistula in its actual access limb; do not assume its side matches the graft. Establish the graft’s location when pelvic positioning, retraction or surgery could affect it.

Asplenic/hyposplenic patients are at lifelong risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) with encapsulated organisms and require vaccination and lifelong penicillin V 250–500 mg twice daily.

Why bond polarity is not the same as molecular polarity

A molecule can contain polar bonds but have no overall dipole if they cancel by symmetry.
Carbon dioxide has two polar C=O bonds pointing in opposite directions, so the molecule is non-polar overall — yet it is very water-soluble because it reacts with water to form carbonic acid.
Volatile agents have asymmetric C–F, C–Cl and C–O bonds, so they carry a net dipole, which contributes to their solubility in blood and tissue.

most drugs bind reversibly through a combination of ionic, hydrogen-bond and van der Waals interactions. Each is individually weak, so binding depends on several fitting together — which is the basis of selectivity.

in a closed sample (no gas exchange), cooling increases CO₂ and O₂ solubility, so their partial pressures fall, and the dissociation of buffer groups — chiefly histidine imidazole on proteins — shifts so pH rises.

water self-ionises (H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻) with ion product Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]. Because the reaction is endothermic, Kw rises with temperature. Neutrality is defined as [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so neutral pH = ½ pKw. At 25 °C Kw ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, giving neutral pH 7.0.

In methaemoglobin the haem iron is oxidised from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ and cannot bind oxygen, while remaining haems bind O₂ more tightly (left-shifted curve) — so tissue delivery falls. Levels >15% cause cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen; >50% cause coma; >70% are fatal.

How does a fuel cell oxygen analyser work?

A galvanic (fuel) cell consumes O₂ at a lead anode (Pb + 2OH⁻ → PbO + H₂O + 2e⁻), generating a current proportional to O₂ partial pressure at the gold cathode (O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻). It is self-powered, accurate to ±3%, and lasts typically 1–2 years because the anode is consumed.
Redox Reactions
Which inhaled anaesthetics are degraded by CO₂ absorbents?

Sevoflurane reacts with strong bases (KOH, NaOH) in soda-lime to form Compound A, a vinyl ether with renal toxicity in rats. Desflurane, enflurane and isoflurane (in descending order of risk; sevoflurane produces little) react with desiccated CO₂ absorbent to generate carbon monoxide.
Free Radicals
Both risks are mitigated by using KOH/NaOH-free absorbents (e.g. Amsorb Plus) and avoiding desiccated absorbent.
